`discover`, `status`, `screenshot`, `logs`, and Android's `describe-ui` are
reads and run under every posture, Plan included, as is `open` of a destination
already booted or booting: it only
shows the pane, changes nothing on the device, and has no host action an
approval could bind to. Every other operation is an effect, including `open` of
a shut-down destination, which boots it. Plan refuses it; Full access
sends it with no approval; under approval-gated and auto-accept-edits the
server asks in the thread (an `approval-requested` turn event, answered like a
Browser session ask) before the pane opens or the host is called, and an
approval mints the host's one-use, five-minute approval bound to exactly that
request and its checkout context — the same receipt a workbench confirmation
yields, validated by the same Apple or Android policy. A denial, expiry, or
thread that went stale or into Plan while waiting refuses the call. Input to a
destination the turn's window already holds open under Allow input rides that
grant without asking; an approved agent input opens or renews it as a pane
input does. `octant_terminal` follows the thread's level: Plan refuses it,
Full access runs it, and below Full access each command the agent types into
it (`run` or `write`) asks the person in the thread with the command shown
first; an approval for a command that starts the terminal also mints the
host's one-use approval for that start. Reading and stopping it ask nothing.
A host that cannot ask refuses it below Full access.

## Modes: Chat, Work, and Code

Modes are server-enforced domain policy, not renderer flags. Chat and Work can
be disabled in settings; Code is always available; disabling a mode never
deletes its data.

The shell shows two modes, **Work** and **Code**. Work presents the Chat and
Work domains together: one sidebar lists both kinds of thread and Project, and
a new-thread composer chooses **Chat** (creates a Chat thread, no folder) or
**In a folder** (creates a Work thread bound to a Project root). The choice is
only which create command the composer sends; the active server mode still
follows the thread or draft on screen, each row opens in its own mode and
reaches its own kind's commands, and nothing in the renderer can turn a Chat
into Work or a Work thread into Chat. Settings' Chat and Work switches still
gate their domains: with one off, the composer offers only the other kind.

| Mode     | Binds to                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | Authority                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Chat** | A virtual, memory-scoped Project, or no Project at all                                                                                                                                                                     | No filesystem or shell authority. Optional safe research tools; scratch space is isolated per thread.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Work** | One OS-confined main folder, plus any [extra folders](#projects-with-several-folders) the person adds                                                                                                                      | The shared capability set at the thread's [guardrail level](#security-and-authority): file reads and writes, shell, Git, local command-line tools, SSH to the person's own machines, provider-native tools, and subagents, as in Code. Focus: documents and artifacts with document adapters (docx, pptx, pdf, image), research with citations, local tasks, and the server-authoritative board; Done by a person. Developer surfaces stay hidden until the person turns them on for the Project (below).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Code** | One main directory, ideally a repository root, plus any [extra folders](#projects-with-several-folders) the person adds; Code threads select a checkout (current checkout or a managed worktree) inside the main directory | The same shared capability set at the thread's guardrail level, which starts in the mode the person picked at first run (Auto pre-selected; Ask first where the provider has no Auto) or later set for the Project or in Settings › Code › Access; any thread switches mode from its composer. Plan mode is always read-only. Focus: Git, terminals, tests, pull requests, review, and managed subagents inside the bound root, with checkouts, managed worktrees, and the objective delivery target. Creating a Code Project may explicitly initialize Git in that folder so a Code thread can prepare a checkout immediately; if that initialization fails, creation is refused and no Project is journaled. Binding without Git remains allowed. |

A No-project Chat thread can be filed into a Chat Project from its thread menu
(**Move to Project…**), picking one or creating it there. The move is the
server's `move-chat-thread` command: it keeps the thread's kind, history, and
settings, accepts only an active Chat Project, and adds no filesystem, shell, or
network authority; the Project's memory applies from the thread's next message.
A Chat already in a Project offers no move. A tool-extension selection resolved
while the thread had no Project no longer matches its new scope and is refused
until it is selected again.

A Work or Code thread can be filed into another Project of its own mode from its
row menu (**Move to Project…**). The server's `move-work-thread` and
`move-code-thread` commands keep the thread's kind, history, and guardrail
level, and add no filesystem reach: the pure `decideThreadMove` policy admits
only an active Project of the same mode whose bound folder is the thread's
folder or contains it, and refuses an archived thread, a running turn, a thread
waiting on the person, the thread's own Project, and any other folder, each with
a plain reason. A person makes the move; a routine acting as the host is
refused. A Work thread takes the destination's binding revision and its working
directory is rewritten to name the same place under the new root, so a
containing folder changes the confinement root but not where the thread works.
A Code thread also needs its checkout to stay valid: the destination's checkout
must be the same repository at the same folder, so a Project that merely
contains the thread's folder is refused. A checkout of the Project's folder is
re-derived under the destination and journaled before the thread; a managed
worktree keeps its own identity. A session grant of Full access is discarded on
the move. The destination's provider policy still applies to the thread's
provider and model. Each move is one journaled thread update by the local
person with its time, and replays like any other thread update.

Stop asks the runtime to end a turn. When the runtime does not end it, a
provider whose sessions each own a process (reported as the `forceStop`
capability, Claude today) lets the person **Force stop** the turn ten seconds
after pressing Stop in Chat, Work or Code. The server commands kill
that attempt's own runtime process tree and nothing else, journals the attempt
`cancelled`, and leaves the thread usable and its session resumable. A runtime
that serves several threads from one process (Codex, OpenCode) reports
`forceStop` unsupported: the command is refused, the UI never offers it, and
Stop settles the attempt at once as before. For a provider that supports it, a
Stop keeps the attempt running until the runtime really ends it, so a Stop that
did not take stays visible. Work returns `stop-requested` while its exact
request-owned supported runtime is still ending. Its force command requires the
same request/thread/turn and an already-aborted owned controller. Code's force
command additionally names the original turn operation, rejects replacement
operations and requires that Stop already reached that controller. Neither path
accepts a PID or kills a shared runtime; the provider owns process verification.
The normal turn lifecycle records completion/cancellation, preserving queued
messages and history. A kill failure leaves an explicit recovery error.

**One authority model, two focuses** (maintainer decision, 2026-10-31: "Work
and Code should essentially be able to do the same, but Work is more for
non-technical users that do not need issue-tracker/Git tools etc. But for
technical users it's a way to differentiate working with documents /
artifacts, local tasks etc. vs coding."). Work and Code differ in what they
show and which tools a thread starts with, never in what a thread may do:

- **Authority is the level, in both modes.** The
  [guardrail level](#security-and-authority) in force (Guarded, Reviewed,
  or Full access) decides who approves a shell command, a write, a
  Git operation, an SSH connection, a native tool, a subagent, or a routine,
  and what confines it, identically in Work and Code. Nothing about Work
  lowers a ceiling: Work threads reach Full access as Code threads do, their writes follow the level rather than always asking, and
  the [Git and pull requests](#security-and-authority) column of the level
  table applies to both. The OS confinement for a Work launch is the one a
  Code launch gets at the same level (the confinement matrix in
  [Security and authority](#security-and-authority)), and a Work turn records
  `shell` and `git` at the level it ran with.
- **Focus is presentation and starting tool set.** Work shows documents,
  artifacts, local tasks, and its board. It hides developer surfaces (Git
  panels, pull request and review surfaces, issue-tracker integrations, and
  the worktree and checkout pickers) until the person turns on **Developer
  tools** for that Work Project; Code shows them. The switch is a person's,
  journaled with who and when; an agent, a routine, or an import never sets
  it, and it changes what a Work Project shows, not what its threads may do.
  A Work thread can run `git` through its shell with the switch off; the
  switch decides whether Octant's Git and pull request surfaces appear for
  it. Work keeps Done by a person; Code keeps the objective delivery target.
  A Work Project with Developer tools on still marks Done by a person, so
  work that needs an objective delivery target moves to Code.
- **Defaults may differ, authority may not.** Work may start with defaults
  suited to people who are not developers, such as approval prompts that
  describe a command in plain language before showing it, or a provider's
  developer-only native tools listed under the Project's Developer tools
  rather than in the composer. Every such default is presentation: a person
  reaches the same capability in Work with the same or fewer steps.

Each provider driver starts a session acquired in Work mode exactly as it
starts a Code session at the same level, and a Work turn journals `shell` and
`git` as the level it ran at (`guarded`, `provider-review` for Reviewed, or `full-access`;
`denied` on a turn accepted before the shared rule was built), with
`confinement` `unconfined` at Full access. Built per runtime:

- **Claude Code:** the Work session starts with its shell tool, at the
  thread's level as in Code (Guarded asks per command, Reviewed uses its
  automatic mode, Full access runs unattended).
- **Codex:** Work threads start and resume with the shell features on and the
  approval policy and sandbox the level maps to in Code; `command` and
  `permissions` requests inside the root reach the person at Guarded. A Work
  thread still starts with a project-doc budget of zero, so it does not read
  the folder's agent brief.
- **OpenCode:** the session rules no longer deny `bash` and `task` in Work;
  the posture's rules apply as in Code.
- **Pi:** the Work session starts with its shell tool.
- **ACP agents, Mistral Vibe included:** an `execute` request reaches the
  person at Guarded as in Code, and a Work launch gets the exec and fork a
  Code launch at that level gets.
- **Octant Harness:** a Work harness thread has the shell port a Code harness
  thread has, on the network its level resolves, under the same harness
  authority.
- **Host:** a Work thread takes Auto, Ask first, Accept edits, or Full access
  from Settings › Work when it is created and switches from its composer
  (`change-work-thread-access`, journaled on the thread); raising a thread or
  the Settings default to Full access is chosen at a local window, as in
  Code. A caller with narrower authority than the thread (a goal-loop round,
  a routine, a delegated turn) runs the turn at the thread's level clamped to
  its own (`clampWorkAccess`).

- **Developer tools:** a Work Project's switch
  (`change-work-project-developer-tools`, journaled as
  `project.work-developer-tools-changed@1` with who and when on the Project)
  is set only from a window on this host; a paired device is refused. It
  shows the Project terminal and Project actions, the developer surfaces Work
  has today; no thread's authority reads it.

An ACP agent whose shell runs in-process with no protocol request reports
`unsupported` at Guarded and Reviewed and runs only at Full access, in Work as
in Code (built: the profile's `shellWithoutRequest`; no shipped profile sets
it). Octant Shield answers a Work thread's approvals at Auto on
every runtime that routes them to Octant, as it answers a Code thread's:
the Octant Harness, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, ACP agents, and Pi, judged
against the Project folder and counted against the Work thread's spend; see
[Octant Shield](#octant-shield).

A driver that cannot run a Work session at the level in force reports so and
keeps the narrower behavior; it never runs commands under a weaker guard
than the level names.

SSH to the person's own machines goes through the thread's shell, in Work
and Code alike: a thread runs `ssh`, `scp`, or `rsync` as ordinary commands.
Octant carries no SSH protocol of its own; the commands use the person's own
SSH agent, or for a server the person chose it for a key Octant made and
keeps in the credential broker, and, at Full access, their own configuration. Below Full access a harness command reaches a registered
server through relays and an agent socket the host opens for that one command,
and a provider runtime's own commands through a folder and an agent socket
the host opens for its launch
([Octant Shield](#octant-shield), servers as built). No mode bans them: in
Work as in Code they are commands at the thread's level. At Guarded, the
first connection to each host in a thread asks the person, naming the host,
even where a remembered approval would cover the command otherwise. Network egress for shell commands follows the level: at Guarded
and Reviewed it follows the Project's egress rules, so a host those
rules do not allow is refused; at Full access the network is open.

Chat's missing filesystem and shell authority is withheld, and by rule, not
only in today's build: a Chat session is acquired on its per-thread scratch
directory, and nothing a provider asks for in Chat is anyone's to approve, so
every approval request is declined at the agent. A provider sandbox that only
blocks writes is not enough, because reads never escalate. Pi starts with no
built-in tools. OpenCode and ACP agents launch confined with process exec and
fork denied and the scratch directory read-only. Claude's gate keeps its reads
inside the scratch directory, and its shell and edits ask and are declined.
Codex threads get no execution environment (`environments: []` on the thread
and on every turn), which removes its shell, `apply_patch`, and `view_image`;
they also start and resume with the shell, image, plugin, and app features
off, so a CLI that ignores `environments` still has no shell, and the user's
own Codex plugins do not load. MCP servers from the user's Codex config run
outside any environment (a `node_repl` server read another repository with
none), and no setting turns them all off, so the driver reads the effective
config and switches each named server off for the thread; a Chat thread whose
servers cannot be listed does not start. Those are the person's own tool
servers, so a person may turn them on for Chat with the account's **Run
Codex as itself** switch (built), or for one thread with its own-setup choice
(built; see the per-thread switch below).
Such a Chat thread keeps no environment, shell, or image reads, and its
servers, plugins, and apps stay as the person's Codex config has them. A server turned on runs with its own reach,
which Chat's no-filesystem rule does not cover, and the switch says so. Octant-managed tools (research,
Canvas) are unaffected; they run on the host, not in the provider's
environment.

Provider-owned memory stays off in every mode. A provider's global memory
follows its own rules into every Project, outside Octant's controls: Codex runs
with `features.memories` off, which also keeps its memory folder out of its
sandbox's readable roots, and Claude runs with no setting sources. Octant keeps
two memories of its own instead: Project memory, scoped to one Project, and
person memory below.

### Person memory

Decided 2026-11-01: Octant should know what other work the person has done
outside the current Project, the way a person expects of a chat assistant, and
the person can turn it off. Memory is automatic and on by default; no entry
asks for confirmation, because confirming each one was rejected as too much
friction. Project memory is unchanged and stays Project-scoped; person memory
is a layer beside it that belongs to the person on this host. It is built,
except where a bullet says otherwise.

- **What is kept.** Short entries about the person and their work, each one
  kind of `preference`, `working-style`, or `past-work`, at most 400
  characters, and for each remembered thread one digest: its title, mode,
  Project, provider, end time, and a summary of at most 600 characters. Every
  entry keeps the threads it came from as its sources (an entry learned again
  from a later thread gains that thread as a second source rather than a
  duplicate). The person can read, edit, and delete each entry and see its
  sources in Settings › Memory, and Forget everything erases all entries and
  digests at once.
- **When it is written.** After a thread ends: a Chat, Work, or Code thread
  the person completed (put away) after memory was turned on. A sweep of the
  three modes' completed threads runs five minutes after start and then
  hourly, and distills
  each such thread at most once, so a thread that was reopened and completed
  again is not distilled twice. Threads completed before memory existed are
  never back-filled, so turning it on never starts a burst of model calls.
  Forgetting everything, switching memory back on, letting a Project back
  in, or allowing a thread again moves that start to the moment of the
  change, so nothing that ended while memory was off, kept out, or just
  forgotten is learned afterwards. A
  thread with nothing the person wrote is recorded as remembered without a
  call.
- **What the distiller reads.** Only what the person wrote in the thread and
  its title: never the agent's answers, tool output, attachments, or files.
  Rationale: an agent's answer can carry outside content (a web page, a tool
  result the Watcher marked) or the contents of a file it read, and a memory
  entry must never be made on outside content's say-so or from a protected
  path; the person's own words carry neither unless the person put them there.
  It also reads the same way in every mode, through reads the host already
  makes for Octant Shield. Secrets are redacted (the same secret shapes as
  approvals, plus private-key blocks) before the text reaches the model and
  again before anything is stored, and an entry or summary that still names a
  protected path is dropped.
- **The model call.** One tool-less, single-use session per ended thread, in a
  scratch folder outside every Project, on the thread's own provider with that
  provider's smallest model, unless Settings › Providers & Models › Automatic
  model calls picks another account. Its usage
  is recorded against the thread as a `person-memory` usage row, so the person
  sees it in the usage dashboard. A reply that read outside content is thrown
  away. The call sits behind one seam (`personMemoryDistillationAllowed`) that
  answers per provider kind, so background use can later be limited for one
  provider without touching the rest; today it allows every kind. Open risk:
  whether a provider's terms allow background calls on a subscription sign-in
  is not settled, and the seam is where an answer would land. If the chosen
  account is off, not ready or at its limit, the thread waits for a later pass;
  it is never distilled on another account. Limits: at most 5 new entries per
  ended thread, 200 entries kept (past that the oldest never-edited entry is
  dropped), 20 sources per entry, 512 Projects kept out, and the distiller sees
  at most the newest 12,000 characters of the person's messages.
- **Where it goes.** Every new Chat, Work, and Code thread, on every provider,
  gets one `person-memory` context block through Octant's own context
  assembly, placed after Octant's instructions and before Project memory and
  the conversation. It holds the entries that existed when the thread was
  created (so it is the same text on every turn and a provider's prompt cache
  keeps its prefix; an entry the person edits or deletes changes it, which
  re-sends the standing context once), newest first, capped at 2,000
  characters. Its text opens by saying it is data about the person from
  earlier threads, not instructions, and each line names its kind. The
  context inspector lists it as Person memory in Chat and Work, so a person
  can see when it was used; a Code window, which is counted by part, counts
  it with Octant's instructions.
- **Searching past threads.** `octant_past_threads` is a read-only host tool,
  offered in Chat (not a Side Chat), Work, and Code beside the thread's other
  host tools. It
  searches the digests and entries above and answers with at most five short
  excerpts, each naming its thread, mode, Project, and date. It reads no
  thread transcript, no file, and no other Project's folder, and it grants no
  file, shell, or Project authority: what it returns is what memory already
  holds. Each call shows in the thread as a tool step.
- **Controls (Settings › Memory).** One switch for all of it, on by default:
  off stops writing, the block, and the tool, and keeps what is stored until
  the person forgets it. A second switch for searching past threads. Per
  Project, Keep a Project out: that Project's threads are not distilled,
  entries and digests whose every source is in it are not shown to other
  threads or found by search, and its own threads get no block and no tool.
  Per thread, Leave no trace (from the thread's menu, listed in Settings
  where it can be undone): the thread is not distilled, gets no block and no
  tool, and what was already remembered from it is erased when it is marked.
- **Deleting.** Deleting an entry or forgetting everything erases those
  events from the journal, not only from the view. Purging or deleting a
  thread erases its digest, removes it from every entry's sources, and erases
  each entry that came only from it.
- **Storage.** Entries, digests, settings, and Leave-no-trace marks are
  journal events (`person-memory-*` aggregates) held in host memory and
  rebuilt from the journal at start, so they are local, owner-only, and in no
  diagnostics or telemetry. A thread's digest names the thread as `threadId`,
  so a thread purge takes it with the thread. Export my data carries person
  memory: a `person-memory` page holding every entry with the threads it came
  from (title, mode, Project, provider account, end time), and no digest or
  setting. Entries were redacted before storage, so the export adds nothing
  beyond what Settings › Memory shows.
- **Who may read it.**
  - A local window: read and change everything in Settings › Memory.
  - A paired device: the memory routes refuse it, and a turn it sends gets no
    block and no tool, because a device may be granted only some Projects and
    memory crosses them.
  - A turn the host starts as itself (a routine's run, a delivered child
    result, a turn resumed after a usage limit): no block and no tool, since
    no person is at the window. A provider session that held the block is
    sent its standing context again once without it.
  - A subagent (child run): neither; it receives only what its lead passes it.
  - A hub, spoke, or peer host: person memory stays on the host that wrote
    it and is never synced or relayed.
  - A provider: sees memory only in a thread on that provider that uses it.
    Memory learned in a thread on one provider can reach a thread on another,
    and Settings › Memory says so in those words.
- **First run.** The first-run flow says in one sentence that Octant
  remembers across threads and that Settings › Memory turns it off.

Work is not cut off from a person's integrations. Work is for files,
browsers, and documents, and what separates it from Code is which developer
surfaces it shows, not the tools a person plugs in. An MCP
server the person installed and enabled as an Octant plugin is selectable in
Work and Code exactly as in Chat (see
[Extensions and skills](#extensions-and-skills)). It runs in Octant's own
supervised session rather than inside the provider, so today's Work-mode launch
confinement does not stop it, and every call it answers waits for a person
unless a remembered approval of that tool in that Project covers it.

A Work or Code thread started without a chosen Project lands in the mode's
**default Project**: the host provisions `<default folder>/Work` or
`<default folder>/Code` on first use, binds it as an ordinary Project marked
`origin: "default-folder"`, and reuses it after. The default folder is the
`defaultFolder` shell setting (`~/Octant` unless changed, always inside the
user's home, and stored by its real path when chosen; see
[host reads of a bound root](#security-and-authority)), and artifact files
mirror under its `Artifacts` subfolder until a mirror setting says otherwise. It sits at the top of home rather than in
`~/Documents`, which macOS guards with a privacy prompt. Work always offers its
default Project. Code has one choice, the `requireGitRepository` setting ("Code
needs a Git repository", on by default). Off, a Code thread may start in a
folder that is not a repository on a `plain-folder` checkout whose head is
`none`, and that includes the Code default Project; every Git-backed feature
reports itself unavailable there rather than inventing a revision. On, both are
refused.

The default folder used to be `~/Documents/Octant`, and threads without a
Project in Code had a separate `allowDefaultFolderThreads` switch beside the Git
requirement. A stored folder is kept, so an install that stored
`~/Documents/Octant` keeps it; only an install that never stored one follows
the new default. A window saves shell settings whole, filled-in folder
included, so in practice any install that saved a setting while the old default
was in effect stored it. Default Projects already bound under the old folder
stay ordinary Projects with their threads, and a changed folder creates a new
default Project beside them. Settings, journal events, and update commands that
still carry `allowDefaultFolderThreads` decode, and the switch is dropped: the
Git requirement each install stored is the one choice it keeps. The host only
ever stored that switch on with Git not required, so on-and-on never existed;
an install that had Git off and the switch off now also offers the Code
default Project, which is the one combination the single choice cannot keep.

Code task creation accepts a plain-folder checkout when the server admits it under
Code settings. The renderer preserves its proposed branch as delivery intent without
claiming a checked-out branch; detached Git checkouts remain refused. Git-dependent
actions continue to report unavailable for plain folders.

A Code Project may be bound to a folder on one of the person's registered
servers over SSH (maintainer decision, 2026-10-31, replacing the 2026-10-29
removal; [Server Projects](design/server-projects.md) owns the detail).
Inference, approvals, every authority check, and the journal stay on this
host; a thread's files, shell, Git, and terminals are on the server. Server
Projects are a catalog of their own, never the local Project catalog, so no
service that reads a local Project's folder can be handed a server path.
Octant connects with this host's own `ssh`, the person's SSH config, and their
agent: keys stay with the host, nothing is forwarded, an unknown host key is
refused, and a call that cannot reach the server fails with nothing run on
this host instead. Built: the catalog, the connection, and the folder check
at binding (Settings › Access › Servers); Code threads there, which run only
on the Octant Harness, with file tools, commands, and Git on the server under
the same levels, approvals, and journal as a local Project; thread
terminals that are logins on the server; the Git tab, whose Git runs on
the server; the dock's Review tool; the Files panel, file editor, and Tests
panel, which read, write, and run on the server; the Project terminal; one
shared SSH connection per server; and a thread's own worktree, made with Git on the server, and its
pull request, opened by repository and branch name. A Work Project may be
bound there too, in the same catalog: its Work threads run on the Octant
Harness with file tools and commands on the server under the same rules, opened from the
Work sidebar and composer. Not built: Work Files, research sources, the status
file and due dates, and the Project terminal for a Work Project on a server;
extra folders; saved Project actions; a Project-level guardrail level or
reviewer. It is tested only against a throwaway local `sshd`, never a real
server. Octant has no sandbox on the server,
so below Full access a remembered approval does not cover a command there. An agent in a local Project still
reaches a remote machine with `ssh` through its shell (above), and Octant on
another computer is a hub-and-spoke member
([Hub and spokes](design/hub-and-spokes.md)). The earlier SSH target binding
was removed, and its records are handled as follows. A journal written by a build that
could bind a Project to an SSH target still replays: its thirteen event names
(`ssh-target.*`, `ssh-remote-*`, `provider-runtime-egress.*`) are retired, and
a thread left on a `remote-root` checkout keeps its history but refuses every
operation, because its Project is no longer in the catalog and no window opens
it. A restart interrupts such a thread's turn that was still running and
withdraws the approvals and questions it left pending. A migration drops the
five `ssh_*` projection tables, which nothing fills any more. The
`<data>/ssh-targets/` folder of host-key pin files is left in place and
listed in the host data map as an unused leftover; Octant never deletes it. An
export written before the removal still assembles: its `ssh-targets` page is
read and dropped.

An authorized repository test remains cancellable while the host rediscovers its
command definition. Cancellation during discovery prevents process launch; runtime
shutdown also cancels pending discovery and waits for it to settle. Thread and
checkout authority checks still precede both run and cancellation.

Every Project, in any mode, may carry one optional **colour**: a theme palette
role (red, orange, yellow, green, teal, blue, purple, or pink) the person picks
as the Project's identity. It lives on the Project record and is journaled as
`project.color-changed@1`, so every client sees the same colour. Absent means no
colour was picked and reads as a neutral mark; older Projects and events replay
without it. `change-project-color` carries the role, or `null` to clear it, and
follows the same rules as a rename: an archived Project refuses it, and a change
that would leave the colour as it is journals nothing. The colour grants no
authority and carries no status.

Any Project may hold a **brand kit**: named colour, font, radius, and spacing
tokens that designs draw with under the Canvas `brand` theme. It lives on the
Project record as `brandKit`, is set by `change-project-brand-kit`, and is
journaled as `project.brand-kit-changed@1`; absent means no kit. The domain
validates every value with the same rule a design's own brand passes
(`designBrandTokenRefusal`), so nothing a kit holds can end a stylesheet
declaration or load a resource. A kit carries no filesystem, shell, or provider
authority, so Chat Projects hold one too. See [Canvas](design/canvas.md) for how
it reaches an agent and a frame.

A Work Project may opt into a **status file**: `STATUS.md` at the top of its
folder, where the work stands, with dated follow-ups and deadlines. The setting
lives on the Project record as `statusFile` and is journaled as
`project.work-status-file-changed@1`; absent reads as disabled, so every
Project, including one created before the setting existed or whose folder
already holds a `STATUS.md`, starts off. The default-folder Project refuses it
on the server: it holds what nobody gave a home, so there is no single piece of
work for a status to describe. Enabling seeds `STATUS.md` if it is missing.
While enabled, the file is read into every Work turn ahead of the thread's
transcript with a standing instruction to update it when the turn changes where
the work stands and to leave it unchanged for questions and conversation; a
completed turn that changed files without touching it gets a `Recent changes`
line appended from the turn's observed-changes record; and a stale status or a
near or passed date makes the next task open by taking stock and asking for an
update, unless its request is a greeting or unrelated to the work, which is
answered first with the update offered at the end. An unconditional "update
before you finish" rule asked the model to rewrite the file after a one-word
greeting. The file reaches the model as keyed standing context, so a runtime
that keeps its own conversation receives it again only when it changed; the
take-stock request is a one-turn instruction on the task's first turn, so the
standing rule's text never changes (see
[Held standing context](#held-standing-context)). The Work Project page, the
Work board's follow-up mark, and the inbox's `follow-up-due` attention signal
read the same file on demand; nothing about its content is journaled. While
disabled, Octant reads nothing from the folder for this purpose, adds no
instruction, and writes nothing there; turning the setting off leaves an
existing file untouched. Octant never writes an agent brief (`AGENTS.md`,
`CLAUDE.md`, or similar) into a user folder, and a Work turn does not read an
existing one: Claude Work turns load no project settings or instruction files,
and Codex Work threads start and resume with `project_doc_max_bytes = 0`, which
skips the `AGENTS.md` discovery Codex otherwise runs from the repository root
down to the Project root. This narrows the always-on
behavior the status file had at first.

Work never silently becomes Code. When coding work is detected in a Work
thread, the server records a **promotion proposal**: an offer to continue in
Code's focus, with its checkouts, worktrees, delivery target, and developer
surfaces. Only explicit user approval creates the linked Code thread. A
promotion moves focus and tooling, not authority: both threads run under the
shared guardrail levels, and the new thread takes the level of its own
Project and scope as any new Code thread does, never a level carried over
from the Work thread.

Rebinding a Code Project supersedes the checkout its existing threads were
created against, and no later observation can produce those threads' checkout
ids again, so the server reports them as unavailable rather than waiting on a
reconnection nobody is attempting. That refusal names
a way out: the thread's fail-closed surface offers an explicit rebind that moves
it onto the checkout the Project binds now. The server authorizes and journals
the move, and it never happens on its own — a matching filesystem root is not
consent to change what authority a thread holds. A session grant of Full access
does not survive the move; the thread lands on its persisted posture. A thread
that owns a managed worktree is refused, because that checkout is the thread's
own tree rather than the Project's.

A Code fork (`fork-code-thread`) is a managed-worktree creation the host
resolves itself: the client names the source thread and a finished turn, and
the host picks the files from its own record — the checkpoint the next writing
turn captured before it ran (a Plan turn in between writes nothing and is
skipped), or a fresh capture of the source checkout when the named turn is the
newest. It refuses a turn that has not finished and a point a writing turn
passed without a capture rather than guess. The worktree starts at that
checkpoint's commit on a new delivery branch, and the captured trees are laid
over it, so uncommitted work arrives too; a failure to lay them down removes
the worktree and creates nothing. The fork starts approval-gated with
current-session persistence and inherits no profile, pending outcome proposal,
running turn, or session grant. Every Code thread creation checks a
`forkedFrom` origin on the server: it must name another thread of the same
Project, and the fork's text handoff (below, "Fork handoff (Code)") must be
selectable from that thread through the named turn right now. A fork or
Restore from here whose handoff cannot be built is refused with the reason
before any worktree is prepared, because the text handoff is the one
conversation transfer every fork can fall back to.

A fork or Restore from here copies its source's conversation, and a harness
fork its tool results too, so a thread made from a source marked with
outside content starts marked. A Code creation with a `forkedFrom` origin
whose source is marked appends `thread.external-content-ingested@1` on the new
thread
(`external-content`, label `code-fork`, content reference
`code-fork-<source thread>-<fork turn>`) before it journals the thread, so no
moment exists at which the thread is created and unmarked; a mark that cannot
be journaled refuses the creation and removes its worktree. The mark and the
thread commit as one journal unit, so a creation that fails after the mark
leaves no mark behind: only a person's clear may forget a mark, so a failed
creation is never undone by a later event. An unmarked source
makes an unmarked thread. The source's mark is read when the creation is
checked, as its handoff reports it. A source a person cleared is unmarked, and
its fork starts unmarked: the clear holds until the next ingestion, and a
fork brings in nothing the person has not reviewed. A source marked again
after its clear marks its fork. The new thread's mark is its own. It
survives replay, a purge of the new thread erases it, and a person clears it
there like any other.

A Chat branch (`branch-chat-thread`, which Chat's Restore from here also
sends) copies its source's messages and completed replies, so a branch of a
marked source starts marked by the same rule: the mark (`external-content`,
label `chat-branch`, content reference
`chat-branch-<source thread>-<branch turn>`) and the branch commit as one
journal unit with the mark first, and a mark that cannot be journaled refuses
the branch with nothing created. The source's mark is read from its
outside-content projection when the branch is made; the cleared-source,
replay, purge, and clear rules above hold unchanged.

A follow-up or side task a model suggested on a marked thread starts marked
too, in every mode, by the same rule (label `follow-up`, content reference
`follow-up-<source thread>-<new thread>`). It copies no transcript, but its
title and prompt are text an agent wrote after reading what marked the source,
nothing bounds what that text can carry, and a side task sends its prompt as
the new thread's first message. Starting one is not a review the way a clear
is. The host's follow-up creator reads the source's mark when it creates the
thread and hands the mark to the Chat, Work, or Code creation as a host-only
input no wire command can carry; a source a person cleared passes on nothing.

A thread a person confirms from a Code planner's proposal starts marked when
the planner thread is marked, by the same rule (label `planner-proposal`,
content reference `planner-proposal-<planner thread>-<proposal>`). The planner
agent wrote the proposal's title and intent after reading whatever marked its
thread, and the intent becomes the new thread's opening prompt; confirming
reviews the proposed work, not what the planner read. The planner service reads
the planner thread's mark at the confirm and hands it to the Code creation as
the same host-only input; a mark that cannot be journaled refuses the confirm,
creates nothing, and leaves the proposal pending.

Fork, branch, follow-up, and planner proposal journal their marks through one
shared step.

A Work-to-Code promotion starts its linked Code thread unmarked. The proposal
names a Work Project, not a Work thread: its summary is text the person typed
into the proposal, its artifact refs are opaque names the host checks for
leaked authority and never reads into the Code thread, and the linked thread
takes only that summary, as its title. No agent-written or outside text
crosses, and there is no source thread whose mark the host could read; marking
from one would mean trusting a thread id the client names. A promotion that
comes to carry a Work thread's transcript or text an agent wrote must mark by
the rule above.

A `#thread` mention or a Side Chat's source brings another thread's
transcript into a turn, so a source marked with outside content marks the
thread reading it (labels `thread-mention` and `side-chat`, content reference
`<label>-<source thread>`). The host reads the source's mark after reading its
transcript and appends the reader's mark before it hands the framed text to
the turn, the order the sibling-thread `read` keeps, so the reader's provider
never sees a marked source's text on an unmarked thread. A mark that cannot be
recorded withholds the text: a mention is answered as unreadable, which costs
the mention and not the send, and a Side Chat turn is refused. The reference
names the source, so mentioning one source again journals nothing new until a
person clears the reader. The sibling-thread `read` marks its caller on every
call, whatever the target, because an agent chose to read; a mention or a
Side Chat is the person's own choice of thread, so an unmarked or cleared
source passes on nothing, as for a fork. A person-returned Side Chat reply inherits the sidecar’s mark under
`side-chat-return`, after the exact selected reply and retained receipt are
revalidated and before ordinary send, queued delivery, retry or resume reads it.
An unreadable reference or a failed mark refuses admission; an edited excerpt
never silently becomes trusted plain prose. Chat, Work, and Code mentions share
one resolver, and a thread that mentions itself is not marked again. A Side
Chat's state section also carries finished subagents' replies, and a reply
marks its parent only when it is delivered, which waits while the parent's
turn runs, so each reply in that section marks the sidecar itself (label
`subagent-result`, content reference `subagent-result-<run>`) by the same
order; a reply that cannot mark it refuses the turn.

A Canvas carries the mark of what wrote it. Every Canvas version commits
through the Canvas event store, and when the thread the Canvas belongs to, or
the managed child writing it, is marked at that moment, the store first appends
`canvas.outside-content-carried@1` (aggregate `canvas-outside-content`, one
event per writer, naming the writer and the first marked version) in the same
journal unit as the version, so no moment exists at which the Canvas holds that
text unmarked; a mark that cannot be read or recorded refuses the version
(a create, revise, board drag, refresh, or adopted version is refused with
`unavailable` and a message to try again, never reported as a race). This
covers an agent's create and revise, a child's, a hand-off document, a person's
edit, and a version taken from another computer, which marks the thread it
lands in first (`Synced from …`). A version taken from another computer is
recorded under its own author, an agent whose id is the version's id, and the
Canvas carries that author whenever the thread it lands in is marked, so a
person's clear of that thread never makes the synced text the thread's own. A version taken before it recorded its own author is named the same way at host start, from the thread's journaled ingestion of it (`replica-artifact:<canvas>:<version>`), which a clear does not erase. The Canvas tool's `read` and `preview` are how
another thread's model reaches a Canvas (any Canvas of its Project, by id; a
Canvas a Chat thread owns outside every Project answers only that thread), so
both mark the reader (label `canvas`, content reference `canvas-<canvas>`)
after the Canvas is read and before anything from it is returned, when the
Canvas records a writer other than the reader or the thread it belongs to is
marked now; the second rule covers a Canvas written before marks were recorded
at write time. A reader that cannot be marked is not given the Canvas. Every mode follows this
rule, Chat included: only a `read` or `preview` that returns content from a
marked Canvas marks the reader, so `describe`, a create, a revise, and a read
of a clean Canvas leave the thread unmarked. A child
is marked under its run, as its other tools are. A writer reading its own
Canvas passes on nothing. The mark recorded at write time is the Canvas's own:
a person's clear on the writer reviews what that thread read, not every thread
that will read the Canvas later, so it leaves the Canvas marked. It survives
replay, and a purge of the Canvas, or of the thread it belongs to, erases it.
A Chat Canvas selection carries only its name into planning, never the
Canvas's text, and a Canvas's mirrored or exported files are files: another
thread that reads them with its own file tools is not marked, as for any file a
marked thread writes.

An in-place restore (`restore-git-checkpoint`, sent by both Restore files to
this point and Undo restore) overwrites a checkout other threads may share, so
the host refuses it, as a `conflict` before Git is touched and before any undo
point is taken, while another thread has a live turn that may write there: a
turn in state `running` or `waiting` whose posture is not Plan. A turn parked
on an approval counts, because it writes as soon as it is answered. "The same
checkout" is the same resolved checkout root path, not the same checkout id:
the id derives from Project and binding revision, so two Projects on one folder
have different ids for one directory, and a managed worktree has its own path
and so never matches. The refusal names the other thread by title (cut to 100
characters) only when it is in the requesting thread's Project; otherwise it
says a thread in another Project is writing. A writing turn counts from just
before the host captures its checkpoint, through the runtime's preparation
(credentials, session seeding, fork preparation), until the runtime has taken
it on, so a restore cannot land between the capture and the launch. A start
that is refused or fails while preparing stops counting at once and holds
nothing back after that. Stopping a turn that is still preparing releases its
root at once, even if a preparation step never returns, and the turn is
refused at its next admission check, at the latest just before the runtime
takes it on, so it never reaches its provider. The stop is journaled as the
start's result when Stop returns, so the transcript shows the turn stopped and a
retry of that operation, including a start recovered after a restart, answers
from the journal instead of launching it. A stopped start whose preparation
settles later clears and settles only its own runtime bookkeeping (pending
start, spend reservation), keyed by its operation, never that of a newer turn
on the same thread. The other order is serialized
by root too: a turn that starts while a restore that passed this check is still
overwriting the same root holds the root, so no further restore starts, and
waits for the overwrite to finish before it captures its checkpoint, so it
starts from the restored files. A second restore of a root that is being
overwritten is refused as a `conflict` as well. Git alone queues only per
checkout id, which would let a turn or a restore in another Project on the same
folder, or a recovered start that captures nothing, run on a half-restored
tree. Restore from here and Fork from here create a thread on its own worktree
and are not subject to the check. The files part of a rewind (below) is an
in-place restore and takes the same check and the same serialization. Discard
uses the same live-writer check and root serialization, checked after approval
and immediately before Git is called. A writing turn that starts during discard
waits before capturing its checkpoint; another restore or discard is refused
until the overwrite finishes, including when it fails. Discard also refuses
while its own thread has a starting or live turn, as a rewind does: that turn
could otherwise write the files being discarded. The existing reviewed-state
token and tracked-path checks still apply. Stage and unstage do not discard
files and keep their existing rules. Reversing selected unstaged hunks uses
this same destructive-operation gate, own-turn refusal and root writer hold.
It reverses only the selected patch; it never substitutes whole-file discard.
No command here reaches commit revert.

Current Review can select exact text hunks from **Index → Working tree** for
stage or reversal, or **HEAD → Index** for unstage. A combined HEAD-to-working-tree
view is not an unstaged comparison. The host retains the canonical comparison,
its digest, hunk identities and an opaque digest of the original host root/binding
witness; commands carry only its operation reference and
selected identities, never renderer-supplied patches. Before applying, the host
revalidates the original live principal, Project binding, checkout and physical
root, current posture, reviewed state and exact canonical bytes. It checks again
after queued work and native preflight, with a final synchronous authority/root
proof after launch preparation. Git receives a bounded patch on stdin with no
three-way or whitespace fallback. The host recounts each selected hunk's
header for omitted earlier hunks that change the line count, so a preflight that
still relocates a hunk is genuine drift and is refused.
A replaced physical root cannot adopt an old comparison even when its Git bytes
match. A missing original witness requires a fresh comparison; the stable host
witness remains usable after restart while the same root and authority remain.
The managed writer hold excludes competing Octant writes during reversal.
Unmanaged external processes can still race after the last native preflight and
state check; this is not a filesystem-wide atomic compare-and-swap.

Binary, rename, conflict, nonregular-file/mode and ambiguous-path comparisons
explain why selection is unavailable. Truncated or non-UTF-8 bytes cannot become
an editable patch. Captured, historical and branch review views remain read-only.
The person confirms reversal and ordinary approval policy still applies. After a
write, Review rereads current state. If authority retires after a launched write,
the private operation stream retains only its minimal mutation outcome, never
fresh comparison or error bytes; the retired caller is told the checkout may
have changed and must Refresh. An authorized replay reads that outcome instead
of applying the same operation again; an uncertain native result stays failed
rather than being presented as proof that nothing changed.

**Rewind and fork instead of edit (maintainer decision, 2026-11-01).** Chat,
Work and Code threads do not edit a sent message: editing rewrites what the
model was told behind its back and leaves a session that still holds the old
turn. Every message of a thread instead offers **Fork from here** and
**Rewind to here**. Restoring a marked checkpoint still forks; a thread can
now also move back in place. Chat's differences are under **Chat** below.

- **Fork from here** on a reply forks through that reply, and on a person's
  message through the reply before it; the first message of a thread offers
  none, because nothing comes before it. A Code fork follows the fork rules
  above. A Work fork is a new Work thread in the same Project that carries the
  source's messages and finished replies through that point as text, starts at
  Ask first with no inherited profile, running turn, or session grant, is
  marked when its source is, and leaves the source untouched. The carried turns
  are copied into the fork's own journal in the same unit that creates it,
  each naming the source turn it came from, so every later read is of the
  fork's own turns. Original attachment references retain their source identity;
  bytes are read only for an admitted continuation, as described under
  **Original inputs in continuations** below. Tool steps and changed-file
  records stay with the source. Its first turn on a provider that keeps its own session starts a
  new session with the carried turns as a disclosed text handoff; a host that
  rebuilds the conversation reads them from the copies.
- **Rewind to here** on a person's message removes that turn and every later
  one; on a reply it removes the turns after it. The person chooses
  conversation, files, or both, and is asked once, in a dialog that reads
  `preview-code-rewind` first and shows how many turns leave and which files
  differ from the checkpoint the files would come back from. Nothing changes
  until they answer.
- **Files** come back from Octant's own checkpoints: the checkpoint the first
  removed turn captured before it ran, or, past Plan turns that wrote nothing,
  the next one a writing turn captured. A writing turn without a capture
  refuses the files part, as a fork does. The files part is journaled as an
  ordinary `restore-checkpoint` result under its own operation, so Undo
  restore offers the way back from it, and it runs first: a restore that does
  not complete leaves the conversation as it was. A Code thread in a Project on
  a registered server takes no checkpoints, a Plan thread writes nothing, and
  Work takes no file checkpoints, so each rewinds the conversation only and
  says why.
- **Refusals.** A rewind is refused while a turn of the thread is starting,
  running, or waiting. Its files part is refused while another thread has a
  live writing turn on the same checkout root, by the in-place restore check
  above. A conversation-only rewind touches no file, so another thread's
  writing turn cannot conflict with it and does not refuse it.
- **The journal stays authoritative.** Removed turns are never deleted. The
  rewind's own completed result (`thread-rewound` for Code,
  `work.thread-rewound@1` for Work) is the record that removes them: every
  conversation read, the transcript, a fork point, a handoff, the context plan,
  and export leave out each turn that started at or after the rewind's first
  removed turn and before the rewind was journaled. Replay folds the same
  records, so a rebuilt projection removes the same turns, and a turn sent
  after a rewind is the thread's own again until a later rewind removes it.
  Readers that place files or a copied session by the order turns ran (fork
  and rewind file points, the harness session copy) still read removed turns,
  because a removed turn captured the files the turn before it left. The
  thread's usage figure counts the turns it holds; the usage ledger, the Usage
  dashboard, and spend ceilings still count every turn that ran.
- **Removed turns stop reaching the model.** A session recorded before the
  rewind still holds them, so it is never resumed as it stands. A provider
  that reports `sessionRollback` continues a copy of its own session cut back
  at the last kept turn (`rewind-native-session`); today that is the Octant
  Harness, whose transcript copy is the one a harness fork makes. Every other
  provider reports it unsupported in its capability report, and the next turn
  starts a fresh session with a disclosed text handoff of the kept turns
  (`rewind`), journaled before the prompt is sent, as a provider switch's is.
  A host that rebuilds the conversation itself each turn rebuilds it from the
  kept turns. With no turn kept the thread starts again as it did at first,
  and a fork's first turn carries its source's conversation again.
- **The composer.** The person's message from the first removed turn returns
  to the composer for editing, which is how a sent message is changed in Chat,
  Work and Code.
- **On the phone.** The Android and iOS client offers Fork from here and
  Rewind to here on every message of a Chat, Work or Code thread it can open,
  through the same host routes and commands, and gains no authority from it.
  A paired device is a remote principal and a Code operation from it is gated
  as an agent's, so the host's own rules decide each part. A fork and a
  conversation-only rewind are allowed. A rewind that puts files back is the
  in-place restore, which the host asks an approval for under Ask first and
  Auto-accept edits, and approvals are taken only at a window on the computer
  (`/api/desktop/*` never reaches a phone); under Full access the host asks
  nothing and allows it. The phone therefore offers files only for a Full
  access Code thread whose preview says files can come back, shows the same
  preview and the same single confirmation, and otherwise offers the
  conversation only and says why in the sheet. Chat and Work have no files and
  say so. Nothing is offered while a turn starts, runs or waits, or while the
  host is stale; the host refuses the same cases itself. The removed message
  returns to the phone's composer above any draft.

  Rationale: the narrower choice keeps the existing boundary. Giving a phone
  its own way to approve a file restore would be a new approval path for a
  destructive effect, and the phone cannot know the host's session grants, so
  it offers files only where the thread's own posture asks nothing and shows
  the host's refusal as it is when the host disagrees.

- **Chat.** Chat follows these rules with the differences below. It has no
  files and gains no filesystem or shell authority: the rewind dialog says so
  and offers the conversation only, with no preview read and no checkpoint
  restore, and the command (`rewind-chat-thread`) carries only the thread, its
  expected version and the first turn to remove, so provider, model and
  Project scope stay the server's.
  - **Fork from here** is the Chat branch (`branch-chat-thread`, above and
    below) and keeps its rules: it copies message text and completed replies,
    never the source's session, and starts a new session with a `branch`
    handoff when the provider keeps its conversation in one. On a reply it
    branches through that turn; on a person's message, through the turn before
    it, so the first message offers none. The reply's own Fork control is the
    same action.
  - **Rewind to here** on a person's message removes that turn and every later
    one; on a reply it removes the turns after it, so the last reply offers
    none. It is asked once, in the same dialog, and is refused while a
    response is running, while the thread is compacting, when the thread or its
    Project is not active, on a stale version, and for a turn that is not part
    of the active conversation. Nothing changes until the person answers.
  - **The journal stays authoritative.** The rewind appends one
    `chat.thread-rewound@1` event, which names the removed turns and carries the
    thread's next version. The projection marks each removed turn `rewound`;
    the turn and its attempts stay journaled. `activeChatTurns` leaves a
    rewound turn out as it does a superseded one, so the transcript, the window
    and its count of left-out turns, context planning, handoffs, mentions,
    subagent context, export, search and the message queue read the kept
    conversation. Replay marks the same turns. A turn sent after a rewind is
    the thread's own again.
  - **Old journals with edits.** Chat once edited a sent message by appending a
    turn that names the one it replaced (`supersedes`). The command is gone and
    nothing writes that marker, but the field, the fold and the display stay: a
    journal that holds edits replays and shows the same conversation it always
    did, and a rewound edit does not bring back the turn it replaced.
  - **Removed turns stop reaching the model.** Chat does not use
    `sessionRollback`. A provider that keeps its conversation in a session of
    its own starts a new session with a disclosed `rewind` handoff of the kept
    turns, journaled with the attempt before the prompt is sent, and with no
    turn kept starts as it did at first. A conversation the host holds is
    rebuilt from the kept turns, a harness session that ran the removed turns
    is not continued, and a compaction summary that reaches past the kept turns
    is not reused.
  - **The composer.** The client already holds the removed message, so the
    command returns no text: the person's message goes back to the composer
    above any draft already there once the host has journaled the rewind.

  Rationale: Chat could copy the Work cut of a provider's own session only by
  trusting a runtime to cut at exactly the kept turn, which no provider has
  proven without a paid live turn, and its Octant Harness conversation is
  rebuilt from the journal anyway. The handoff or the rebuild is the path whose
  content the host chooses and journals, so Chat takes it for every provider
  and leaves `sessionRollback` to Work and Code.

Rationale: provider-owned runtimes (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, ACP agents)
each have their own way back in a session, but Octant could not prove any of
them cuts at exactly the kept turn without a paid live turn, and a wrong cut
would hand the model a turn the person removed while the transcript says it is
gone. A fresh session with a disclosed handoff is the one path whose content
the host chooses and journals, so those providers report `sessionRollback`
unsupported until a driver proves its own rollback. Rewinding only the
conversation changes nothing but the thread's own record, so it is gated as a
read (it runs in Plan and asks for no approval); any rewind that puts files
back is gated as the in-place restore it performs.

A child AgentRun starts only when the thread's agent delegates through
`octant_agents`, the one child-run tool, offered to an Octant Harness lead and
to a provider runtime's agent alike. Its operations are `capabilities`,
`delegate`, `status`, `wait`, `cancel`, and `follow-up`; `wait` with a zero
timeout reads a finished reply without blocking. Either parent harness can
target either child harness; provider-owned hidden subagents remain disabled.
Every child appears in the Agents surface, where the person can watch, stop,
or resume it, and `cancel` is the agent's way to stop one it started.

Rationale: the harness once offered its own `delegate` tool beside
`octant_agents`, with different words (`start`, `collect`) for the same
actions over the same admission, so a Harness lead saw two tools that did
one job. `octant_agents` was kept because it alone could cancel a child, and
because its `wait` answers at once for a child that is waiting for a free
request slot or on a provider limit, where the harness tool blocked until its
timeout and held the slot the child needed. What the harness tool had that
`octant_agents` lacks, a `wait` over several children at once, is a wait per
child in turn. A journal that names the retired tool still replays: its name
stays readable in turn records and approvals
(`NATIVE_HARNESS_RETIRED_TOOL_NAMES`). The host's AgentRun routes read and control
existing runs but create none. Reads, the Agents center list, acknowledgements,
and cancellation are authorized per window: the window's own workspace must
currently hold the parent thread on the matching Project, so the center lists
only the runs of threads the window has open. Admission (`admitAgentRunControlRequest`) prepares the child's workspace
on the server: Chat a research-only virtual workspace, Work the current
confined Project root and binding revision, and Code an isolated managed
worktree that is confirmed before admission. No client supplies a path, a
receipt, or a claimed `verified` flag. Admission, restart, and replay refuse
stale, expired, foreign-thread, foreign-Project, parent-checkout, unavailable,
or wider-than-parent grants. Whether the agent may delegate is one host
setting, on by default; a stored Ask from the retired "only when I start them"
choice reads as off.

Each Code child allocation is keyed by its parent and delegation request. Two
sibling requests receive distinct managed worktrees; only the same request can
reuse its verified receipt. The host checks the actual Git worktree inventory
and records the starting commit. Committed revision is the default source.
The person can instead open the parent task's **Worktrees → Child source**,
capture **Current edits snapshot**, inspect the included paths, then explicitly
select it for children prepared from that task. Capturing alone does not enable
it. Selecting **Committed revision** clears the selection. Existing children
never change when this selection or the parent's files change.

A current-edits source reuses Git checkpoints, with a separate worktree tree and
index tree, without committing to or changing the parent's branch, files or
staging. Capture enumerates tracked changes and eligible untracked files,
including nested untracked files; ignored files are excluded. Protected changes,
truncated or oversized manifests (over 256 paths), unreadable objects, and an
unstable capture refuse rather than silently copying a subset. A capture has a
thirty second bound and is checked against a second capture and observation.
The selected snapshot is bound to the parent thread, checkout, binding and base
revision; a stale selection must be replaced or explicitly cleared before a
child can start.

Each child records its committed base, snapshot identity and included paths in
its managed receipt and admitted workspace. The parent's child details and the
child's provider context identify the source. Copying preserves staging in that
child's independent checkout. The host journals applying and completed copy
states before admission; an incomplete, failed or interrupted copy refuses
confirmation and execution. It is never automatically reapplied over a child's
files, including after a lost reply or restart. Prepare a new child to recover
an incomplete copy. The checkpoint anchors follow existing checkout retention.
This source choice transfers files, not model attachments.

Provider-owned child reports are read-only observations through the existing
`child-agent-activity` SDK event. Chat attempts, Work turn updates, Code operation
frames, and managed-child conversations retain the normalized facts in their
existing journals or purgeable content. Identity includes the mode, root thread,
optional managed parent, provider instance, session, and provider child ID.
An observation never receives an AgentRun ID, workspace grant, or managed control.
Missing child model or task metadata stays unknown; the lead model is not a
substitute. Status is the provider's last report, not proof of a live process.
Replay is idempotent; conflicting reported identities become unknown, and missing
or circular child lineage is excluded. Each source retains at most 16 observed
children and eight history entries per child, with explicit partial/truncated
history. Parent reads include at most 64 observations. No current in-tree adapter
advertises native-child observation support: their existing child-disable and
provenance gates remain in force. SDK fixture coverage does not establish
real-provider native-child acceptance.

Child result packets retain at most 16 generations, including the current
generation's availability, immutable execution target and workspace receipt.
The reported summary is a bounded 4,096-character view of the generation's
existing result content. Lifecycle blockers come from recorded settlement facts.
Normalized file-change reports and host-executed tool returns are stored beside
the generation's reply, atomically with settlement, in the same subject-owned
content store. Each section retains at most 32 records and 60,000 serialized
characters; tool output is bounded to 2,048 characters. File paths outside the admitted workspace are omitted and
make the section truncated. Provider file reports are explicitly unverified;
host tool returns remain an unknown check outcome even when their output says
a test passed. No result implies parent delivery, review, merge, or deployment.
Writable managed Code children capture their isolated workspace before execution
and after confirmed provider teardown through the host's Git checkpoint port.
The same path covers Octant Harness and provider harnesses. The private session
record preserves the original tree and workspace identity across waits and retries
within one generation; a new follow-up generation starts its own comparison.
Git captures include tracked and non-ignored untracked files without changing the
real index, HEAD, or branch. Captures describe observed workspace changes, not proof
that the child alone authored them.

A settled comparison retains at most 128 paths and 65,536 diff characters, with a
120,000-character serialized ceiling, in subject-owned content beside the result.
Comparison captures create no Git refs, so a crash cannot leave pinned source
content behind. The retained diff remains readable after later edits or Git object
collection; collection before comparison can make the capture unavailable. A resumed generation
whose original tree was collected cannot substitute its current midpoint and
reports review unavailable. Waiting generations can advance their snapshot at the
next settlement; completed generations keep their original comparison. Failed
captures invalidate an earlier partial comparison for that same generation.
Review reads accept only the managed run and generation, check current parent and
child read authority, and never resolve a client-supplied filesystem path. Summary
polling carries metadata only. The existing Review surface opens the saved diff
without checkout mutation or parent-file navigation. Chat, Work, Plan, legacy
sessions without a baseline, and unavailable captures report review unavailable;
a parent checkout is never substituted.
Parent and child scope checks precede reads, streams recheck scope before each
frame, and a parent purge removes all generations' text and evidence. Nested
observations retain the authorized root thread and identify their managed parent
separately. Result reads do not consume or acknowledge delivery.

Settled managed attempts record active milliseconds and the chosen limit through the existing subject-owned result evidence, atomically with lifecycle persistence. Waiting intervals are excluded. The child detail shows its latest recorded attempt and cumulative recorded time, and labels historical, cancelled or lost-startup gaps as unavailable rather than inventing wall-time totals. Existing cumulative Project/thread ceilings remain independent and authoritative.

A managed child's lifecycle moves from Starting to Running once its workspace
is verified and its provider session starts, not at completion. One turn,
from provider acquisition to its terminal event, has a default 30-minute working-time limit. The person can choose 1–240 minutes in Helper agents settings before the next attempt; agents cannot change that setting. Retry and Resume each read the current setting and start a fresh timer, never inherit the old attempt's remainder. Provider acquisition and startup each have an independent two-minute readiness bound, so raising the task limit does not enlarge a stuck startup. A turn that reaches its working-time bound
is recorded as Interrupted and releases its capacity. The bound counts working
time only: it pauses while the child waits for a person's approval or answer and
resumes with the remaining time once every pending request is answered, because
a child cut off with its approval card still open lost its work to the person's
pace rather than its own. No separate overall wall-time cap exists, by decision: the working
deadline is the only bound, since a cap that counted a person's wait would
cut off the work it protects. A waiting child keeps its capacity slot until
the request is answered, the run is cancelled, or the host restarts.

Managed children retain a private provider-session cursor and a bounded,
purgeable conversation alongside their journaled lifecycle. A cursor is bound
to the run, provider, model, workspace, context, and authority. Resume uses that
same native session only when the provider supports it and the binding still
matches; it never silently starts a fresh session. Missing or invalid continuity
requires Retry. Restarted conversation views are marked stale until execution
reconnects, and a purged subject cannot restore its session or conversation.

Children on either harness use the host's approval and question stores. Each
prompt identifies its child, provider, and model and is checked against the
live parent and child authority before and after the answer. A child approval
permits only that request, never consumes or creates a remembered lead-session
grant, and cannot approve an opaque provider action in Plan mode. Cancelled or
expired requests and requests whose transport was lost at restart cannot be
answered. The composer lists eligible child approvals and questions beside the parent's own request, in a bounded scroll region with keyboard-selectable requests and an Open child action. It reads and answers the same authoritative pending IDs as Agents, names the child, provider/account and recorded target folder, and disables responses on a failed refresh or lost connection. A paired device receives a restricted child-request view with only eligible approvals and questions; parent sessions, turns, tool results, tasks, steering and follow-ups are never included. It may read and answer only requests from a child execution admitted by that device's own turn, approve once or deny; another device's, a local window's and host-owned executions remain unavailable. Admission and explicit Retry/Resume bind the execution to the authenticated scope; reads never transfer ownership, restart loses live ownership, and live parent/child authority is rechecked before the response can run. Settings, launch, pause, steering and remembered grants gain no remote route. The same
request is a Needs you row naming the parent thread and the child (see
pending requests across modes); the row has one action, which opens the parent's
Agents tab on that child, and no way to answer.

Live child steering is optional on a provider connection. Codex uses its
current-turn steering command; Octant's harness inserts a note after a complete
tool-results step or response and persists it before acknowledging delivery.
Only notes retained in the fitted provider request are recorded and acknowledged;
notes omitted to fit the context limit are refused.
Unsupported steering is reported as such; a saved note alone is not evidence
that the running child received it.

Delegation resolves explicit provider/model selections against the parent's
current eligible catalog, including Project policy and supported reasoning
values. A provider that can answer counts even when its catalog is
degraded (a Foundry deployment its models route does not list); a direct
endpoint model is a target only once its tools are verified. With no explicit target, both harnesses use the same role-to-slot
mapping and host/Project model slots (Settings names them model roles). An unconfigured route can inherit the
authorized parent target; a configured but unavailable or disallowed route does
not bypass its settings. The selected target and routing decisions remain
visible. Off, paused, tainted, and unauthorized parents cannot start helpers.

Parent conversation context is opt-in and fixed at admission. Chat uses its
admitted conversation; Work and Code expose bounded accepted prompts and
completed replies with source attribution, provider/model identity, taint, and
omission metadata. Work/Code selections contain at most 24 blocks of 4,000
