  same ceiling. Automation-origin execution cannot create, edit, run, pause, or
  archive a routine (`automation-recursion`). No agent or provider tool reaches
  the routes. An agent takes part only through the proposal and the routine
  tools below: it may read routines, propose one, ask the person to pause or
  archive one that is its thread's own, and report its own run's result.
  Every change still happens as a person's principal confirming it; resume,
  edit, run now, and cancel stay the person's alone.
- **Proposed from a thread.** A Work or Code thread's agent may propose a
  routine with the app-managed `octant_propose_routine` tool: a name, a task
  prompt, a trigger (once at an explicit instant, every N minutes within the
  bounds above, or weekly at a local time in an IANA zone), and a missed-run
  policy. It names nothing else: the thread's own Project and mode are implied,
  and the agent cannot choose another Project, a profile, a model, or any
  authority. Chat is never offered the tool, a turn that runs as the host (a
  routine's run, or a usage-limit resume) is refused it as
  `automation-recursion`. A turn in Plan is offered and may call it, as it
  may offer a side task: a proposal records only a suggestion the person
  confirms, and the routine takes none of the thread's posture, so it runs
  asking first (or at the level the person later picks for it), never in
  Plan; a follow-up's turn in its own thread is still narrowed by that
  thread's posture, as any turn is. A proposal creates nothing, whatever
  the thread's posture: a remembered Full access does not let an agent create
  or confirm a routine, and the routine it leads to is approval-gated anyway.
  The host holds it for ten minutes as a suggestion chip at the foot of the
  thread, listed and
  answerable only by the window or paired device whose turn raised it; with
  no such window open, or once it goes away, the proposal is withdrawn
  unanswered. The chip's one click confirms and dismissing it declines.
  Confirm is the `POST /api/automations/proposals/decide` route, under the same transport
  principal and Project check as `commands`. On confirm the host builds the
  definition from the thread's live facts (Project version and binding, the
  Code thread's own available checkout, the thread's provider and model, and
  an approval-gated profile that allows that model, the thread's own when it
  qualifies) and creates it through the ordinary create command as the
  confirming principal, so every ceiling and revalidation above applies
  unchanged: filesystem and tools only, no network or subagents, Work without
  shell or Git, Code asking first, and session-only permission kept
  session-only in both the authority receipt and the execution profile each
  run's thread is created from. A thread that left its Project, an archived
  thread, or an unavailable checkout refuses at confirm and creates nothing; a
  thread in Plan does not, since the routine is built at the approval-gated
  authority above whatever the thread's posture. The first answer takes the proposal off the list, so a
  retry cannot create a second routine. The call waits for the answer and
  reports `confirmed` with the routine id, `declined`, `expired`, `cancelled`,
  or the host's refusal. The tool rides the `appManagedTools` capability in
  the matrix under [security and authority](#security-and-authority): a
  provider or model without it is not offered the tool, and its degraded form
  is the person creating the routine in Automation Center.
- **Routine tools in a thread.** A Work or Code thread's agent is also offered
  the app-managed `octant_routines` tool, on the same capability and never in
  Chat, with `help`, `list`, `get`, `pause`, `archive`, and `report-result`.
  `list` and `get` read the routines of the thread's own Project and mode from
  the projection (a routine elsewhere reads as absent), with each routine's
  schedule, state, prompt, and recent runs, and flag a routine proposed or
  created from this thread, the routine whose run started this thread, and the
  run this turn belongs to. They answer at any posture, Plan included, and in
  a routine's own turn. `pause` and `archive` only ask: the request waits as a
  card in the thread under the proposal rules above (the raising window or
  paired device only, ten minutes, the shared cap of 32, withdrawn with the
  turn), and the person's confirmation is their own pause or archive through
  the `proposals/decide` route and the ordinary command, under the same
  Project check, at the routine version the agent saw, so a routine changed
  since is refused rather than changed. An agent may ask only about a routine
  that is its thread's own: `originThreadId` is this thread, or one of the
  routine's runs started this thread. A Code turn in Plan is refused, and so
  is every turn the host runs on its own, the routine's own run included:
  nobody is present to confirm, the card is listed only to the window that
  raised it and a host-run turn has none, and acting without a confirmation
  would be automation-origin execution pausing a routine. A run that should
  stop says so through `report-result` instead. `report-result` takes an
  outcome (`succeeded`, `nothing-to-do`, `needs-attention`, `failed`) and a
  summary of at most 1 KB, and is accepted only from the turn the dispatcher
  started for that run: the dispatcher hands the run's identity to the turn it
  starts through host-only start options that no wire command carries, and
  the host checks it against the run's journaled thread, so neither the host
  scope alone, a usage-limit resume, nor a person's later turn in the same
  thread can report. It is journaled once per run as
  `automation-run-result-reported@1`; replay keeps the first, it never
  changes the run's lifecycle, and Automation Center shows it beside the
  run's own status. Push notifications stay redacted and do not carry it. A
  reported summary is the run agent's own words, so a thread that reads it is
  marked as having read outside content.
- **Created from a thread by a person.** The person may also create a routine
  from a Work or Code thread's Environment with
  `POST /api/automations/thread-routines` (`create-thread-routine`: thread,
  name, prompt, trigger, missed-run policy). The host builds the definition
  from that thread's live facts exactly as for a confirmed proposal, so its
  Project, mode, binding, and approval-gated profile are the thread's and the
  body cannot name wider ones; a thread outside the named Project, or Chat,
  refuses. It is created as the requesting principal
  through the same create command.
- **Origin thread.** A routine confirmed from a proposal, or created from a
  thread by a person, records that thread as `originThreadId` on its journaled
  definition. Only the host sets
  it, never a command body, and later revisions keep it, so the projection
  rebuilds the link on replay. It links the routine and the thread in the UI
  and grants nothing.
- **Follow-ups in the same thread.** A follow-up is a routine with a `once`
  trigger, missed-run policy `run-once`, and target policy `same-thread`; the
  contract refuses `same-thread` with any other trigger or policy, and a
  persisted one without `originThreadId`. Its one run sends its fixed prompt as
  a new turn in its origin thread, under the host's heading
  (`Scheduled follow-up you set up earlier in this thread:`), so the agent has
  that conversation and the transcript marks the turn as scheduled rather than
  typed; the mark is presentational and the run's journaled dispatch intent is
  the evidence. It is made two ways, both through the create path above as a
  person's principal: the agent proposes it with `octant_propose_routine`
  (trigger `follow-up`: an instant and a prompt) and the person confirms the
  chip, or the person sets it up from the thread with
  `POST /api/automations/follow-ups` (`schedule-follow-up`: thread, time,
  prompt), which builds the definition from the thread's live facts exactly as
  a confirmed proposal does. Chat threads cannot have one, and the proposal
  refusals above apply. Moving it (`reschedule-follow-up`) is an ordinary
  update of its time; cancelling it is the ordinary archive. An edit cannot
  change any routine's target policy, and Run now is refused for a follow-up,
  because its one turn is its scheduled one. Its turn runs as the host under
  the same ceilings as any routine run: a Work turn uses the thread's own
  folder and runs ask-first, a Code turn asks for `approval-gated` and is
  clamped by the thread's grant, so a person widening the thread never widens
  the follow-up, and the turn's tools refuse new routines
  (`automation-recursion`).
- **Follow-up revalidation.** At fire time, after the routine checks above, the
  host checks the thread itself and refuses with a typed reason rather than
  adapting: `thread-unavailable` when the thread is gone, archived, or in
  another Project; `thread-done` when a person marked it Done (Work) or
  Complete; `full-access-ineligible` when the Code thread now has Full access;
  `execution-profile-mismatch` when its provider or model changed; and
  `thread-busy` when a turn is running or being started in it. A busy thread
  is skipped, not waited on: waiting would put a scheduled turn behind the
  person's own at a time nobody chose. A refusal fails the run with its
  reason in the journal and sends nothing; unlike other routines, a follow-up
  is not left paused, because the once trigger then ends it.
- **Follow-up missed window.** A follow-up missed while the host was asleep or
  off runs once on return if it is at most 24 hours late. Past that it fails
  as `follow-up-missed` and sends nothing: a check made a day late is stale.
  Either way it runs at most once and then ends itself as `exhausted`, the
  state every spent one-time routine reaches, with its run history kept.
- **Asleep or offline.** The scheduler is an in-process timer in the running
  host over journaled definitions. Nothing wakes the computer or runs in a
  cloud today. A self-hosted wake service on a person's hub, which only wakes
  a spoke and never holds or runs its routines, is built
  ([Hub and spokes](design/hub-and-spokes.md#wake-service)); it has run only
  between hosts on loopback with a fake socket. On return it reconciles missed occurrences by the routine's policy:
  `skip` records them as skipped; `run-once` records all but the newest as
  skipped and runs the newest once. No catch-up burst. More than the missed-run
  cap blocks the routine as `missed-run-cap-exceeded`. A routine with an active
  run never overlaps itself.
- **Runs as the host.** A routine is host-owned, so its run creates the thread
  and starts the first turn as the host, never through a window: it runs with
  no window open, and an open window lends it neither identity nor Project
  binding. The routine scope is minted per process and never registered, so no
  route, renderer, or paired device can act as it; it reaches only active
  Projects of the routine's mode, after the revalidation above, and every
  ceiling here still applies. The thread's creation, and a Work run's first
  turn, are journaled as the host's `system` actor, so the journal tells a routine's thread from one a person
  started. A browser-origin approval a routine's turn raises has no window of
  its own, so it is offered to every local window that may drive that thread's
  browser (one bound to the routine's Project); answering settles only that
  prompt, and an "always allow" is journaled by the answering window.
- **Journal.** Definitions, revisions, lifecycle changes, occurrence claims and
  skips, runs, dispatch intents and claims, cancellations, and a run's
  reported result are journaled. A
  claim commits the deterministic run before the occurrence ledger, so a crash
  repairs forward to the same run and never dispatches twice. Run-now and
  cancel are idempotent by request id.
- **Work first-turn outcomes.** The existing scheduler observes the retained
  Work turn request after acceptance, matching its runtime receipt, thread,
  Project, host, binding, provider and model against the run's captured snapshot.
  Only journaled terminal truth releases that run's active slot; missing or
  mismatched evidence stays active, and a changed current definition never
  replaces the captured owner. A cancelled/interrupted Work turn records an
  interrupted run; a failed turn records runtime failure. The status commits
  before another occurrence may be claimed. Replay and notification failure
  never send the old provider call again. This observes first-turn completion,
  not proof that delegated children or background processes are quiescent.
- **Turning one off.** Pause stops future occurrences; Resume restarts from the
  next occurrence; Archive ends the routine and keeps its history (there is no
  delete). Cancel stops a run before its first turn starts; afterwards the
  thread's own interrupt applies. A thread's agent may ask for a pause or an
  archive of its own routine under the routine tools above; only the person's
  confirmation does it.

A `#thread` mention points at another thread the sender can already Open. The
host resolves a bounded, read-only title, status, and transcript window at send
time. Dragging a sidebar thread onto a composer, or choosing Attach as context
from that thread's row menu, uses this same path: the mention search, given
the thread's id, returns that thread only when this window can Open it, so
where its title would rank does not matter, and the renderer does not read the
transcript to attach the chip. In Chat, an explicit mention of a Chat thread also grants the source
provider the bounded `octant_ask_thread` tool for that turn: it may send one of
the user's instructions to the mentioned Chat thread and receive its completed
reply, at most three times a turn. The target's own Chat turn, provider,
Project, and authority remain authoritative; an active target returns Waiting
rather than being interrupted or duplicated. Coordination is one hop (the
target's turn is offered no ask) and unavailable, unauthorized, or deleted
targets fail closed. Work and Code mentions remain read-only: a turn whose
mentions name no Chat thread is not offered the tool, and a Work or Code
thread named in a call refuses. In Work and Code, an `@file`
mention completes a path inside the thread's bound root; the host refuses a path
outside that root before reading it. Chat Projects have no filesystem authority,
so `@file` is absent there. In local desktop Work and Code composers (drafts and
existing threads), dropping a native folder or local `file:` URI inserts an editable
absolute `@folder/` reference after the host validates the current Project or
checkout roots, extra folders, and pinned filesystem identity. The window names
this computer and the canonical folder. Validation reads metadata only: no
recursive listing, attachment contents, turn, grant, or working-directory change.
Remote client paths, inaccessible/deleted directories, and escaping symlinks refuse
with an explanation. A draft targeting a future managed checkout refuses until
that thread exists; it never remaps a dropped Project path into another checkout.
Names retain spaces and Unicode; duplicate canonical references are inserted once.
Draft edits and ordinary image attachments survive validation and refusal.
Unknown `@` text stays ordinary text. `@` is the one composer
picker in every composer: it lists the effective snapshot's available skills,
effective plugin MCP servers, and connectors the person added (a disabled or
untrusted item is absent), plus the thread's files in Work and Code. Choosing a
row makes a structured selection chip that the host re-resolves at send; it
never installs, trusts, enables, or elevates anything. `/` lists commands only,
and `$skill` stays a typed alias. Side Chat is a Chat-mode sidecar about
exactly one source thread: ordinary Chat with no inherited Work or Code
authority and no agent path that messages, approves, steers, or appends to the
source. A person may explicitly choose a finished reply’s **Use in source draft**
action. The host resolves that exact reply and its linked, still-openable source;
the client appends only that reply to the source’s editable unsent draft, keeping
existing text and caret, including while the source runs. It neither sends nor
queues, steers or approves anything. Other replies, attachments and tool output
are omitted visibly, and an overlong answer says it was truncated. The draft
retains a typed reference to the sidecar, turn, attempt and original answer
digest even if the person edits its text. New replies retain a bounded receipt
on their existing Chat attempt: versions observed at the host’s actual source
reads, context digest, read range and omissions. Independent reads are not an
atomic snapshot; older replies say their original source snapshot was not
recorded. On ordinary send, queued delivery, retry and resume, the host checks
the exact reference and receipt again, refuses missing/purged/unauthorized or
wrong-destination references, and records inherited outside-content provenance
before the provider reads. Choosing a reply grants no execution authority.
Each turn the host re-resolves the source on the sender's window and
frames it as the conversation's subject: the newest 40 messages within 32,000
characters, with truncation stated, plus a current-state section capped at
8,000 characters. For Code that section names the branch, clean or dirty with
line totals, up to 50 uncommitted paths from Git (status joined with numstat
against HEAD, untracked files included), up to 50 paths the thread's turns
changed, and the delivery target; for Work, the Project folder and working folder; for every mode, the
newest five subagent results. Each state part that cannot be read says so on
its own; an unreadable transcript refuses the turn. The source block is a
required context entry, so the planner blocks with its usual remedies rather
than silently dropping the thread the Side Chat is about. On a provider that
keeps its own conversation, a byte-identical snapshot whose previous delivery
completed is replaced by a one-line "unchanged" notice, and the full snapshot
is resent at least every fifth turn. A Side Chat about a Work or Code thread
also gets read-only list, search (Code only), and read tools over the
source's files as app-managed tools; see
[security and authority](#security-and-authority).

A Chat attempt that fails or is interrupted carries a bounded failure code,
and the client-safe process diagnostic when the provider supplied one. The
transcript states Octant's sentence for that code. The provider's own message
stays off the attempt. A refusal Octant itself authored before the provider
answered (for example an unsupported capability or an unready provider) also
journals that host sentence, so replay after a restart shows the same refusal
the live turn did; provider-originated text is never persisted there. App-managed tool and research calls use the turn's own
deadline; a call that never returns ends the attempt instead of leaving it
running, and a cancellation is not recorded as that call having failed.

A turn stopped by the provider's own usage-limit signal additionally carries a
provider-neutral `usageLimit` fact in every mode: `temporary` (a live rate
window or overload), `exhausted` (the provider says the allowance is spent), or
`billing` (the provider reports an account/credit problem), plus the
provider-declared `resetsAt` instant when one exists. Only an explicit protocol
signal — Codex's `turn.error.codexErrorInfo`, Claude's assistant `error` and
result `terminalReason`, a rejected rate-limit message — produces the fact;
message-text matching never does, and account usage telemetry alone does not
prove this turn stopped. Providers without such a signal keep their ordinary
honest failure. An unknown reset stays unknown: the notice states the provider
did not say when the limit clears rather than fabricating a countdown, and a
billing stop gets no reset line at all. The fact is bound to the single
affected turn: each later attempt transition, successful recovery, provider or
account switch, and replacement error clears it. In Chat the fact rides the
parked `waiting` attempt (which records no failure); in Work it rides the
turn's `rate-limited` failure category; in Code it rides the journaled turn
failure and parks the turn as `waiting`. Drafts, queued input, and completed
tool results are untouched.

A refused resume is the other fact that parks a Code turn as `waiting`: the
provider's `stale-resume` failure journals as Code's own `stale` failure
category, and the transcript's recovery — the waiting status row offering a
new task in the Project, the composer left ready to send — keys on that
stated category, never on the absence of a request or a limit, which a
different parked wait could also satisfy.

A stop that disclosed `resetsAt` additionally offers an explicit per-thread
opt-in: Resume when the limit resets. A billing stop never offers it, and a
stop that preserved no resumable provider state — the parked Chat attempt's or
Work turn's `resumeCursor`, or the Code turn's journaled evidence — cannot
take it. Accepting journals `usage-resume.scheduled@1` on the thread's own
aggregate with a record naming the exact turn or attempt, provider instance,
limit fact, and reset instant; the same commit emits the mode's
`thread-updated` so every connected client sees the scheduled state and its
cancel affordance. At the reset instant a host-owned scheduler re-reads the
journaled record, rechecks the thread's mode, lifecycle, provider account, and
that the bound stop still waits on the limit, then continues through the
ordinary serialized turn-admission path — the same command shape a manual
retry takes — so capacity gates, admission ordering, and the single-continuation
bound all hold unchanged. The dispatch settles by appending
`usage-resume.settled@1` plus the mode's `thread-updated` in one commit; the
outcome it records (`dispatched`, `invalidated`, or `failed` with the refusal
detail) stays on the thread until a newer thread event replaces it.
The old stop's notice describes a dispatched recovery as started, rather than
implying that the resumed turn is still running after it settles.
Cancellation, a manual retry, archival, a provider change, or any superseding
turn transition settles a stale recovery as `invalidated` rather than letting
it fire against newer state; a dispatch the admission path refuses settles as
`failed`. The dispatch runs as the host, under the same per-process host
scope a [routine](#modes-chat-work-and-code) runs under, never through a
window: it resumes with no window open, and an open window lends it neither
identity nor Project binding. The admission path still rechecks the thread's
Project access (an inactive Project refuses and settles `failed`), mode, and
posture exactly as for a person's retry, and a Work resume refuses while Work
is turned off, since no window stands in for the mode switch; a Work continuation is journaled as
the host's `system` actor. Any approval the resumed turn raises is offered the
way a routine's is: a browser-origin or extension-tool prompt goes to every
local window that may drive that thread (one bound to the Project the prompt
recorded), and
answering settles only that prompt. This resume timer is deliberately narrow and separate from
[routines](#modes-chat-work-and-code): an in-process host timer over journaled
opt-ins that only continues a stopped turn — no cloud wake, no background claim
beyond the host's own running process, and no billing automation. A host that was down or unreachable at the reset instant
rescans `status = scheduled` rows on return and dispatches the still-valid
ones; a record that cannot be re-validated settles `invalidated` and never
re-arms.

A child AgentRun stopped by the same provider usage-limit signal parks as
`waiting` with the normalized `usageLimit` fact on the run — never `failed`,
which would report a bounded wait as a dead run and offer Retry where the
honest action is waiting out the reset. The fact rides the run's own
aggregate on `agent.run-status-changed@1`, so the run's row, the parent's
delegated-task read, and the managed `status`/`wait` tools all report the
limit and any armed recovery rather than a pending result or a perpetual
Working child. A run still parked on a journaled limit survives a host
restart as `waiting`, the same as a run waiting on its immutable pool
decision. The same explicit opt-in exists on the run: a person arms or
withdraws it through the same `usage-resume.*@1` journaled contract — the
record binds the run's id, its execution provider, and the disclosed reset —
and the provider or parent agent cannot arm it silently. Dispatch goes
through the ordinary `start` path with the parent thread's live grant
re-derived at dispatch time (a Code parent contributes its execution policy
only while still active), so capacity gating, authority clamps, workspace
checks, and approval freshness apply unchanged; a run whose parent grant is
gone settles `failed` instead of being orphaned awake. The run leaving its
waiting state for anything but the resume's own dispatch — cancellation,
subtree withdrawal, a different disclosed reset — settles the opt-in
`invalidated`; a wait re-entered on the same declared reset leaves it armed.
The settle journals `usage-resume.settled@1` on the run's aggregate and folds
the outcome back into the run, so the opt-in's version stays the aggregate
head and a stale `expectedVersion` cannot overwrite it.

Agent-to-agent messaging is a separate, host-delivered channel beside mention
excerpts and that Chat one-hop ask. A Code turn reaches it through the `send`,
`acknowledge`, and `receipts` operations of `octant_threads`, the tool it also
sees its sibling threads with (below). Its threats are recorded in
[security/agent-to-agent-messaging-threat-model.md](security/agent-to-agent-messaging-threat-model.md),
approved by the maintainer on 2026-10-12. This section is the effective rule.

- **Who may message whom.** A thread may message only another active thread of
  its own Project; any other id (unknown, another Project or mode, a child
  run, itself) refuses `unauthorized` in the same words, so a refusal never
  confirms a thread exists. Only Code turns are offered the messaging
  operations and a Project has one mode, so this means Code to Code inside one
  Project. Chat threads, Work threads, and child runs neither send nor
  receive: Work turns carry no messages, so a Work thread's `octant_threads`
  offers no `send` (see the rationale below). A recipient is named by the same
  `<thread id>@<project id>` reference `list` returns; one whose Project part
  is not the sender's current Project refuses `unauthorized` in the same
  words, even when its thread part names a thread the sender could reach, and
  is journaled as `agent.message-refused@1` like any refusal that names a
  recipient. The tool judges the raw recipient list before the delivery
  service sees it: more than four entries, any malformed reference, or any
  reference of another Project refuses the whole send, and nothing is sent to
  the rest.
- **Sending.** The messaging operations are left out of the enum of a turn in
  Plan and of a profile whose non-empty tool allowlist does not name
  `octant_threads.send`, and a call made anyway, or after the thread dropped to
  Plan mid-turn, is refused before anything is stored. A refusal made
  there, for a call that names a recipient, is journaled as
  `agent.message-refused@1` without a body. An admitted
  send journals `agent.message-sent@1` on the `agent-message` aggregate, one
  message per recipient, and keeps the body in the host's store under an
  opaque reference; bodies never enter the journal. The sender is told `sent`
  and nothing more: sending starts no turn, grants no authority, and returns
  no reply. Bounds are four recipients per send, a 64 KiB body, and eight
  messages per sender that no turn has carried yet; a waiting message whose
  recipient closed or left the Project is refused at the sender's next send,
  so it stops holding a slot.
- **Delivery.** Admission is not delivery. When the recipient's next Code turn
  assembles its context, the host rechecks that the sender is still active,
  that both threads still share a Project, and that the recipient is active,
  and journals `agent.message-refused@1` otherwise. A message that passes
  marks the recipient with `thread.external-content-ingested@1` and is added
  to that turn as one context block: a host sentence naming only the sender's
  thread id, then the body inside the shared external-data frame. A turn
  carries the oldest waiting messages up to 64 KiB, at least one, and the rest
  wait for the turn after. `agent.message-delivered@1` is journaled once the
  provider has accepted that turn's prompt and context, not when the turn was
  taken on: a turn that was refused, cancelled, or failed before its send, and
  a host that stopped before it, leave the message waiting for the next turn.
  Delivery is therefore at least once. A host that stops after the provider
  accepted the turn and before the event is appended carries the same message
  into the next turn too; a host stop never drops a message unread. The block
  reaches every Code provider the way a `#thread` mention does and is part of
  that turn only.
- **Bodies.** A body lives only while its message waits: delivery and refusal
  delete it, purging either thread deletes it with the message, and at start
  the host keeps only the bodies of waiting messages. A message an earlier
  host journaled as delivered without a turn carrying it stays as journaled
  and is never offered.
- **Acknowledgement and sender read-back.** The host-authored envelope names
  its immutable messageId. `octant_threads` takes explicit `acknowledge` and
  `receipts` operations for up to 20 durable IDs per call; `send` is always
  named. An acknowledgement is the current
  recipient reporting receipt: the host checks the exact delivered record,
  current sender and recipient Code authority and same-Project relationship.
  A sender cannot acknowledge its outgoing message or name another recipient;
  the caller thread comes from the running turn. Duplicate acknowledgements
  and replay retain one fact. Neither prompt acceptance nor turn completion
  automatically acknowledges a message. Acknowledgement proves no understanding
  or action. Sender status reads only that thread's own queued, delivered,
  acknowledged or refused metadata, never a body, target title or peer lookup.
  The authenticated existing facts route lists bounded recent receipts and
  refusals only for sender threads the window may open. Its provider-delivered
  count includes acknowledged messages; acknowledgement is a later receipt,
  not an additive delivery total. The messaging operations remain omitted and
  refused in Plan, on excluded profiles and cancelled turns; managed children,
  Chat and Work gain no messaging rights. Sending again, including retrying a
  send, creates a new durable message; receipt retries use the existing ID.
- **Expiry.** Each newly admitted message records an explicit deadline 24 hours after admission under the maintainer-approved lifetime policy. The host journals `agent.message-expired@1` before deleting a queued body or freeing its slot; expiry is a separate receipt and never counts as provider delivery or refusal. Delivery rechecks expiry before carrying a message, startup reconciles it, and a scoped host sweep checks at most once a minute. An append failure retains the body for retry. Older records without a deadline retain their existing lifetime; no timestamp is reinterpreted as consent. A message already journaled delivered or acknowledged does not expire. The Chat mention path is unchanged.
- **Refusals in the Agents center.** A refusal is journaled at the send, at
  the tool (a turn in Plan, a profile without the tool, a call with no
  message; a cancelled turn is not a refusal), and at delivery, with these
  limits. A send naming more than four recipients is refused as a whole and
  journaled for its first four. A turn journals each distinct (recipient,
  reason) refusal once and at most eight in all; past that a refusal is still
  the answer the sender gets but is not journaled, because every journaled
  refusal is read back at each start under a fixed scan bound and a model
  looping on a refused call must not fill it. A call too malformed to name a
  recipient is not journaled. The refusal event names its sender and
  recipient threads, because a message refused before admission has no
  `agent.message-sent@1` to say who sent it, and a purge of either thread
  takes the message aggregate with it, so a restart replays neither. The
  projection keeps the newest fifty such refusals per sender and counts the
  rest, beside the messages that were refused later. The Agents center lists
  the newest five with the sender, the thread named, the reason, and its age,
  and states how many more there are. The `/api/agent-messages` read is
  scoped by the sender thread: a window sees the counts and refusals only of
  messages sent by a thread it may open, asked afresh on every read and never
  remembered, so a refusal never reveals a thread to a window that could not
  already see its sender. The recipient id shown is the one the sender's own
  transcript holds. A refusal journaled before the event named its endpoints
  is not shown.

Seeing sibling threads is the read-only companion to messaging, approved by
the maintainer on 2026-10-13 and extended to Work on 2026-11-05, when the
maintainer folded messaging and the planner's board into the same tool. The
`octant_threads` tool lets a Work or Code turn see the other threads of its
own Project, and a Code turn message one or wait for one to finish. Its
operations are `help`, `list`, `read`, `wait`, and in Code `send`,
`acknowledge`, `receipts`, and the planner's `board`. No operation creates,
steers, completes, archives, or stops a thread.

- **Rationale for Work.** Work and Code share one authority model, so the
  read-only operations, which change nothing outside the caller's own record,
  reach Work under the same rules as Code. Messaging does not: a message is
  carried by the recipient's next turn, and only Code turns assemble that
  context, so a message to a Work thread would wait unread for good. Until a
  rule says how a Work turn carries, frames, and confirms a message, Work
  threads neither send nor receive, the most conservative reading of the
  approval.

- **Who may see whom.** The caller is a Work or Code thread's turn; the
  targets are the other threads of the same Project, which are all of its
  mode, that are neither completed nor archived (in Work also neither marked
  Done nor being deleted). Threads of another Project, the caller itself,
  child runs (they have the managed `status` and `wait`), deleted threads,
  every Chat thread, and a thread of the other mode are never listed or
  readable. The host decides the set from the
  caller's own thread on every call; the model supplies no Project, path, or
  window.
- **Operations.** `list` returns, for each target, a reference, the title, the
  state (`working`, `waiting-for-person`, or `idle`), and when the state last
  changed: at most 32 rows, most recently changed first, with `truncated`.
  `read` returns one target's title, state, and the same bounded transcript
  window a `#thread` mention resolves (12 messages within 8,000 characters,
  truncation stated), and no tool payloads beyond that window, files, or diff.
  `wait` returns when the target leaves `working`, or after the caller's
  timeout, 30 seconds by default and at most 120 like a child run's `wait`,
  with the state only; `working` in its answer means the time ran out.
- **References.** A reference is `<thread id>@<project id>`, the one form every
  operation names a thread by, `send` included: the thread part is the id
  messaging journals, and the Project part keeps the same text from ever
  naming a thread of another Project. It grants nothing; `read` and `wait` re-decide
  the set at the call, so a reference refuses once its thread is completed,
  archived, deleted, or in another Project than the one it was listed in, and
  it never resolves to a different thread. `read` decides again after its
  transcript read, and `wait` on every look, so a thread that closes or moves
  meanwhile refuses too, as does one the `#thread` mention read cannot serve.
  A reference does not carry the thread's working state, since `wait` exists
  to see that state change. Every reference outside the set, malformed text
  included, refuses `unauthorized` with one sentence, so a refusal confirms
  nothing outside the caller's Project. A call
  whose input fails the tool's schema (an unknown operation, an extra field, a
  timeout out of range, a reference over 128 characters), whose turn was
  cancelled, whose profile leaves the tool out, or whose caller is unknown,
  completed, or archived refuses `policy`; none depends on another thread.
  The caller and the turn are re-checked wherever the target is. Inside
  it, `list` makes the set visible on purpose; a `sent` answer from messaging
  already confirmed it.
- **Taint and framing.** A `read` or `list` answer joins the turn inside the
  shared external-data frame, like a delivered agent message. `read` and
  `list` (a title is text a person or an agent wrote) mark the caller with
  `thread.external-content-ingested@1` before the result returns, every time;
  a call that cannot be marked returns `unavailable` and nothing else. Each
  call journals its own mark, under the source label `sibling-thread`,
  whether or not the caller was already marked. `wait` returns a closed set
  of states and does not mark. A thread that lists its siblings therefore
  asks for single-use confirmation on risky actions afterwards, and that mark
  clears only by a person.
- **Offer and bounds.** The read operations are offered in Plan, since none
  changes anything outside the caller's own context, and left out for a
  profile whose non-empty allowlist does not name `octant_threads`; the tool is
  omitted when no operation is left. In Work they reach every turn whose
  provider carries app-managed tools, as Work's other tools do. A turn may make 8 `read` and 4 `wait`
  calls; the next refuses `rate-limited`. Every `read` and `wait` whose input
  decodes counts, refused or not, so probing references spends the same
  budget as reading them. `list` is not counted. Each answered `read` and
  `wait` is journaled as `thread.sibling-observed@1` on the reader's own
  `sibling-thread-observation` stream with reader, target, action, time, and
  the bytes returned, never the text; purging the reader purges it. A call
  the host cannot journal returns `unavailable` and nothing else. A refused
  call is not journaled, and `list` is recorded only by its mark.
- **Carriage.** The Code and Work runtimes add the tool to each turn's
  app-managed tool set, created once per turn so the bounds above are that
  turn's. It
  reaches the provider on the transport that runtime already uses for every
  app-managed tool: an in-process MCP server for Claude, dynamic tools for
  Codex, a loopback MCP bridge for ACP agents and OpenCode, a loopback
  custom-tool bridge for Pi, and function calling for direct endpoints. A thread whose runtime carries no
  app-managed tools (OpenCode without Octant's isolated
  configuration, an ACP agent that does not take the bridge, a direct-endpoint
  or Ollama model nobody verified for tools) is offered none, this one included. Child
  runs compose their own tool sets and are never offered it.
- **Facts.** The host answers from its own records on every call. Threads
  are the persisted Code threads, or the projected Work threads; a deleted
  thread's row is erased and a child run never has one, so neither resolves.
  A Work thread's state comes from the activity that files it on the Work
  board (a running turn is `working`; an open request, an interrupted turn,
  or a finished turn that asked the person to decide is
  `waiting-for-person`), its `stateChangedAt` from its newest turn, and its
  `read` from the Work `#thread` mention read. A Code thread's state comes
  from the evidence that files it on the Code board: running work is `working`;
  an unanswered approval or question, a step whose outcome is unconfirmed or
  that waits on a decision, an interrupted last turn, or a finished turn that
  asked the person to decide is `waiting-for-person`; anything else is
  `idle`. `stateChangedAt` is the newest update among the latest provider
  turn and every other runtime work record, or the thread's creation when it
  has never run; a turn parked on an approval keeps its running record, so
  its time is when that turn last moved. `read` takes its transcript from
  the Code `#thread` mention read for the window the turn runs for, judged on
  that window's standing authority like every Project check in a turn's tool
  call (see [Security and authority](#security-and-authority)).

### Projects with several folders

A Work or Code Project has one **main folder** (its bound root) and any
number of **extra folders** the person adds, up to 16 (maintainer decision,
2026-10-31). An extra folder gets the same access as the main folder at each
thread's [guardrail level](#security-and-authority). New tasks may choose an approved working folder; Code checkouts and Git remain bound to their own checkout. Built.

- **Adding and removing.** Only a person adds or removes one, from the
  Project page's folders card. Add folder… opens the native folder picker on
  desktop (the host folder browser elsewhere), which issues the same
  single-use binding receipt a Project's creation or relink consumes, so the
  path is the folder's real path and an agent, a routine, or an import never
  supplies one. `add-project-extra-folder` and `remove-project-extra-folder`
  journal `project.extra-folder-added@1` (the folder, who added it, and
  when) and `project.extra-folder-removed@1` (the folder, who removed it,
  and when), each with the whole Project after the change, so replay rebuilds
  the list. A Project journaled before the field existed replays with none.
- **Task working folder.** At creation, the person chooses a server-issued
  folder identity from the current Project and an optional relative subdirectory.
  The identity binds the Project's main binding revision and the extra folder's
  journaled addition revision; remove/re-add produces a new identity even if the
  path and timestamp match. A request supplies no arbitrary absolute root.
  The provider, terminal default, saved actions and new Work artifacts use this
  choice. The composer and Environment show it. The choice is immutable for that
  task, including its subdirectory; a different choice starts a new task. Existing
  threads without an identity retain their main-folder/checkout interpretation and
  their existing relative-directory control. This avoids resuming a retained native
  session against a different root. Missing, removed, relinked or replaced working
  folders refuse rather than redirect output. A running turn checks its selected
  identity and physical directory until settlement and cancels on revocation.
  An extra working folder is shared, including for a child worktree. Code Git,
  PRs, changed-file receipts and Review still describe that thread's primary
  checkout only; the UI states that limit.
- **What can be a folder.** The domain policy refuses the home folder and
  any folder above it, a system folder (`/`, `/System`, `/Library`, `/usr`,
  `/etc`, `/private`, `/Volumes` itself and their peers) or a folder inside
  a system-owned tree, a credential folder in home (`.ssh`, `.aws`,
  `.azure`, `.gnupg`, `.kube`, `.docker`, `.password-store`,
  `.config/gcloud`, `.config/gh`, `Library/Keychains`), anything inside or
  containing one of those, the main folder, a folder inside or around the
  main folder or another extra folder, and a seventeenth. Relinking the main
  folder onto or around an extra folder is refused until that folder is
  removed. A Chat Project has no folders.
- **What the folders grant.** Every place that confines a thread treats
  main and extra folders as the Project: the OS profiles give each extra
  folder exactly the main folder's rule at that level (Seatbelt reads, and
  writes or a trailing write denial; Bubblewrap a writable or read-only
  bind), Claude's sandbox lists them in its read and write allow lists and
  its `additionalDirectories`, Codex's wrapped profile and its approval
  scope include them, OpenCode's session rules allow reaching them as a
  folder of the session rather than an outside directory, ACP and Pi
  profiles bind them, and the Octant Harness file tools accept an absolute
  path in one, and Octant Shield's fast rules allow reads and edits in one
  as in the main folder (its command rules keep to the main folder). Plan
  reads them and writes none, as it does the main folder.
  Full access stays unwrapped. The deny rules for secrets and the
  `DEFAULT_DENY_READ_PATHS` refusal of ancestor roots apply to extra folders
  unchanged. A folder missing on disk at launch is left out of the profile
  rather than failing it. The lease or connection a runtime reuses is keyed
  by its folders, and a change applies from the next turn. A Codex thread
  that resumes after its folders changed first closes the idle lease of the
  same root and mode that still holds it, as after a posture change.
- **What the agent is told.** The runtime only sees its working directory,
  so each Work and Code turn carries an instruction naming the extra folders
  by absolute path and saying that commands, Git and checkouts start in the
  main folder.
- **Code.** Worktrees, checkouts, Git and pull requests stay keyed to the
  main folder; an extra folder is a plain folder with no checkout
  management. Language services, debug sessions and repository tests do
  cover an extra folder: a file there is named by its absolute path, and the
  root authority places it in one of the Project's current extra folders (and
  refuses any other absolute path) after resolving the checkout, so a window,
  thread or checkout the main authority refuses reaches no extra folder. A
  language server or debug adapter for such a file runs with the folder as its
  own bound root, in a server keyed by the folder; the folder has no file
  watch, and a debug session's breakpoints and stack frames belong to the
  folder its program runs in, so one session never spans two folders. Test
  discovery also reads each existing extra folder's `package.json` and
  `.octant/tests.json`, with ids of their own and the folder's absolute path
  as the working directory; a run starts there, with that folder as its root
  for artifacts, and the sandbox binds the folder as it binds the checkout. Octant's own shell port
  for the harness starts in the main folder but reads and writes each extra
  folder as it does the main one, and the ACP client file and terminal tools
  accept an absolute path or working directory inside an extra folder and
  bind every Project folder for the command they launch; a path outside all
  of them is refused. The editor and the Files explorer open, read and save
  a file in an extra folder under the same checkout authority and the same
  confinement as the checkout's own: the request names the file by absolute
  path, the root authority places it in one of the Project's current extra
  folders after resolving the checkout, and the folder is then the file's
  root. The explorer lists each extra folder as its own tree beneath the
  checkout's, labelled with the folder's last component. The explorer watches
  the checkout and all sixteen eligible extra folders over one shared authenticated
  stream per thread/window authority. Duplicate views share that stream; the host
  shares an OS watcher for the same physical root. Each notice identifies its root
  and names paths relative to it. The host rechecks the current binding and folder
  membership before registration and delivery; removal or relink ends the stream.
  Reconnection and truncated notices reconcile every visible tree. Language services
  watch extra roots too and reconcile open documents after a dropped watch.
  Requests may name only the checkout or an exact current extra root; a child path
  is refused. A save there is
  journaled like any other save of the thread.
- **Terminals and Project actions.** A Project terminal starts in the main
  folder unless the person picks an extra folder. A saved action previews its
  host-resolved task working folder when selected, otherwise the active checkout
  in a Code thread. Work task actions and new terminals use their task folder;
  Project-level actions without a task use the main folder. The action's directory is relative to that
  folder. Explicit picks accept only the main folder or an extra folder the
  Project record lists, compared as the exact path. See the Project actions
  rule under [Security and authority](#security-and-authority). Every Project terminal
  binds all of the Project's folders that exist like the main folder, so the
  shell can move between them; the pick only chooses where it starts. The
  header's action buttons and the start screen's quick tools offer the pick
  once a Project has an extra folder. A Code thread's terminal binds every
  Project folder that exists as a Project terminal does, and its start command
  may name an extra folder to start in, compared as the exact path the Project
  lists; the host refuses any other, and a folder missing on disk is left out
  of the binding. The Terminal tab's menu offers **Restart in** each extra
  folder (a Project with none shows no pick, and Plan shows none). The pick
  opens a confirmation naming the destination and explaining that restart stops
  the shell and every command running in it. Only an explicit confirmation stops
  it; Cancel preserves it, and New terminal offers a separate shell when available.
  This terminal-only choice does not change the task's recorded working folder.
  The first terminal a task opens starts in its recorded working directory.
- **Work files.** A path relative to the main folder is always the main
  folder's; a file in an extra folder is named by its absolute path, and the
  host honours an absolute path only inside one of the Project's current
  extra folders, never anywhere else. The Work Files listing walks the main
  folder and then each extra folder under the same confinement and bounds,
  names an extra folder's entries by absolute path, and opens one through a
  preview token that resolves to that folder. The Work overview's folder
  list adds each extra folder's top level after the main folder's, sharing
  the item limit and naming each by its last component, so it carries no
  host path. A turn's record of the files that changed while it ran watches
  every folder the same way, so a file written in an extra folder lists as
  Work's own. An artifact the host creates for a Work thread takes a name with
  no path and is placed in the folder that thread works in: its working
  directory relative to its selected approved root, read from the thread by
  the host and never from the create request. Without a thread it goes to the
  main folder. The artifact's record retains its folder identity and relative
  destination, so revise, rename, conversion, export and preview continue there
  after replay; a later thread change cannot retarget it. Removing/re-adding or
  relinking that root refuses these operations without a fallback. Legacy records
  without an identity retain their main-folder interpretation.
- **`@file` picker and Code search.** A mention is the main folder's relative
  path or the absolute path of a file inside one of the Project's current
  extra folders; the host reads an absolute path only there and reports any
  other as out of root. The picker lists each existing extra folder with the
  main folder under the same confinement and root identity checks, and the
  Code picker offers those files by absolute path. Code search walks the
  checkout and then each extra folder under the shared budgets, and a match
  there carries its folder; choosing it opens the file in the editor by the
  folder's path joined to the match's.

## Agent task display

Providers that report their own task plans (Claude, Codex, ACP, OpenCode) emit
`task-progress` runtime events, and the host journals them. Claude's checklist
is its `TodoWrite` tool: the driver offers it in every posture, Plan included,
and lets it run unasked, because it changes only Claude's own session state
(no file, shell, network, or person). Each call restates the whole list, and
a task id follows a list position, so the panel keeps Claude's latest order and
wording.

`task-progress` adds or updates one task. Because every one of these providers
restates its whole plan, each restatement ends with a `task-list` event naming
the ids the plan now holds, in order (at most 64, the per-turn task cap). Each
surface keeps only those tasks, in that order, so a step the provider drops
leaves the panel, a moved step moves, and an empty list clears it. `task-list`
belongs to the `taskProgress` capability: a driver that reports it supported
may send either kind. Code journals it as its own operation event; Chat and
Work fold it into the list they already journal whole. A journal written before
`task-list` existed holds only `task-progress` and replays exactly as it did,
dropped steps included.

Each thread surface shows the agent's restated plan as a live "N of M tasks
completed" panel while any task is open or the turn is still writing: Code from its journaled
operation events, Chat from `ChatAttempt.tasks` carried on
`chat.attempt-updated@1`, and Work from `WorkTurnState.tasks` journaled on
`work.turn-updated@1` with a live `turn-tasks` stream frame. The panel is a
projection of journaled state, never a renderer-owned plan; per-step detail
stays in the transcript's activity rows.

## Tool calls in Chat and Work

Every mode shows a turn's tool calls as the same compact group in the
transcript (see [DESIGN.md](../DESIGN.md) Transcript). Code replays them from
its journaled `tool-activity` events. Chat and Work record exactly the same
step per tool call and nothing more: the provider's tool call id, the tool
name, a state (`started`, `running`, `completed`, `failed`), and an optional
progress or result message of at most 2048 bytes, redacted before it is kept. No tool
input and no tool output is captured, except the `published` page a call put
outside this host (its `https` address and title, and the host's own snapshot
of the file it sent; today only a Claude artifact), which Code's
`tool-activity` and its conversation steps carry too and the transcript shows
as a link card beside the drawn snapshot. A turn keeps at most 64 steps in arrival
order and sets a truncated flag when it called more. Chat carries them as
`ChatAttempt.toolSteps` on `chat.attempt-updated@1`; Work carries them as
`WorkTurnState.toolSteps` journaled with the settled `work.turn-updated@1`,
with a live `turn-tools` stream frame while the turn runs. That frame restates
every step at each change, so it carries a published page's link but not its
snapshot (up to 256 KiB, resent once per later tool event); the snapshot
arrives with the settled turn. They live on the
attempt or turn record, so they are thread content and purging the thread
removes them with it. Both fields are optional, so a turn saved before they existed
still decodes, and the group draws nothing for a turn that called no tool. This
changes rendering and recording only; Chat's and Work's authority, and Work's
shell posture, are unchanged.

### Web search

Octant has one web search, `web-search` (`WEB_SEARCH_TOOL_DEFINITION`): one
name, one argument schema, and one result shape wherever a model meets it. It
searches the SearXNG endpoint in Chat settings for a query of 1 to 512
characters and returns that query with each result's title, URL, and snippet,
5 results unless the call asks for 1 to 10. It opens no page.

- **Where.** A Chat thread is offered it on every provider while its research
  is on and its research route is ready through SearXNG; a provider-native
  route uses the provider's own search instead. The native harness offers the
  same definition as its own tool in Work and Code, and in Chat under the
  same research grant ([Native harness](#native-harness)). A harness Chat
  thread gets it once, from the harness's own tool set: the turn adds no second
  copy beside it.
- **Invalid queries.** A call with a missing, empty, blank, or over-long query
  is refused as `invalid-query` and searches nothing. It never stands in
  other text for the query: Chat's earlier search, `octant_web_research`,
  searched the person's whole prompt when the query was missing, sending text
  they never meant as a query to the search service. A search the endpoint
  does not answer comes back to the model as `search-failed` rather than
  ending the turn.
- **Outside content.** A successful result marks the thread as having read
  outside content. On a harness thread the call also passes the harness's
  tool-call policy, which refuses a tainted thread's query that looks like it
  carries data ([Search queries on a tainted thread](design/search-query-taint.md));
  a Chat thread on another provider searches through its research route, as
  its search did before, without that refusal.
- **Rationale for the name.** `web-search` was already the harness's tool, with
  its policy, Plan rule, and outside-content label keyed to it. Giving every
  Chat provider that name, rather than keeping `octant_web_research` beside it,
  is what lets a harness Chat thread carry one search instead of two, one of
  which skipped the taint rule. The earlier label `octant_web_research` still
  reads in a journaled outside-content list.

## Workspace shell

[Workspace behavior](design/workspace.md) owns navigation, Projects, panes,
content tabs, dock tools, and their presentation lifecycle. [DESIGN.md](../DESIGN.md)
owns their visual treatment. Those current specifications replace the earlier
shell and visual-language migration descriptions; server authority and durable
state remain owned by the architectural sections here.

### Zen assistant tool

Zen's assistant arranges the Zen space in front of its window through one
family, `octant_zen`, offered only to the Chat thread bound as that space's
assistant on that window ([Workspace](design/workspace.md)); no other thread,
and no other window's space, is reachable through it.

- **Operations.** `get-space` returns the space's version, its dimming and
  element opacity, and each element's id, kind, title, geometry, stacking, and
  whether it is minimized, and nothing of what a note, checklist, or pinned
  thread says. `search-threads` finds threads this window can open, and
  `pin-thread` pins one as a card. `create-widget` adds an empty Notes,
  Checklist, or Timer widget, the only kinds it can create; a recipe widget
  comes only from `preview-recipe`, whose preview creates nothing until the
  person confirms it in Zen, expires after ten minutes or when the space
  changes, and is limited to four open at once. `place-element` moves,
  resizes, focuses, minimizes, restores, or removes an element, and
  `update-appearance` changes dimming and element opacity. `help` returns the
  full usage without touching the space.
- **Versions.** Every change names the version it applies to
  (`expectedVersion`) and returns the new one. A change against an out-of-date
  version changes nothing and comes back as a `conflict` carrying the space's
  current version, so a model reads the space again and retries rather than
  failing blind. `get-space` is how a model learns the version and element ids
  before its first change.
- **Authority.** The host decides every call against the window's own space and
  the assistant binding; input naming a window or space is refused. A timer
  runs at most eight hours (25 minutes by default).
  A successful result is journaled as outside content under `octant_zen`; the
  seven tools it replaced were journaled under their own `octant_zen_*` names,
  which still read.
- **Plugin switch.** Zen is a bundled first-party plugin (`zen`, a `ui-surface`
  component allowed in every mode) that is on by default. While it is off, the
  host refuses every `/api/zen` route, including the background routes, with a
  typed `plugin-disabled` result, offers no `octant_zen` tool to any thread, and
  the renderer cannot open Zen. Switching it off deletes nothing: layouts,
  backgrounds, focus zones, and events stay on disk and reappear when it is
  turned back on. The built-in background catalog stays in the host because app
  backdrops use it too.

## Persistence

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  cmd["Command<br/>(validated by contracts)"] --> policy["Domain policy<br/>mode · capability · authority"]
  policy --> version["Expected aggregate version"]
  version --> append["Append events<br/>(atomic, versioned envelope)"]
  append --> journal[("event_journal<br/>aggregate_heads")]
  journal --> proj["Projections<br/>(idempotent, checkpointed)"]
  proj --> read[("Read tables<br/>chat · work · code · project · usage · theme · …")]
  append --> publish["Publish committed sequence"]
  publish --> reactors["Reactors<br/>provider turns · tools · subagents"]
  read --> clients["Renderer / remote clients"]
  journal -. "db:rebuild" .-> proj
```

- **Store.** One SQLite file under `OCTANT_DATA_DIR` (default
  `~/Library/Application Support/Octant`), created with owner-only permissions.
  A single narrow SQLite port has two adapters — `bun:sqlite` in production
  and `better-sqlite3` for the Node portability smoke — that pass the same
  conformance suite. Journal, migration, and projection code depend only on
  the port. Both adapters run the store in WAL mode with `synchronous = FULL`:
  a Chat reply's streamed deltas batch into one journal commit per short burst,
  so the authoritative journal fsyncs a bounded number of times per second
  instead of once per token, and a power loss loses at most the burst that was
  still open — never a committed one.
  Settings → Data & storage exposes a read-only, server-authoritative data
  map of those locations (and per-Project facts) so a person can see what
  this host stores without opening a document. Categories the host cannot
  verify are `unknown`; the map never carries secret values.
- **Envelope.** Every event carries schema version, event id, aggregate id and
  version, global sequence, correlation and causation ids, actor, host id, and
  timestamp. Unknown or future events are quarantined rather than dropped.
- **Projections.** Each feature owns its projection and persistence schema
  (`persistence/*Projection.ts`, `*PersistenceSchema.ts`). Projections are
  checkpointed by sequence, detect lag, and can be rebuilt individually or
  wholesale (`db:status`, `db:verify`, `db:rebuild`). A projection whose state
  lives only in process memory (AgentRuns, Canvases, image jobs, managed
  GitHub clones, artifact replicas) declares `holdsStateInMemory` and replays
  from the start of the journal at every host start, because its stored
  checkpoint describes the previous process rather than this one. It names
  the aggregate types it applies, and that replay reads only those rows.
  Automations are also in memory; the host rebuilds them with their own
  hydration after catch-up instead, which leaves them empty and reported
  unloaded rather than partial when it cannot finish (see the next item).
- **Startup hydration reads a store's own rows.** Every in-memory store and
  projection rebuilds at start from its own aggregate types, read in journal
  order through the (type, sequence) index, so no store reads, decodes, or
  counts another store's rows: a journal dominated by Code turn frames (one
  row per streamed provider delta) cannot lock out an unrelated store or slow
  its start. The start-up compatibility check still decodes every row, so a
  row that no longer decodes stops the start as before. Each scan cap counts
  only the store's own rows, and what passing it does differs by store:
  - Work threads, Work settings, Work turns, Work artifacts, and agent
    messages apply rows one batch at a time under a 1,000,000-row cap, and
    refuse to start the host past it.
  - Work promotions and workflows collect every frame in memory before
    applying them, keep a 100,000-row cap, and refuse to start the host past
    it.
  - Work research keeps a 100,000-row cap; past it the host starts and
    research reports unavailable.
  - Automations apply rows one batch at a time under the 1,000,000-row cap.
    Past it the host still starts, but the Automation list reports that
    history could not be loaded (the Automation Center says so and that
    nothing is scheduled), Automation commands are refused, and the
    scheduler does not start, so nothing fires against history the host never
    read. The journal is untouched; the state clears on a start that can read
    it.
  - Work requests and the uncapped stores read all of their own rows.
- **Reads while a window is open stay off the full journal.** Every service
  checks that the store is usable before each read, and that check answers
  from the latest store inspection (the integrity check plus a decode of every
  journal row): the one startup ran, or a newer one host diagnostics asked
  for. It never starts one itself. A Code thread's whole operation history,
  which the board, the sidebar's pull-request join and child observations
  read every few seconds, is read through a (type, thread, sequence) index
  and kept decoded between reads: a later read decodes only the rows appended
  since, and a thread whose slice shrank (a purge) is read afresh. The kept
  histories are shared by every reader of the journal and bounded at 100,000
  frames across threads, least recently read dropped first. A Chat thread's
  events stream holds the same rule: its frames journal on several aggregates —
  the thread's own events, its work-list and follow-up entries, and the context
  ledger that settles a compaction — all keyed by the thread id, so the stream
  reads each slice through the (type, aggregate, sequence) index (migration 89)
  instead of replaying the global journal, and a held stream that wakes on every
  machine change decodes only its own thread's rows.
- **Migrations.** Ordered, forward-only, checksum-verified, applied in
  transactions before the server reports ready. A changed checksum or an
  unknown newer migration fails closed; a store backup is taken before a
  migration runs. Restart integration tests prove replay per feature.
- **Untrusted-content taint.** Browser observations, tool results, and imported
  external content that already carry tainting provenance append
  `thread.external-content-ingested@1` with thread identity and bounded source
  labels. Raw bodies never enter the payload; a provider runtime's own web tools
  append it too, as the next item describes. The thread-lifetime taint
  projection rebuilds from the journal; session, turn, and restart boundaries
  never clear it. Irreversible or authority-bearing actions on a tainted thread
  still require fresh confirmation after replay. That gate follows the
  thread's [guardrail level](#security-and-authority): on at Guarded and
  Reviewed, and off at Full access, where the mark is recorded and shown
  but never prompts or blocks;
  a person turns it down for one thread by setting its level, or for a
  Project's new threads by setting the Project's level, in Work and Code
  alike, and back up the same way (`outsideContentRecordedOnly`). No
  switch turns it down at a level below Full access: the gate is what keeps
  a marked thread's irreversible calls asking there, so turning it down
  means choosing Full access for that scope. The mark
  itself is recorded at every level, because the journal records what came
  in. One gate enforces it today:
  `resolveThreadElevation` in `packages/domain/src/toolCallPolicy.ts` asks
  afresh, under every posture below Full access that allows the tool at all,
  for each closed-catalog entry marked `irreversibleUnderTaint`
  (MCP tools, computer-use, the harness's `web-fetch`, `bash`, `edit`,
  `write`, and `goal-check`); Plan refuses all of these but `web-fetch`
  before that check. At Full access in Work and Code the taint is recorded only (see
  [modes](#modes-chat-work-and-code)). A contract test refuses a catalog entry in a
  destructive, credential, outside-Project, or privilege-expansion class
  without that flag. A Code Git action a person takes from a window is that
  person's own per-action act, and no agent tool issues one.
  The prompt that asks says why. A harness approval asked for the thread's
  own call (`singleUse`), an MCP tool prompt, and a Computer use approval on
  a marked thread carry `outsideContent`: the sources that marked it, most
  recently read first, each with its read count and first and last read
  time, at most eight, and the total number of sources. The host reads them
  from the ingestion projection when it asks; no client supplies them, and
  they hold labels and times only, never content or a content reference. The
  web, phone, and terminal prompts say the thread took in outside content,
  so the call is approved once, and list them in the words the Clear review
  uses (one definition in `@octant/domain`), ahead of the answer controls.
  The full-screen terminal panel cannot scroll, so it runs the source names
  and counts together on a few wrapped lines and leaves times to the plain
  prompt and `--json`.
  The collapsed Computer use strip never offers Approve for a marked
  approval: it offers a review that opens the full prompt. A
  Computer use approval the host gates as marked but whose sources it cannot
  read carries an empty list, so it still says so. A child run's approval
  names no sources: it is never remembered in the first place.
- **Provider runtimes' own web tools.** A runtime's built-in web search or page
  fetch, or a tool the model's provider runs on its own servers, hands its
  result to the model without Octant seeing it. The adapter reports the call
  as a normalized `outside-content-read` event when it first sees it:
  `web-search`, `web-fetch`, or `hosted-tool`, the runtime's tool name, and the
  query or address as one redacted line bounded in UTF-16 units, when the
  runtime gave one. A call that later fails, is denied, or is cancelled may
  already have returned a page, so the start marks. A driver may report it
  whether or not it reports tool activity.
  - Chat, Work, and Code turn runners mark the thread. A child run's runner
    marks the run's own id, which is where its harness tools read the mark.
    Each runner marks before it looks at its event budget or a Stop, since
    the read reached the model either way.
  - The label is `runtime-web-search`, `runtime-web-fetch`, or
    `runtime-hosted-tool`, with origin `tool-result`. The reference is
    opaque: `runtime-web-`, the tool's name when it is a plain identifier, and
    a SHA-256 of the tool, the turn, the call, and the query or address. No
    query, address, or page content is journaled.
  - A mark that cannot be recorded stops the turn, because the content has
    already reached the model. The read stays owed in the host process: the
    thread's next turn records it before it starts, or is refused with the
    same reason, so retrying cannot resume the provider session that read it
    while the thread is unmarked. A host restart forgets what is owed.
  - Marking does not gate a tool the runtime executes itself. A Code turn
    whose approvals the runtime's own reviewer answers (harness auto-review)
    is stopped at the mark and tells the person why, because the reviewer was
    chosen for the session while the thread was unmarked. The next turn
    starts without it, as auto-review is off on a marked thread.
  - A single-shot request (a context summary, a hand-off document, a commit or
    pull-request draft, a harness single shot) has no thread of its own to
    mark, so an answer written after such a read is not used.
  - Codex: its `webSearch` item, on `item/started`. A start may carry an empty
    query. Octant does not switch Codex's web search off.
  - OpenCode: `webfetch`, `websearch`, and `codesearch`, and any call its
    provider executed (`provider.executed`, or `executed` on the 2.0.22
    stream), on `tool.called`. A call a person then denies has already marked.
  - ACP agents: a tool call whose kind is `fetch`, or whose kind is `search`
    with a `rawInput.query` and no path, pattern, glob, or other place to
    look, the first time the agent reports it. A web search an agent reports
    under `search` with a path-like input, or with no `query`, is not marked;
    `search` also covers local file searches, so that residual stays.
  - Claude: `WebSearch` and `WebFetch`, on the call's first content block,
    and the same two inside one of Claude's own subagents, read from the
    subagent's reply. The driver offers both only to a session that carries
    the person's own setup with web tools on
    ([Key providers run as themselves](#providers)), asks before each below
    Full access, and refuses a session that reports either otherwise.
  - Pi and the direct endpoints have no built-in web tool. Pi is launched with
    only its file and shell tools, and a direct endpoint fails a turn whose
    stream carries a hosted or server-side tool's output.
- **Clearing taint.** Taint keeps its thread lifetime, and a person at a local
  window may clear it. A clear records that they reviewed what the thread read.
  - It appends `thread.external-content-cleared@1` on the thread's
    `thread-external-content` aggregate with actor `local-user`. The payload
    holds the thread, the window, the cleared source labels, and the ingestion
    count, never content.
  - The request names the aggregate version the person was shown. A newer
    ingestion refuses it as `stale`; an untainted thread answers
    `already-clear` and journals nothing. It is refused while the thread's
    turn is running or queued, when its last turn ended without the host
    learning how (Code's `ambiguous`), and when the thread's own mode cannot
    be read for that window. A message still in the thread's message queue
    counts as a queued turn, whether the queue is moving, paused, or held.
    The message queue answers all of this for every mode, and the check and
    the append run under its per-thread ordering, so a send through the queue
    cannot land between them.
  - Only the local-only `POST /api/thread-external-content` clears. Its `read`
    returns each source with its count and first and last time, and the
    version a clear must name. The private listener answers a paired device
    404, the handler refuses a paired device and the host's own scope, and the
    route sits on the loopback chain only. No tool, command, model output,
    structured reference, agent message, or host-run turn (routine, goal
    loop, usage-limit resume, child-run delivery) can clear.
  - The mark is keyed by the bare thread id, and Chat, Work, and Code
    threads share one id space: the journal refuses to start a thread under an
    id another mode's thread already holds, so a client-chosen id cannot share
    another mode's mark or, by being purged, erase it. A mark that threads of
    two modes already share (history from before that check) cannot be told
    apart, so a clear of it is refused as `thread-unavailable`.
  - One clear covers that thread and only it. A child run and a fork keep
    their own taint; a Code fork, a Chat branch or restore, a follow-up or
    side task, and a thread confirmed from a planner proposal start with their
    source's mark when they are made, and a mention or Side Chat of a marked
    thread marks the thread reading it (see the Code fork rule under Modes).
    A Canvas written while its writer was marked keeps that mark after the
    writer is cleared, and marks the next thread that reads it.
  - Measured deterministic Auto/Shield scenario (2026-11-06): research ingestion,
    an in-root edit, then the declared local `bun run test` command produces zero
    outside-content prompts with or without a person clearing after review. A
    subsequent GET to a configured safe network produces one such prompt without
    clear and zero after clear. This is a policy/journal fixture measurement,
    not a live provider turn count; provider-owned review can differ. It gives
    no basis for weakening taint policy or recommending Full access.
  - A clear removes the mark only. Nothing leaves the model's context and the
    provider session is not restarted, so what the thread read can still steer
    the model.
  - A clear holds for nothing. The next ingestion taints the thread again,
    including a content reference recorded before the clear: the clear
    forgets the thread's ingestion rows, which are what deduplicate a
    reference. Until then everything taint was gating applies as on an
    untainted thread: Full access, remembered harness approval classes,
    remembered MCP tool grants, computer-use grants, auto-review, and helper
    starts.
  - It covers every mode and provider because it changes only Octant's own
    gate. It cannot cover a provider runtime's own tools: those run under the
    runtime's approvals and sandbox, and a clear changes nothing about them.
  - On replay a clear deletes the thread's ingestion rows and zeroes its taint
    row, and the projection ignores an event at or below the last one it
    applied for that thread. A journal without the event replays unchanged.
  - The surface is one notice in the composer of a Chat, Work, or Code thread
    that a local window has open, drawn only while the thread is marked, with a
    Review action. The notice reads the mark when the thread opens and again
    when a turn starts or settles. Review lists the sources in plain words
    with their counts and times (a row projected before the host recorded
    times shows none), says that clearing removes nothing the model read and
    that the next outside content marks the thread again, and holds Clear the
    mark back while a turn is running or messages are queued. Every refusal
    is shown as its own sentence, and a `stale` one reloads the list. A client
    that is not on a loopback host (`externalContentAvailable`) neither
    reads nor draws it. Approval prompts do not yet say that the mark is why
    they ask: neither the MCP tool approval view nor the harness approval
    carries that reason.
- **Browser captures.** Only a screenshot the agent asks for with the browser
  tool, or the person takes with the Browser pane's Screenshot control, is kept
  with the thread that owns the Browser, and so is a short recording (an
  animated PNG) of the agent's page during one call that asked for it with
  `record`. The bytes live in the host's managed
  attachment store and the journal holds only a reference, the page origin, URL,
  title, content hash, and time. A thread keeps its newest 32 captures and they
