  - Consent is one explicit submission in the card. Host-generated privacy
    text describes this specific consumer, not a general guarantee about every
    tool. A future credential-bearing command needs a separate consumer and
    its ordinary execution approval; it cannot reuse this card's grant.
    Administrator passwords and arbitrary command/file delivery are not
    supported. The person may instead submit a field reference from an already
    linked 1Password store. The authenticated broker reads that exact reference
    once, checks its link revision before and after lookup, and returns transient
    material only to the host's already claimed card operation. The host rechecks
    expiry and authority after lookup and before network dispatch. No reusable
    slot or reference is saved. Lookup failures consume the card and show a
    bounded actionable cause; a new card requires new consent. There is no
    automatic linking, unlocking, fallback or retry. Item references resolve at
    use, including rotated values, under the existing linked-store rules.

<a id="linked-secret-stores"></a>

- **Linked secret stores.** A person may link a secret store they already use
  and point a credential at an item in it. Octant never holds the value: the
  broker fetches it at use, returns it to the one caller that asked, and drops
  it. Built for the 1Password CLI; the seam is a closed list of adapters
  ([`linkedSecretStores.ts`](../packages/host-runtime/src/linkedSecretStores.ts)),
  each answering `probe` and `read`, so another tool (the Bitwarden CLI, a macOS
  Keychain item) is a new adapter and no change to the broker, the journal, or
  Settings.
  - **Link.** Settings › Secret stores sends `link-store` to the host-only
    `/api/secret-stores/commands` route (a local window; `/api/secret-stores` is
    a remote local-only prefix, so a paired device is refused). The broker's
    `/v1/secret-stores/link` links a store only while its tool is installed and
    the store is open, and records the store and the link time in
    `secret-stores/linked-secret-stores.json` in the data directory (mode 0600,
    removed by a complete-data removal). A locked store, a missing tool, or an
    unreachable store is reported as a value (`store-locked`,
    `tool-not-installed`, `store-unavailable`) and nothing is linked. Unlinking
    leaves every pointer in place and makes each fail closed
    (`linked-store-not-linked`) until the store is linked again.
  - **Point.** `point-provider-key` names a provider instance, a store, and an
    item reference. The host accepts it only for an instance that sends an API
    key or bearer token, only after the broker proved the item resolves right
    now (a locked store or missing item refuses and writes nothing), and never
    over a key the person stored: that refuses as `key-already-stored`, so the
    person removes it first. The pointer replaces only another pointer.
    The host rereads the provider after the item check: a provider removed or
    reconfigured meanwhile has already had its key cleared, so the new pointer is
    deleted and the change refused (`provider-changed`), the same protection the
    pasted-key route applies, so a delayed write never sends an old endpoint's
    key to a new one.
    A connector's secret does the same: in Add an MCP server, a secret row
    marked "From 1Password" sends `linked: { store, reference }` with an empty
    value, the host points the generated secret id at the item (refusing the add
    when the store is locked or the item is missing) and journals it with a
    `connector-secret` target, and removing the server clears and journals the
    pointer. The id resolves through the broker's connector namespace; no other
    namespace follows a pointer, and no route returns one as a value. A pasted value that looks like a pointer is
    refused by the broker's `set`, and the desktop's key operations refuse to
    replace or edit a pointer, so a reference changes only through the
    journaled route.
  - **Use.** The provider's existing path asks the broker to resolve the
    instance id. The broker reads the pointer, runs the adapter (for `op`:
    `op read --no-newline <reference>`, with the reference validated as an
    `op://vault/item[/section]/field` address and passed as one argument, never
    through a shell, with Octant's own `OCTANT_*` variables removed from the
    tool's environment, a timeout, and a size bound), and returns the value in
    that response alone. The tool's own words are read once to classify the
    outcome and dropped. A fetch is never cached: a rotated item is used at the
    next request.
  - **Failure is a value and fails closed.** `locked`, `missing`, `unavailable`,
    `not-linked`, and `invalid-reference` each answer with a typed cause and no
    value, and the provider's turn fails with its existing unauthenticated or
    unavailable state and a message that names the store and never an item or a
    value. There is no fallback to a stored copy, a file, or an environment
    variable.
  - **Journal.** `secret-store.recorded@1` on one host-wide aggregate
    ([`secretStoresJournal.ts`](../apps/server/src/secretStores/secretStoresJournal.ts),
    [`secretStores.ts` contract](../packages/contracts/src/secretStores.ts))
    records `secret-store.linked`, `secret-store.unlinked`,
    `credential-reference.set` (store, reference, whether it replaced one) and
    `credential-reference.cleared`, each with the local window id. A reference
    names an item and is journaled; the value is not an input to any record, and
    the schema rejects any other field. A change is made and then journaled; when
    the journal refuses, a link or a new reference is undone and the answer says
    nothing changed, and an unlink or clear that cannot be recorded says it was
    made but not recorded. An earlier pointer is put back through the broker's
    `restore`, which writes the pointer without reading its item (the item may be
    gone or its store locked by then); if it cannot be put back, the new pointer
    is removed and the answer says so, so an unjournaled pointer never stays
    active. Google command-line selection additionally records
    `credential-reference.requested` before dispatch, after fresh local-window
    admission. This is the person's exact consent, not proof that the broker
    committed a change. An unknown reply tells the person to read the current
    account; it is never reported as an unchanged or confirmed selection.
  - **Browser credential-use permission.** Vendor partner autofill access for
    Octant is unverified and is not assumed or required by this CLI-backed
    binding. No partner signup or extension compatibility is implied.
    A local window may review a selected
    1Password account/vault/item and record a distinct
    `browser-credential-grant`, never an OAuth identity or a store unlock.
    The Browser derives the owning task, Project, profile and exact HTTPS
    origin, including port, from a live native context. Review and save need
    its sign-in or take-over hold. This first binding supports only the top
    frame; iframe targets, paired clients, unattended callers and headless
    contexts are refused. Arbitrary page scripts remain a separate capability.
    The broker requests only the selected item with explicit `--account` and
    `--vault` IDs. CLI item JSON may contain concealed values; the adapter
    projects only IDs, bounded title, item version and saved HTTPS origins.
    Metadata responses contain no field values, OTPs, raw JSON or diagnostics. Missing,
    malformed, non-HTTPS or more than eight saved websites refuse uncertainty;
    excess URLs are never silently dropped. A separate broker-session/link
    revision prevents a relink from matching earlier metadata. Legacy
    two-field credential pointers retain their strict decoder and behavior.
    Permission is scoped to one Project's eligible threads, or the stricter
    task/context. Private permits only task/context; Personal remains
    Project-bound. The reference-only grant and revocations are journaled;
    live grants are memory-only, expire at host restart or after eight hours,
    and are never restored from journal history. Website cookies do not renew
    them. Clearing a profile invalidates its reviews and grants.
    A saved grant is a permission snapshot, not executable credential
    authority. Metadata and page reads are separate observations, not an
    atomic transaction. Changed account/item version, link revision, site,
    frame or profile refuses matching on the next read; changed matching
    metadata removes and journals the grant. No immediate background
    invalidation is promised.
    Every fill revalidates the grant, selected account/item version, link
    revision, current held owner, profile and exact top document/form before
    use. The person reviews the username/current-password labels and exact
    submission/return origins, then approves **Fill selected fields**. Both
    exact origins, including ports, must appear in fresh selected-item metadata
    before the native reservation admits a private read. Missing sites require
    manual sign-in or the person correcting the item’s saved websites; Octant
    does not change metadata automatically.
    **Submit sign-in form** is a separate explicit action. Only one unambiguous
    top-frame form with fixed username/password fields, HTTPS action, POST
    method and same-tab target is supported. Changed fields, document, owner,
    profile or item refuse; MFA, CAPTCHA, passkeys and ambiguous forms remain
    manual.
    The broker's private consumer resolves only the selected Login item's fixed
    username/password fields from the same versioned result. Values stay in
    host memory between that consumer and the native form effect, never in a
    server runtime port, broker HTTP response, app UI, journal, workflow or diagnostic.
    A short-lived native one-shot reservation holds actions, snapshots, peek
    and diagnostics throughout private read and effect. Reservation epochs
    discard an overlapping read even if it finishes after release. The server
    applies the same publication fence to point descriptions/crops; native
    point implementations must preserve it when integrated. A cancelled read
    retains exclusion until it settles, including when the prepared plan
    expires during that read. The native effect checks the earlier of the grant
    and plan deadlines after final DOM validation. Expiry invalidates eligibility
    without releasing custody-owned observation exclusion. Point selection cannot release the
    independent fill hold.
    Native commit start consumes the validated plan once. Cancellation or
    revocation before start invalidates it; after start, a receipt reports
    possible/completed effect without claiming undo. Submission has its own
    validation, cancellation and receipt, independent of the earlier fill.
    Final DOM refusal with no effect leaves no added navigation permission.
    Explicit SSO submission may temporarily admit only its exact HTTPS outbound
    and original return origins, for the submitting view's top frame, for at
    most ten minutes. It changes neither the agent allowlist nor permanent
    person-origin grants; subframes and other tabs do not inherit it. No
    credential use on an unmatching SSO site is authorized. Unexpected hops
    refuse, while approved hops keep the same task/profile. Electron's frame
    navigation/redirect events must provide main-frame evidence; unknown frame
    identity receives no temporary permission.
    A filled form is not authentication. Outcomes distinguish filled,
    authentication-required, denied, cancelled and failed. Resuming requires
    the person's existing handoff after the protected operation ends. The
    website receives the credential and its own scripts can retain or reflect
    it. Observation exclusion during the operation and credential-free broker
    results do not prove callbacks are gone, that a reload erased them, or that
    later page content cannot reflect credentials. Consent states this limit;
    the separate [bounded Browser script operation](design/browser-agent-tool.md#bounded-page-scripts)
    explicitly authorizes ordinary DOM/account access only at Full access in
    its current implementation. It cannot overlap private credential custody,
    but previously installed callbacks may persist. Fixed-reader redaction and
    credential-free broker results are not an arbitrary-script password
    non-observation guarantee.
  - **Named credential commands.** Settings › Secret stores saves a fixed
    reference-only binding for one Code Project: canonical recipient executable
    and SHA-256 digest, bounded fixed arguments, relative Project directory,
    explicit account ID and 1–8 immutable vault/item/section/field environment
    references. The installed `op` 2 executable, version and digest are pinned
    at save time through the same discovery locations as the linked-store adapter;
    replacement requires a new binding. The discovery invokes only `--version`.
    Reserved process, loader, Git, SSH, credential-tool and Octant environment
    names cannot become mappings; this is not an exhaustive defence against
    arbitrary runtimes or a hostile recipient at Full access.
    A normal Code task's credential tool `run-saved` operation selects only a
    binding ID; the Code conversation offers the same review/run service to the
    person.
    Every run needs a separate one-use credential approval within three minutes,
    the originating registered local window, and ordinary Code command policy.
    Ask for approvals and Auto-accept edits keep the recipient OS-confined;
    Full access permits ordinary unrestricted commands. Plan and unknown postures
    refuse. Ordinary approvals and Auto Shield remain additional to credential
    consent; saving a binding never approves an ordinary command or destination.
    No routine, managed-child tool set,
    paired scope or headless caller inherits it.
    The server derives the current Project, checkout, profile, provider and
    active-turn posture. After process preparation it rechecks Project/checkout
    authority synchronously, asks the owning root seam to verify the managed
    receipt and root identity, and checks the broker's linked-store revision.
    Same-process window revocation, unlink, binding edits and authority changes
    invalidate pending use; across broker/filesystem awaits these are the last
    observed revisions, not an atomic distributed revocation transaction.
    The broker's fixed `/v1/secret-stores/command-use` route validates references
    and link revision only. It cannot launch a process or return a secret.
    The existing owned process port executes `op run --account ID --` followed
    by the host-prepared target and the reviewed recipient arguments, with
    references, a sanitized inherited baseline, bounded output and a
    1–300 second run timeout. The approval deadline stops governing after actual
    child start. After any credential-tool authentication wait, the bootstrap
    checks the recipient's canonical path, bounded SHA-256 digest and file
    identity again, then replaces itself with that recipient through `execve`.
    A replaced recipient refuses silently. This closes the authentication-wait
    gap; the final hash-to-exec syscall race remains, so the pin is last-observed
    identity rather than an atomic executable-file-descriptor guarantee.
    The bootstrap uses the server's canonical trusted runtime, whose file
    identity is rechecked before parent spawn. Packaged desktop uses its own
    Electron runtime in Node mode; supported Node and Bun hosts use their own
    runtime. Missing `execve` refuses without retry. Runtime loader environment
    variables are excluded before startup, and bootstrap-only Electron flags
    are removed before the recipient. The runtime remains part of the trusted
    host installation; its replacement is not covered by the recipient pin.
    Below Full access, `op` authenticates outside confinement and can launch only
    the already prepared Seatbelt or Bubblewrap target. The policy, read roots
    and pin derive from the recipient, not `op`. The capsule runs only fixed
    host code before the recipient: native env promotes the launch proxy URL
    inside confinement and removes its private source, then the host runtime
    verifies the recipient pin. The confined bootstrap preserves only the
    host-owned `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1` activation; user mappings cannot set Node,
    Bun, Electron or proxy configuration variables. The auth parent receives no
    ordinary proxy variables. Recipient network uses the current per-launch
    egress rules and one-use confirmed hosts; closure and audit/taint summary
    settle before output may return. Ordinary authority/posture and forge branch
    checks run again at final parent admission. Recognizable forge writes below
    Full access require the structured tools. Failed audit withholds output.
    A missing wrapper, unsupported runtime or preparation failure never retries
    without confinement. Ordinary system reads remain permitted; this is not a
    denial of every path outside the Project. Protected provider accounts lose
    their own-account exemption, and the default `~/.op` and `~/.config/op`
    directories stay denied even beneath broader roots. Credentials remain in
    the recipient environment; no file or callback returns them to Octant.
    At Full access the recipient and descendants have ordinary Full access.
    All postures receive credentials directly from `op`; default vendor concealment cannot
    prevent encoding, file writes or network disclosure. Octant does not claim
    exact-value redaction for values it never receives.
    Cancellation before spawn has no command effect. After spawn, cancellation
    requests owned process-group termination and reports possible effects,
    including uncertain cleanup; it cannot undo effects or revoke a credential.
    Exit zero proves process exit only, not account authorization or success of
    the intended business operation. Journal records reference bindings,
    revisions and approved/started/outcome metadata, never resolved values or
    process output. Restart restores bindings, not approvals or output.
    Preparation operation IDs replay only while their in-memory request/receipt
    is retained. After eviction or restart, preparation needs a distinct request
    and fresh approval; an old approval ID refuses. A new approval does not
    imply an earlier process or its effects stopped. The one-time HTTPS token
    card and AWS temporary-session path remain independent.
  - **AWS command line.** Settings › Secret stores › AWS command line points
    the AWS command line at the two items that hold the person's access key
    pair (`point-aws-cli-key`; the broker proves both resolve now, as for a
    provider key). The pointer lives beside the linked stores in
    `linked-secret-stores.json`, and naming items, it holds no value. Each
    Octant Harness shell command, at every level, asks the broker
    (`/v1/cloud-cli/aws/session`) as it starts; the broker reads both items,
    asks AWS STS for a session with `GetSessionToken` (one hour, signed with
    the platform's Signature Version 4 like cloud request signing), and
    returns the session alone, which the command gets as `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`,
    `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`, and
    `AWS_CREDENTIAL_EXPIRATION`. The long-lived pair never leaves the broker
    and is never kept. A session is handed out again while more than 15
    minutes of it are left, and forgotten when the pointer changes or is
    removed; an unlinked store hands out none. A failed attempt answers for
    30 seconds before the store and AWS are asked again, and a command waits
    at most 15 seconds for its session, then runs without one. The session's secret and token
    are noted as issued, so redaction removes them wherever a command's output
    is kept. A locked store, a missing item, a refused key, or an unreachable
    AWS gives the command no credentials, and the AWS command line says it
    found none. A change journals both items in one append as two
    `credential-reference.set` or `credential-reference.cleared` records
    (target `aws-cli-key`, part `access-key-id` or `secret-access-key`), and
    a change the journal refuses is undone as a provider key's is. A provider
    runtime's own commands get no session: its process outlives one.
    - _Rationale._ The person pointing the pair is the grant, so every
      harness command gets the session, a marked thread's included: the
      command still passes the thread's level, its approvals, Shield at Auto,
      and the egress rules, and a session without multi-factor sign-in cannot
      call IAM. `GetSessionToken` over `AssumeRole` because it needs no role
      for the person to set up and gives the same reach as the pair, never
      more. One hour so a long command does not lose its credentials midway;
      AWS's shortest, 15 minutes, would cut off a long sync.
  - **Google Cloud command line.** Settings › Secret stores › Google Cloud
    command line accepts a linked 1Password item containing service-account
    JSON, the exact expected service-account email, and explicit Google OAuth
    scopes. Review and confirmation are separate from entering the reference;
    a read of Settings never issues a token. The public pointer and scopes
    live in the existing `linked-secret-stores.json` sidecar; the key does not.
    Only a live local host window can change this selection. The account's IAM
    roles can reach several Google Cloud Projects: an Octant Project or a
    default `gcloud` Project does not narrow those roles.
    - The broker alone reads the JSON and signs an RS256 JWT with the selected
      email as issuer, the exact selected scopes, and
      `https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token` as both audience and exchange
      endpoint. It ignores the item's `token_uri`; delegated subjects,
      impersonation, and arbitrary endpoints are not supported. A JWT lasts
      at most one hour. Store reads and token exchange each have a ten-second
      bound. The broker caches only the resulting short-lived access token,
      uses a conservative expiry, and refuses a different returned scope set.
    - Each ordinary Octant Harness shell command receives only a token file
      through `CLOUDSDK_AUTH_ACCESS_TOKEN_FILE` and a private `CLOUDSDK_CONFIG`.
      The file is mode 0600 in a host-owned mode-0700 command resource directory;
      confinement grants that resource read access and only its configuration
      child write access. Confined harness launches deny the shared Google
      resource root before reallowing their own resource, including launches
      without a selected account; an overlapping writable binding is refused.
      Full access retains its existing unconfined, soft boundary. No grant
      widens the shared script directory. File
      logging, usage reporting, and prompts are disabled. The broker's reusable
      key, provider-native harnesses, worktree setup, ADC, `gsutil`, and `bq`
      are outside this channel. A command receives no mid-command refresh.
    - Selection changes and unlink invalidate pending issuance and prepared
      launches, checked again synchronously at the actual spawn boundary.
      A running command may retain its already-issued token until expiry;
      Clear removes future use, not Google-wide revocation. Issued tokens are
      registered for output redaction. An unavailable or expired configured
      channel receives an empty token file and isolated configuration with a
      recovery message, so it cannot fall back to the host's saved sign-in.
    - Startup first reconciles the existing owned harness process receipts.
      Each recovery stage has a ten-second bound. Only confirmed process
      recovery permits removal of prior `google-*` resources beneath this
      dedicated root. Failed or uncertain recovery leaves those files intact,
      disables Google issuance, and keeps the rest of the host available.
      An unrelated command can still run with the token-free configuration.
      Normal command completion removes only its owned resource directory.
    - _Rationale._ The selected token-file interface is supported by `gcloud`
      and gives each command an explicit lifetime and isolated configuration.
      Current `gcloud` also supports a direct access-token environment value;
      this adapter does not use it. Installed SDK, OS confinement, and live
      account acceptance remain separate from fake-token protocol tests.
    - The host-wide Octant credential guard includes `harness/cloud-cli`
      beneath the data directory. Other confined processes cannot read its
      running tokens through an ancestor grant; Octant's file tools refuse
      reads, writes and searches there at every level. Only the owning
      ordinary harness launch receives the narrow OS resource exception.
- **Organization sign-in on a host without the desktop app.** An Azure AI
  Foundry endpoint that signs in with a directory account and opted in to it
  (`deviceCodeSignIn`) signs in with a device code from
  `octant provider sign-in <instance>`
  ([`providerSignInCommand.ts`](../packages/cli/src/providerSignInCommand.ts),
  [`providerDeviceSignInRoutes.ts`](../apps/server/src/providers/oauth/providerDeviceSignInRoutes.ts)).
  Its `/api/desktop/provider-sign-in/begin` and `/poll` routes take exactly
  the caller the provider key routes take (bridge secret, window capability,
  no `Origin`, loopback), and the private listener never forwards them; the
  browser sign-in route never begins a device code, so a code appears only in
  the terminal that asked for it. The broker builds the tenant's device
  authorization URL from its closed issuer host and refuses a verification
  page off a closed list; the server follows an issued code until the broker
  settles it, so an interrupted command never leaves a grant without a
  pointer. An Amazon Bedrock endpoint signs in at its organization's single
  sign-on portal only this way, with no opt-in, since the portal's device
  authorization is its one flow; the broker accepts a verification page only
  on the portal region's device host or the organization's own access portal
  host. Settings' sign-in route answers a Bedrock instance's status and Sign
  out only, refusing a remote principal's Sign out before the pointer is read.
  [Enterprise provider identity](design/enterprise-provider-identity.md)
  owns the rules.
- **Cloud request signing.** The credential broker signs cloud requests
  itself ([`cloudIam.ts`](../packages/host-runtime/src/cloudIam.ts),
  [`sigV4.ts`](../packages/host-runtime/src/sigV4.ts)): Signature Version 4
  from the published algorithm with the platform's crypto, never a cloud SDK.
  A sign request names a credential reference and the request's own fields
  and nothing else; a digest, a date, or a scope of the caller's own is a
  malformed request, and a request outside the scope stored at sign-in (one
  partition, service, host, path prefix, and method from the broker's closed
  table) is refused before any credential is renewed or signature made. The
  portal session, its refresh token, the client registration, and the role's
  secret key never leave the broker; the raw resolve route refuses the grant.
  A signature answer carries the authorization, the date, and the role's
  session token, which the cloud requires beside every signature and which
  signs nothing without the secret key. Removing the endpoint, or changing its
  region, portal, account, or role, ends the portal session and deletes the
  grant before the change is journaled.
- **Artifact replica membership.** Each replica entry carries a detached
  Ed25519 signature from the device signing key the writing host holds for its
  replica instance, in a credential namespace of its own that provider
  credentials cannot reach — not a paired client's device key. There is no
  replica key. The entry names that key, and the instance id is derived from
  it, so a record that fails verification under its own key, names an id
  that is not its key's, or is not the canonical encoding of its entry with
  the canonical base64 text of its signature, is not valid and is journaled as
  unreadable.
  Membership is derived from the valid records a host holds and the founder it
  pinned; an entry counts only when its writer is admitted through a chain of
  signed approvals and acceptances from that founder and the entry sits at or
  before any cut on it and, when a revocation names the slots its writer read
  as the subject's own (`kept`), in every such revocation's kept slots, so a
  slot the revoker did not read as the subject's stays closed to its key. A new computer joins by writing a join request into
  the store, signed over the time it was written; a request older than a day
  is not offered for approval. A member in good standing approves it by name,
  and only the store's own copy of the request can be approved, not a copy a
  caller hands over. A short matching code, compared on both screens, is a
  consistency check that the request, the approving computer's key, and the
  founder are the ones the joining computer means. It is not a secret and not
  a tamper proof: six digits leave room for someone who can write the store
  to search offline for a substituted join request that yields the same
  code. The signatures and the verified approval chain, not the code, make
  the records authoritative. The joining
  computer then signs its acceptance of that one approval, which makes the
  approver its only parent. Revoke writes a signed revocation, and only a
  computer that brought the revoked one in, directly or through others, can
  revoke it. A member leaves by signing a left record with its own key, which
  cuts it just before that record; it then forgets its identity and deletes
  its device key. Store setup, joining, revoking, and leaving happen on the
  host, never from a paired phone. Store credentials live in the host credential store — macOS
  Keychain or freedesktop Secret Service — and are not written into the
  replica. An S3-compatible store is contacted only over authenticated TLS. A
  plaintext endpoint is refused, and store credentials are not sent on it.
  The storage provider can read the synced content: the artifact versions and
  tombstones are plain files. Settings and the user guide
  (`octant-site/docs/guide/sync-artifacts.md`) say so before sync is turned on.
  Opt-in encryption of replicas is not this rule. A replica import appends
  versions to this journal and adopts nothing else. Membership accepts an
  entry signed by an admitted instance's device signing key, within its cut
  and its kept slots, as authentic. It does not delegate host authority between hosts.
- **Replica store endpoints.** A bucket endpoint must be `https` with no path,
  query, or user info, and must not be link-local — IPv4 `169.254.0.0/16` or
  IPv6 `fe80::/10`, literal or IPv4-mapped — where cloud instance metadata
  answers; the contract refuses it before any request is signed. Loopback and
  private ranges stay allowed, because a self-hosted bucket server such as
  MinIO on the same machine or LAN is a legitimate store. A host name is not
  resolved to check where it points; the endpoint is whatever the person on
  the host typed, and only that person can set it.
- **Hosts never trust each other.** Multi-host views merge read models
  client-side without transferring authority. Federation shares no
  credentials; the explicit
  [Shared sign-ins](design/hub-and-spokes.md#shared-sign-ins) API-key copy
  requires a fresh own-unlock on each host and a one-use receiving ticket.
  Subscription sign-ins refuse copying. Completing
  all-hosts honesty, pairing at scale, and conflict presentation is client
  registry work, not a new trust boundary. Conflicting facts stay under their owning host;
  create and mutation routing name one destination and refuse when that host is
  not routable — they never queue offline work or convert one host's read model
  into authority on another. An all-hosts list keeps every registered host;
  an unreachable host's cached items stay listed as stale and read-only, and
  an authority-bearing mutation is allowed only on a host whose read model is
  ready. The hub-and-spoke design keeps this rule: a hub introduces hosts and
  devices to each other, an introduction grants only what the receiving host's
  person allowed when it joined the hub (by default full membership, which
  never reaches Full access, and an agent from another member never answers
  an approval), each host
  stays the only authority over its own threads and journal, and what one host
  may do on another is only the grant the receiving host keeps
  ([Hub and spokes](design/hub-and-spokes.md#journal-and-authority-boundaries)).
- **Host platform in copy.** The host's identity report (`GET /api/hosts`)
  carries the host's `platform`, set from `process.platform`; it is optional
  in the contract because an older host does not send it. Only the loopback
  listener answers that route, so only a window on the host itself learns the
  host's OS. The private listener refuses `/api/hosts` before and after
  sign-in and never hands it to product dispatch, so a paired device or
  remote browser learns no platform and its copy stays neutral. The renderer
  reads it from the window's own host's answer, not from federation registry
  entries, which are the client's records and carry no platform, and copy
  that names the host's computer or credential store follows it. Before the
  answer arrives, or from a host that sends none, copy uses the neutral "this
  computer" rather than the window's platform, which is wrong exactly for a
  remote window. Copy the server writes itself never follows
  `process.platform`, because a signed-in paired device can read it:
  destination labels such as the folder export's, refusal reasons such as the
  gist destination's, and refusals that name the host's window say "this
  computer" on every host. Only copy for a macOS-only capability, such as
  Computer use or the Apple workbench, names the Mac, which tells a reader
  nothing the capability does not.
- **Local servers and Running services.** Listener observation is ephemeral,
  scoped to listening sockets of the current user, and never journaled. One
  classifier decides what may be listed at all: a system daemon, another user's
  process, or an interpreter with no project and no editor lineage is omitted
  rather than shown disabled, so no surface can be read as a host process
  inventory. On Linux a Node main thread renames itself `MainThread`, so the
  scan names such a listener from `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` (program and script)
  before classifying; a command line it cannot read stays unclassified. The
  Code Environment reads it per thread. The start screen's
  Running services reads the same service host-wide (`list-running-services`
  on the same authenticated route; no thread or Project in the command) and
  adds one filter before anything is probed: a listener is published only when
  its working directory sits inside an active Code Project the Project
  bootstrap lists (today every active Code Project on the host, the same set
  the per-thread route resolves against; it does not vary by window), or inside
  the worktree of one thread of such a Project, which a host-written ownership
  receipt vouches for. A listener outside those roots gets no row and no health
  probe. Rows are Octant-owned (a live terminal descendant) or not owned. A
  not-owned row is any other admitted current-user listener in those roots
  whose lineage names no editor; an earlier Octant session, a terminal, Claude
  Code, or Codex could have started it, and Octant cannot tell which, so the
  row and its Stop confirmation say only that Octant does not own it. The same bounded scan, health phase and
  deadline apply, and a scan that cannot finish is a refusal, never an empty
  list. Open and Stop re-observe and re-classify by an opaque id that is not a
  process id and differs from the per-thread id for the same listener. Stop is
  judged under the origin's posture (a server in a Plan thread's own worktree is
  never stoppable; the Project folder is no one thread's, so a server there is
  judged approval-gated even when a Plan thread works in it), a server Octant
  does not own needs the confirmation naming process, folder and port, and a
  paired device may stop only a server Octant owns; the actor comes
  from the request's authenticated principal. A window reads the host it is
  connected to; All Hosts federation does not carry these rows, with one
  exception: a desktop window whose Environments filter is narrowed to one
  connected paired computer reads that computer's Running services over its
  paired session, as that device (for a computer paired through Other
  computers the request travels through the desktop's main process, which
  holds it to the pinned key, since the window's page policy reaches loopback
  only; see Desktop pairing above), and opens its servers only live (below),
  never as one of its own Browser tabs; while that computer is not connected
  the card reads nothing and says so, never this computer's rows.
- **Proxy sessions and server grants.** A paired device asks for a grant to
  open one dev server from its own computer, under a proxy session that is
  separate from its product session. The rules in force:
  - **Proxy session.** Minted at `/api/remote/auth/server-proxy-session` from
    the ordinary device challenge, signed over a proxy transcript that differs
    from the product one only in its label, so neither signature becomes the
    other kind of session. It lives in the host's memory only, travels in its
    own `HttpOnly` cookie scoped to `/api/server-proxy/`, and reaches only the
    routes under that prefix, which are their own route-policy surface: never
    product routes, never forwarded or classified as product actions. A
    product session never reaches a proxy route. Each request carries the same
    signed envelope product routes use, re-reads the device, and spends a
    nonce from the session's own store (16,384 in the retention window). The
    proxy surface has its own concurrency: 64 on the listener and in the route
    policy, 32 per device in the session store, answered 503 with a one-second
    `Retry-After`, apart from the product budget, and a device decides one
    grant request at a time. A device holds at most four proxy sessions (a
    fifth ends its oldest) and the host 64. A session whose device is found
    revoked, expired, or rotated, by a request or by the minute sweep, ends at
    once, as a backstop to the credential hooks. A host restart ends every
    proxy session.
  - **Grant.** `POST /api/server-proxy/grants` names the listing its listener id
    came from. The host gathers every fact itself: the principal, whether the
    device can open the thread (an archived thread counts as unreadable), the
    listener re-observed and re-classified by that id, its ownership and health,
    the thread whose own worktree it runs in, and that thread's posture, and
    decides with the grant policy in its fixed order. A device holds at most 8
    open grants and the host 32, refused `grant-limit` after every other rule.
    The thread is read again just before a grant is minted, and a thread or
    server closed while the request was being decided mints nothing. The same
    session opening the same server again gets the same grant. A
    listing the host could not finish answers 503, never a refusal. A local
    window reaching the route on the loopback listener is answered
    `local-principal` and nothing about the server is read.
  - **Record and revocation.** Each opening (actor: the device) and closing
    (actor: the host) is journaled as `remote-server.grant-opened@1` and
    `remote-server.grant-closed@1` with the grant, device, thread, and port,
    never the endpoint, and an open-grant projection is rebuilt from them. A
    starting host closes every grant still open as `proxy-session-ended`. A
    grant closes when its proxy session ends or expires, when its device is
    revoked, rotated, expired, or signs out (before that credential change
    returns), when the listener is disabled, when its thread is archived or
    purged, and when Octant stops its server. A thread purge erases the grant's
    records with the thread's. Nothing erases a device's records, so a revoked
    device's grant history stays with its revoke.
  - **Relay.** `/api/server-proxy/<grant id>/<path>` relays one request to the
    grant's dev server. Each carries the proxy session's signed envelope, with
    its body (at most 8 MiB, any media type, 413 above) hashed into the proof.
    The proof signs the canonical query (sorted and normalized) while the dev
    server gets the query as the page wrote it; the two differ only in order
    and percent-encoding, which a request carried over TLS with a single-use
    nonce gives no one else a chance to choose. A proxy request whose cookie
    names no live proxy session, or one whose device no longer stands, has at
    most 4 KiB of its body read, 413 above, and one source holds at most four
    such requests at once (429). Before every request, which gets its
    own upstream connection, the host checks again: the grant is open and bound
    to this device, credential generation, and proxy session; Code is on; the
    thread is active and this device can still read it; and the process the
    grant was minted for (pid, untruncated name, and port, from one `lsof`
    narrowed to the port) still holds the port under an Octant terminal, and
    no other process listens where it could answer the loopback address the
    host connects to (a wildcard counts for both families, and an IPv4-mapped
    bind for the IPv4 loopback). The check and the connection are two steps:
    a server that exits and whose port another process binds in that gap
    (milliseconds) receives that one request, and the next request's check
    closes the grant; for an HTTPS dev server the pin refuses it first. The
    host does not confirm the accepting process per connection, since that is
    a host query per request and a socket still waiting to be accepted is not
    yet visible to it. A
    request never relies on a check that began before it arrived; a burst
    shares the running check's successor. A lost check closes the grant
    (`server-stopped`, `server-changed-hands`, `thread-archived`,
    `thread-unreadable`, `code-disabled`) and the request is refused
    `grant-closed`, the same answer as a grant that never existed or belongs
    to another device; a check the host could not make answers 503 and keeps
    the grant. The host connects only to the grant's `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]`
    endpoint, within five seconds or `server-unreachable`, follows no redirect,
    and sends the request's path and query with `Host: localhost:<port>`, an
    `Origin` (admitted only as the listener's own) as the dev server's origin, a
    `Referer` under the grant's path as that path on the dev server (any other
    is dropped), and `Connection: close`. Hop-by-hop headers, `x-octant-`
    headers, fetch metadata, forwarding claims, and cookies named `octant-`
    (after any `__Secure-` or `__Host-` prefix) never cross; the page's other
    cookies and `Authorization` do. The response comes back with hop-by-hop
    headers, `Content-Length`, `x-octant-` headers, `Clear-Site-Data`,
    `Alt-Svc`, and `Set-Cookie` for an `octant-` cookie removed, marked `x-octant-server-proxy: relayed` so the
    device can tell it from the host's own answers, without the listener's
    security headers or response budget, streamed with no size cap and closed
    after five minutes without a byte. An HTTPS dev server's certificate is not
    checked against a trust store; the first one under a grant is pinned for
    its life, and another closes the grant as `server-changed-hands`. Each
    request is registered under its grant before connecting, and holds its
    place in the device's proxy budget until its response ends; closing the
    grant closes the upstream socket and cuts the response before the call
    that closed it returns. `OPTIONS` is not relayed. The listener admits
    bodies up to the relay's 8 MiB, and up to 10 MiB on each mode's
    attachment upload route; every other route keeps its own budget.
  - **WebSockets.** The relay route is the only one that switches a
    connection: a signed `GET` asking to upgrade to `websocket` takes the same
    checks as any relayed request, then the host opens a WebSocket to the
    grant's endpoint with the same header rules, its own handshake key, the
    page's subprotocol list, and no extension, within the connect bound. Only
    when the dev server answers 101 with the right accept value, no extension,
    and no subprotocol or one the page offered does the page's connection
    switch, answering that subprotocol; a dev server that declines, and any
    upgrade to another protocol, is refused `upgrade-refused` (501). Every
    other route on either listener answers an upgrade request as an ordinary
    one and never switches. After the switch, messages carry no proof of their
    own: each socket is registered under its grant before the host connects,
    and closing the grant for any reason above closes the page's end with 1008
    and the dev server's with 1001 before the call that closed it returns. A
    grant holds at most four sockets and a device sixteen, answered 503 with a
    one-second `Retry-After` past either; a socket does not hold a proxy-budget
    slot once switched. A message is at most 16 MiB in either direction, and a
    larger one closes the socket with 1009 before the host buffers it; writes
    one end does not read close the socket with 1008 past twice that. The host
    answers pings itself and relays whole messages, text or binary, and close
    codes. An open socket counts as use of its proxy session, so the session
    does not idle out under it; its absolute expiry still ends the session,
    the grant, and the socket. The listener's transport (Node or Bun) switches
    a connection only when the route's answer carries an accepted upgrade, so
    an answer that does not is written as plain HTTP and the connection closed.
  - **Forwarder and signer on the device.** Only the desktop app opens a
    page live. Its main process starts a forwarder on the first Open that
    binds `127.0.0.1` and `::1` only, on the port it recorded, else the next
    free one in 47610–47619 (said once; all taken refuses Open with that
    range), and serves each granted server at
    `<port>-<label>.octant.localhost`, `<label>` the first 10 bytes of a
    SHA-256 over the host and thread in base32, so the same server keeps its
    name. It routes by the exact `Host`, refuses an unknown name, and admits a
    request only with that name's secret (a header Octant's browser adds for
    the exact origin only, or an `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict`, host-only
    cookie the default browser gets from a one-time claim token in a URL
    fragment) and, where the browser sends them, `Sec-Fetch-Site`
    `same-origin` or `none` and the page's own `Origin`. It holds no key: for
    each request it sends the method, full proxy path, and body digest (8 MiB
    cap, 413 above) to the Octant window that opened the page, which refuses
    unless the canonical path is under the proxy route of a grant it holds and
    builds and signs the envelope itself; the main process takes back only
    Octant's own headers, from that window only. The window holds its proxy
    session (minted by `issueServerProxySession`, which never clears the
    product session) and its grants in memory. The forwarder reaches the host
    through the listener trust rule with no cookie jar, rewrites the page's
    origin and `Referer` to the listener's and the grant's path, never sends
    the page's secret, and hands the page only a response marked relayed, with
    a `Location` naming the dev server's own origin moved to the name, a
    loopback `Set-Cookie` `Domain` dropped, and HSTS dropped; anything else
    becomes a failure page in the plan's copy. Octant's browser is a sandboxed
    window per name in a persistent partition, with every permission refused,
    kept on the page's origin, and not a Browser tab, so no agent can drive
    it. Removing a host, revoking this device from it, or forgetting a paired
    computer closes that computer's page windows, clears every persistent
    partition for its recorded page names through `clearRemotePageStorage`, and
    forgets the names; a name that could not be cleared stays for a retry. A page's WebSocket upgrade (live reload) takes the same admission,
    secret, and window signature as any request, signed as a `GET` with an
    empty body, and goes to the proxy route through the same listener trust.
    Once the host switches protocols with the accept value for the page's own
    key and no extension, the forwarder answers the page 101 and passes bytes
    through both ways unchanged, so the host's message cap, buffer bound, and
    close codes apply as on any relayed socket; a closed grant, a revoke, or a
    session's end closes it from the host, and closing the host's pages or
    stopping the forwarder closes it here. Any other answer reaches the page as
    the request's failure status, and no frame is sent.
- **Host-driven provider sign-in.** A local principal may start a descriptor-driven
  PKCE or device-code sign-in. The host, not a provider child and not the
  renderer, owns the loopback redirect, the device poll, and refresh. State and
  the code verifier are checked, the redirect is one-shot, and an unanswered
  consent times out. Tokens stay in the credential broker. The journal records
  the terms acknowledgment (who and when) and the public sign-in state, never
  an access token, refresh token, authorization code, or verifier. A remote
  principal cannot acknowledge terms, start the flow, or refresh. Starting a
  sign-in without a recorded acknowledgment of that descriptor's terms is
  refused (`terms-required`). A revoked,
  expired, or reused refresh token is a typed sign-in-again state and drops the
  stored grant. The API-key path remains available beside that sign-in.
- **Subscription sign-in dialects.** The host OAuth runner also speaks vendor wire
  dialects beside the standard PKCE path: OpenRouter exchanges the code for an
  API key, and the ChatGPT plan dialect registers the host as a user-defined
  agent. Each keeps the host-driven sign-in rule above, and tokens stay in the
  credential broker. In the ChatGPT plan dialect, the identity token is
  validated before a grant is stored, a replaced grant's local material is
  deleted, and a request the plan route's profile cannot express is refused
  before send. The wire details are in
  [Provider runtimes](design/provider-runtimes.md#subscription-sign-in-dialects).
- **Account usage endpoints.** Devin and OpenCode Go report plan windows only from an account endpoint, so the
  host reads the sign-in their own CLI saved and asks that endpoint. Devin:
  `windsurf_api_key` (and an `https` `api_server_url`, else
  `server.codeium.com`) from `~/.local/share/devin/credentials.toml`, sent in
  the body of a Connect `POST` to
  `SeatManagementService/GetUserStatus`; daily and weekly remaining
  percentages become windows, and the overage balance is not shown. OpenCode
  Go: the `opencode-go` key from the `credential` table of OpenCode 2's
  `opencode*.db` in its data directory (`$XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode`, default
  `~/.local/share/opencode`), opened read-only with no pragmas, else
  `auth.json` when no database keeps sign-ins; sent as a bearer token to
  `GET opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/usage`, whose 5-hour, weekly, and monthly
  used percentages become windows. The reads run in the host process, only
  for an enabled instance of that provider. Only a refresh a person asks for
  waits on the endpoint. Every other caller, the limits service's
  five-minute schedule and the service-limits read before each Chat turn,
  gets the last reading at once and starts at most one background read per
  five minutes, so a turn never waits on the endpoint and frequent turns
  never multiply the calls. The request sends nothing else and follows no
  redirect. Octant never writes, copies, or stores either key. It
  stays out of logs, the journal, snapshots, and errors: every failure carries
  a fixed message. A missing sign-in reads as not ready, an OpenCode sign-in
  without Go as plan limits not applying, a refused key as unauthenticated,
  and a 429 keeps its `Retry-After`. The Devin call is not a published
  interface; an answer whose shape stops matching fails as a protocol change
  and keeps the last reading rather than guessing.
- **Update feed signing keys are per ring.** The desktop updater verifies a
  feed's Ed25519 signature against the compiled-in keys of the ring the signed
  release names, before any other field is believed. Stable trusts only the
  stable key (`OCTANT_UPDATE_PUBLIC_KEY`); preview and candidate trust the
  preview key (`OCTANT_UPDATE_PREVIEW_PUBLIC_KEY`) and the stable key. The
  preview workflow builds unreviewed `main` without an approval gate, so
  anything merged there can read the key it signs with; a shared key would let
  that code sign a `ring: "stable"` feed and make the stable approval
  meaningless. The stable key may sign previews because its holder can already
  sign stable, and it is how installs that predate the preview key reach a
  build that knows it. Those installs read `<ring>/<platform>-<arch>.json`;
  key-aware builds before the release named its app read
  `<ring>/<platform>-<arch>.preview-key.json`, and current builds read the
  app-named files above. Installs built before `product` existed decode a feed
  strictly and call a document carrying it malformed, so no product-bearing
  document is written at a name they read. Each candidate run also writes an
  old-shape document (no `product`, signed over the old encoding) at
  `candidate/<platform>-<arch>.preview-key.json`, moving those Octant installs
  to a build that reads the new name. The old preview names are left as last
  published (the last Octant preview build), because the installs reading them
  are Octant and the ring now carries Nightly: they are offered nothing and
  move on by choosing Octant's Preview channel (`candidate`). The bare
  `candidate/<platform>-<arch>.json` holds an old-shape bridge feed that the
  approval-gated `release-preview-bridge.yml` signs once with the stable key,
  pointing at a published candidate build that ships the preview key; it
  refuses preview tags. Nothing overwrites it, so an install offline for any
  length of time still finds a release it can verify. The release wizard mints a ring's key
  only when the app ships none for it: replacing a deployed key strands every
  install that trusts it, and rotation would need a staged overlap. The private
  halves are environment secrets:
  `OCTANT_UPDATE_FEED_PRIVATE_KEY` only in `stable`,
  `OCTANT_UPDATE_FEED_PREVIEW_PRIVATE_KEY` only in `preview`.
  `scripts/sign-update-feed.ts` reads the secret for the ring it signs and
  refuses a key whose public half the app does not trust for that ring, so an
  unset preview public key fails the release job instead of publishing a feed
  no install can verify. The signed ring must still equal the ring the app
  follows. The feed's publish credential is not part of this trust: a writer
  that can replace a feed file can withhold a ring's updates, never install
  something no trusted key signed.
- **The feed is published to GitHub releases.** Each ring has one fixed
  mailbox release, `feed-preview`, `feed-candidate` or `feed-stable`, a
  prerelease that holds only that ring's feed JSON files. The release workflows
  upload with the job's own token (`contents: write`) through
  `scripts/publish-update-feed.sh`; no server credential exists. The app keeps
  its compiled base `https://octant.sh/updates` and requests
  `<ring>/<file>`; octant.sh redirects that path to
  `https://github.com/Ogard-Labs/octant/releases/download/feed-<ring>/<file>`.
  The updater follows that cross-host redirect, and the signature and artifact
  hash checks never depend on the host that served the bytes. The mailbox tags
  do not start with `v`, so no rule scoped to version tags reaches them. Whoever
  can write release assets in the repository can withhold a ring's updates, and
  nothing more, for the reason above.

**Proposed, not accepted: Claude sign-in inside Anthropic's terms.** Octant
would not mint, store, or inject a Claude setup or OAuth token. Claude
subscription sign-in would stay in Anthropic's own flow, and confined Claude
launches would sign in from a Claude-owned config directory. Step 0 of the
remediation plan was measured on 12 Oct 2026, and the maintainer chose the Keychain read
it found. The rule is still not in force: it needs Anthropic's Commercial
Terms or an explicit Anthropic exception. Until that is recorded, the rules
in this document describe the build as it ships.

### Secret guard

Below Full access, secret files stay out of every agent's reach by an OS rule;
at Full access they are guarded softly (maintainer decision, 2026-10-31:
"softer guard — full access is full access"). Full access stays "no sandbox,
no prompts": a shell command there can read a protected file. The Google
Cloud channel is the bounded `gcloud` service-account adapter below. Azure uses
only the fixed one-use Resource Manager HTTP read described under credential
cards; general Azure CLI credentials remain unavailable by design.

- **One list, every runtime.** The list is
  `packages/domain/src/secretGuardPolicy.ts`; the host turns it into rules in
  `apps/server/src/process/secretGuard.ts`. Below Full access (Ask first, Accept edits, Auto, Plan) it joins every
  confined launch through the shared builder: the deny-default Seatbelt profile emits
  it after every grant (Seatbelt applies the last matching rule), so a
  protected file inside a granted root, such as a home folder opened as a
  Project, stays denied; the Bubblewrap capsule covers each protected file
  inside a bound root. At Full access no launch is wrapped (see
  [Sandbox](#security-and-authority)), so the list is not an OS rule there.
  The built-in groups, per platform:
  - **SSH private keys:** files in `~/.ssh` (two levels) named `id_*`,
    `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.p12`, `*.pfx`, `*.ppk`, or `identity`, and any file
    that has a `name.pub` companion, found from the folder listing alone.
    `*.pub`, `config`, and `known_hosts` stay readable, and so does an agent
    socket in the folder.
  - **Cloud command-line credentials:** `~/.aws/credentials`,
    `~/.aws/sso/cache`, `~/.aws/cli/cache`, the credential and token files
    under `~/.config/gcloud`, and the token caches under `~/.azure`. Each
    tool's configuration file stays readable.
  - **Cluster configuration** (`~/.kube/config`), **container registry
    sign-in** (`~/.docker/config.json`), **package registry tokens**
    (`~/.npmrc`, `~/.pypirc`, `~/.gem/credentials`, `~/.cargo/credentials`),
    **Git and network credential files** (`~/.git-credentials`,
    `~/.config/git/credentials`, `~/.netrc`), and the **forge command-line
    sign-in** (`~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`). The registry files are protected
    whole: a token line cannot be told from the rest without reading it.
  - **Keychains and password vaults:** on macOS every file under
    `~/Library/Keychains` except the login keychain database and its SQLite
    companions, and the local vault folders of password managers; on Linux
    `~/.local/share/keyrings` and the vault folders. The login keychain stays
    readable because the Security framework opens it in the calling process:
    `git credential-osxkeychain`, `security`, and a runtime's own Keychain
    sign-in fail without it, and its items stay encrypted and unlock only
    through the keychain service. A confined launch gets that exception back
    for reading only, and only when a granted root already reached the folder.
  - **Browser cookies and saved logins:** profile cookie, login, and key
    stores under `~/Library/Application Support` (five levels) and the
    browser cookie folders on macOS; under `~/.config` and the browser
    profile folders on Linux.
  - **Octant's own secrets:** the bridge secret, the data directory's
    `remote` and `integrations` folders, and the runtime directory's
    `*.secret` files.
  - **Provider sign-ins:** each provider's stored sign-in file in the home
    folder, and Octant's managed account homes (`providers/` in the data
    directory). A runtime may read its own sign-in and no other tool's: a
    launch names its own account paths, and a sign-in entry at or beneath
    one is left out, one containing it is denied with the own path
    re-allowed. A confined launch also counts as its own the read and write
    roots it was granted by name, except the bound root and the temporary
    directory. No own path ever reopens a file in another group.
- **The person can add paths and remove built-ins.** Settings › Permissions
  › Protected files (`ProtectedFilesService`, `/api/protected-files`) shows
  each group with the paths it covers on this host and the channel that
  replaces it. A person adds an absolute or `~/` path and removes it again;
  removing a built-in group needs an explicit confirm, and the command
  carries `confirmed: true`, so an unconfirmed removal is not representable.
  Every change is journaled under the `protected-files` aggregate with the
  actor; only a window on this host may change the list, never a paired
  device. The journal holds changes, not the list, so a group a later Octant
  adds is protected on every host. Changes reach every launch prepared after
  them.
- **Work goes through the channel instead of the file.** SSH through the
  agent socket in `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, a password manager's SSH agent included;
  Git over HTTPS through the system credential helper, which reaches the
  keychain through the Security framework; provider, connector, and package
  keys through the credential broker; cluster access through a `KUBECONFIG`
  the person keeps outside the list. The AWS command line in Octant's own
  shell gets a short-lived session from the broker once the person points its
  key pair at a linked store ([AWS command line](#linked-secret-stores)).
  The Google Cloud `gcloud` command line in Octant's own shell receives a
  command-owned access-token file and private configuration from the broker
  after exact account/scopes consent ([linked secret stores](#linked-secret-stores)).
  Azure offers only the fixed broker-owned Resource Manager GET through a
  private one-use credential card; it exports no token to a CLI or file.
  General Azure CLI credentials remain unavailable. A confined command must not
  bypass a protected Azure store through another tool.
  - _Rationale._ AWS first because a session needs nothing on disk: the
    session's three values go in the command's environment, which the AWS
    command line and every AWS SDK read before any file. The Google Cloud
    adapter uses its supported token-file interface and a private config
    directory to bound each command's resources; it does not assume that
    Google supports only file input. Azure needs its own consumer-specific
    contract rather than an invented generic access-token environment variable.
    The tested `az rest` interface follows same-origin redirects with the bearer;
    a fixed initial URL therefore does not bound the final authenticated path.
    The approved Azure HTTP alternative enforces the fixed URL itself and refuses
    every redirect instead of giving a command a credential lease.
- **A refused read names its rule and channel.** Octant's own file tools
  (the Octant Harness's read, write, edit, and grep; the ACP client's file
  read and write) and Claude Code's file tools, through Octant's tool gate,
  answer a protected path at every level, Full access included, with the
  group, the path, and the channel to use instead (`protectedFileRefusal`). The Octant Harness's
  search across a folder skips protected files without opening them.
  Claude Code's Grep, Glob, and LS take no exclusion and, at the postures
  where the runtime runs outside Octant's profile (approval-gated,
  auto-accept-edits, and Full access), run in its unwrapped process, so a search rooted at or
  above an existing protected file, or inside a protected folder, is refused
  whole (`secretGuardSearchRefusal`). The refusal names the resolved search
  root and protected rule/channel, explicitly says no results were returned,
  and suggests an ordinary subfolder with no protected entry. It never claims
  partial results or recommends bypassing the protected entry through another
  tool. Relative roots and a relative Glob's fixed `..` prefix are resolved
  against the bound search folder before the same lexical/real-path check.
  Parent traversals retain both lexical and kernel symlink interpretations;
  direct file-tool paths are resolved against the bound Project root too.
  Its own sandbox cannot carry the list,
  because its `allowRead` takes precedence over `denyRead`. Protected entries
  are matched in their lexical and resolved forms, so a linked folder's target
  is refused too. In the Seatbelt profiles each exception follows only its own
  rule's denial, and the person's added paths are denied last, after a
  launch's extra rules. A command's refusal is the
  operating system's `Operation not permitted`; Octant does not rewrite
  command output.
- **Secret redaction everywhere.** Known key formats (private key blocks,
  provider, forge, registry, cloud, and chat-service tokens, JSON web
  tokens, a URL's password, an `_authToken` value) and every value the
  credential broker handed out in this host process are redacted
  (`redactSecrets`) from a runtime's normalized events at the shared driver
  boundary (`redactProviderRuntimeSecrets`), so tool output, transcripts, the
  journal, exports, and diagnostics built from them carry the mark instead.
  Thread exports and the service log pass the same redaction. Tool and
  approval requests are left as asked, so redaction never changes what an
  agent does. A key split across two streamed chunks is not caught, and the
  model still sees what a tool returned to it.
- **Shield links in.** The Judge, built for every runtime that routes
  approvals through Octant, sends a command or call that reaches a secret file to the person (`secret-path`) and refuses a command that reads
  secrets and sends something off the computer (`reads-secrets-then-egress`);
  see [Octant Shield](#octant-shield). It reads the list in force, the
  person's additions included (`isProtectedSecretPath`), beside its own
  secret-path patterns. The Watcher flags every call of Octant's own tools
  that names a protected path, in a path field or as a word of a shell
  command, refused or not, as the `secret-path-read` label. At Full access,
  where Shield judges nothing, an Octant Harness command that sends something
  off the computer after the thread reached for a secret, or while naming
  one, is journaled as a `shield-tags.recorded@1` tag
  (`reads-secrets-then-egress`) under the thread. These never block, because
  nothing else stands between a shell command and the file there. The Watcher
  also flags a call of Octant's own shell that prints an environment variable
  whose name says it holds a secret, as the `secret-env-print` label, at every
  level: the command hands one to `echo`, `printf`, or `printenv`
  (`echo $GITHUB_TOKEN`), or its output lists one with a value (`env`,
  `export -p`).
  - _Rationale._ The Judge keeps its own patterns beside the list rather than
    replacing them: they also cover files the list leaves out (`.env`,
    `.gnupg`, a stray `.pem`), and a built-in group the person removes takes
    away the OS rule, not Shield's habit of asking, which only ever sends a
    call to the person. The flag reads a command's text only, so a path the
    command builds at run time, or a relative path in a tool's arguments, is
    not seen; it is a record for the person, never what stands between a
    command and a file. A refused attempt is flagged too, because what the
    agent reached for is what the person needs to see. A tag that cannot be
    journaled withholds the command's output, as an unrecorded `ssh` command
    does; the command itself has already run. A provider runtime's own
    commands at Full access reach no Octant shell and are not tagged.
  - _Rationale (printed variables)._ The name decides, never the value: a
    word of the name is a secret noun (`TOKEN`, `SECRET`, `PASSWORD`, `AUTH`,
    `API_KEY`, `ACCESS_KEY`, and the like), and a name ending in a word that
    says where or which secret (`_FILE`, `_PATH`, `_SOCK`, `_ID`) holds none,
    so `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` and `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` are left alone. A variable
    handed to another program (`curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"`) is a
    use, which the Judge weighs, not a print. A `sh -c` body is read as a
    command of its own, two levels deep; a command is read for its first 64
    KB and 256 simple commands, so one padded past that is not seen, which
    leaves the thread as guarded as before. Its output is read for `NAME=value`
    lines, so a `.env` file a command prints is flagged as well. Only a call
    with a shell command is read: a file tool's result is the file, which the
    list covers. The
    label is a record like `secret-path-read`; it does not feed the Full
    access egress tag, which still keys on a protected path, so the tag means
    what it meant.
- **Measured friction** (macOS 27, below Full access, fake files in a
  throwaway home): a planted `~/.ssh/id_test` is refused while
  `~/.ssh/config`, `known_hosts`, and public keys read; `ssh-add -l` lists a
  key through an agent socket inside `~/.ssh`; `git` commits and runs `ssh`
  for an SSH remote. Not measured: a push over SSH or HTTPS to a real server,
  a real publish, and a container pull.
- **Known gaps.** At Full access a shell command, or any program the agent
  starts, can read a protected file: only Octant's own file tools and
  redaction stand in the way, by decision. On Linux a protected file absent
  when a confined runtime starts is not covered, because Bubblewrap would
  have to create a placeholder in the person's home folder first; a file
  created mid-session is covered from the next launch. Below Full access
  Claude Code's commands run in Claude Code's own sandbox, which the guard
  cannot join; the Project-root rule and the approvals hold them, and its
  file tools are refused by Octant's gate. Linux launches are covered by
  tests of the covers they build, not yet by a measured run.

### Octant Shield

Octant Shield is Octant's own automatic approval reviewer (maintainer
decision, 2026-10-31). Its Judge is built for every runtime below, subagents
included, with the picker and the Settings and Project choices (build order
steps 1 to 3), its Watcher for the results Octant hands a model (step 4),
safe networks for provider runtimes and harness commands (step 5), and the server registry with
its SSH rules (step 6), with the gaps each part names below. It answers the
approval prompts
that would otherwise go to the person, for every runtime that routes
approvals through Octant: Octant Harness, Claude Code (`canUseTool`), Codex
(app-server approval requests), OpenCode (`permission.asked`), ACP agents
(`session/request_permission`, Mistral Vibe included), and Pi (through its
extension). It is the model-reviewed approval reviewer first planned for the
harness, extended to every runtime. Shield has two parts that never share
input: the Watcher reads outside content and the Judge answers approvals.

**Place in the levels.** At the Reviewed
[guardrail level](#security-and-authority) the person chooses the reviewer:
the provider's own, or Octant Shield. The picker label stays Auto, and Auto
is offered for every runtime that routes approvals through Octant. The
default reviewer is the provider's own where it has one (Claude Code, Codex,
and Mistral Vibe's auto-approve mode) and Octant Shield everywhere else.
Settings › Access sets "Auto reviewer: Provider's own / Octant Shield" as an
account default with a Project override. Auto falls back to Ask first only
when no reviewer can run, for example when no Shield model is reachable, and
the picker says why.

**Judge.** Each prompt passes three stages in order:

1. **Hard lines and deny rules.** Anything outside Shield's authority goes to
   the person or is refused; Shield never allows it. The malicious-call rules
   below belong here.
2. **Fast allow rules,** with no model call: reads and edits inside the bound
   root or one of the Project's extra folders, the Project's own test or build
   command, read-only Git, and SSH to a registered server within its
   profile. Egress to a safe network is allowed: a call that names its
   destinations (a fetch, or a `network-access` prompt naming a host and
   port) passes when every one is a place the person trusts for the
   thread's Project, while Network limits are on (rule `safe-network`).
3. **Model judgment** for everything else. The Judge sees only the person's
   own messages in this thread, the pending call (tool, arguments, working
   directory), the bound root, the level, the thread's taint state, and the
   Watcher's labels. It never sees tool results, file contents, or fetched web
   content, so text injected there cannot steer it. It answers allow, ask, or
   deny with a one-sentence reason. A malformed answer, a timeout, or an
   unreachable model means ask: Shield fails closed to the person.

**Malicious calls.** Rules first, then the Judge, catch these, and they go to
the person or are refused, never allowed by Shield: reading secrets followed
by network egress, piping a download into a shell, obfuscated commands
(encoded payloads, eval of fetched text), persistence (login items, launch
agents, cron, shell startup files), credential and keychain access, mass
deletion, rewriting history on a shared branch, and disabling security
settings.

**Authority limits.** Shield grants per call only. It never creates a
standing rule or a thread or Project grant and never widens the OS sandbox
past the thread's level; a `network-access` answer yields `call` rules only,
as the [egress rules](#security-and-authority) state for the reviewer. Once a
thread is tainted, Shield cannot allow irreversible, publish, or new-egress
classes; those go to the person, as taint already withdraws the provider's
own reviewer. After 3 denials in a row, or 20 in one thread, Shield pauses
and the next call goes to the person.

**Watcher.** The Watcher reads outside content as it enters the thread, with
deterministic detectors and no model call. Built for every successful result
of an app-managed tool and of a plugin MCP server, and of what an adapter sees
a runtime's own web search or fetch return (an ACP agent's content items,
the results Codex reports on a standalone search, and the text items of an
OpenCode web tool's result); a search Codex's model provider runs itself
reports no results and is marked but not read. Allowed; not built yet:
remote command output of a runtime other than Codex (an Octant Harness
command's output is an app-managed tool result and is read). It labels injection-shaped content: instructions aimed at the
agent, hidden or encoded text, requests to exfiltrate, and fake authority. It
can only raise: it marks the thread tainted, puts a visible marker on that
tool row, and tells the Judge "tainted". It never allows anything. It runs at
every level; at Full access it only records and marks: a quiet tag on the
tool row and a small mark on the thread card, never a prompt or a block. Each
label is journaled as an outside-content source, so it names the finding in
the person's review of the mark and is forgotten when the person clears it;
the Judge is told the label kinds, never the text, and a subagent's labels
count beside its parent's.

**Safe networks.** The person names trusted places in Settings › Access
(account default, Project override): hosts, domains, address ranges, and
private-network tags. Egress to a trusted place passes by rule; anything else
goes to the Judge at Reviewed and to the person at Guarded. Each decision is
journaled per host. Built for provider runtimes on macOS and Linux and for
Octant Harness commands, behind the Network limits switch, which
ships off ([provider runtime network](#provider-runtime-network)): a `host` place
matches that name, a `domain` the name and every name under it, a range is
CIDR, and the tags are `this-mac` (loopback), `local-network` (the private
IPv4 ranges and IPv6 unique-local addresses), and `overlay-network`
(100.64.0.0/10); any place may name a port. A range that reaches a
link-local address is refused. Each list is journaled whole, journal first, as
`safe-networks.places-set@1` on the `safe-networks` aggregate (the account's
fixed id, or the Project's), and `safe-networks.project-override-cleared@1`
returns a Project to the default, and `safe-networks.limits-set@1` records the
Network limits switch; startup replays them. Only a person at a
local window changes them (`GET`/`POST /api/access/safe-networks`). A harness
command's proxy falls back to the places of its thread's Project after the
thread's and Project's rules refuse, and a private answer passes for it only
through a place, as for a runtime. Taint suspends places for a command as it
suspends standing rules, so a marked thread's command reaches only the hosts
a person confirmed for it. A runtime's own bytes taint no thread, but a
launch that names its thread (Claude's own process and its sandbox, through
the session a running Code turn holds or a Work request's thread) loses its
places while that thread is marked, and an open tunnel a place carried
closes at once; a launch no thread holds (a probe, and OpenCode, ACP
agents, Pi, and Codex, which serve a folder) keeps them. A mark that cannot
be read counts as marked. The Judge's `safe-network` rule comes after its
taint limits, so a marked thread's network call goes to the person whatever
place it names. _Rationale:_ the Judge reads places only from a call that
names its destinations, never from a shell command, because `curl -d @file`
sends more than its words show; and only while limits are on, so turning
the switch off returns Shield to exactly the thread's and Project's own
rules, as it does the proxies.
Bytes a command receives from a place taint its thread as any other
command's do. With limits on, an unlisted host goes to Shield where Shield
reviews the thread at Auto, for a runtime that says it runs at Auto (Claude's
own process and its sandbox) and for every harness command, whose
`network-access` prompt it answers per call; anything Shield does not allow
goes to the person. _Rationale:_ places apply to commands only while limits
