are on, like everything else here, so turning the switch off returns every
command to exactly its thread and Project rules.

**Servers over SSH,** in Work and Code alike:

- The person registers their own servers: a host alias from their SSH config,
  a user, and an action profile (Read-only, Operate, or Admin).
- Keys stay out of the agent. Octant hands the SSH session the person's SSH
  agent socket or the credential broker; the agent never reads key files, and
  Shield refuses reads of key paths.
- SSH to a registered server passes by rule; to an unregistered host it goes
  to the person.
- Each remote command is judged like a local one, by the server's profile.
  Read-only allows status, logs, disk, process, and service-status reads.
  Operate adds service restarts, package updates, and deploys the person
  described. Admin adds config edits. Destructive or lock-out actions
  (firewall changes that can cut access, user or key removal, disk and
  partition changes, deleting data, rebooting a production host) go to the
  person at every level below Full access.
- Every remote command and its exit status is journaled with the host, and
  remote output passes through the Watcher.
- A per-server notes file (runbook) the person points to is given to the
  agent as context, never as authority.
- A Project bound to a folder on a server is judged by that server's profile
  too, and never by this host's safe places or protected paths
  ([Server Projects](design/server-projects.md#threads)).

**Servers as built.** The registry is Settings › Access › Servers: an
account list, and per Project an optional list of its own that replaces the
account list for that Project's threads. A server is its alias, user, profile,
the deploy commands the person described (Operate and Admin run them exactly
as written), an optional absolute runbook path, and how it signs in: the
person's SSH agent (`ssh-agent`, the default and what a server registered
before the choice means) or a key Octant keeps (`octant-key`). Each change is journaled
whole, journal first, as `shield-servers.server-set@1` or
`shield-servers.server-removed@1` on the `shield-servers` aggregate; a
Project's list is journaled whole as `shield-servers.project-servers-set@1`
under the Project's id, and `shield-servers.project-override-cleared@1`
returns the Project to the account list. Startup replays them; only a person
at a local window changes them (`GET`/`POST /api/shield/servers`, with
`?projectId=` for a Project's list). The Judge, the confined path below, the
record, and the notes all read the thread's Project's list. An alias is unique without regard to case, as ssh
matches `Host` patterns, and a runbook inside a key or credential folder is
refused. The rules are pure policy in `packages/domain/src/shieldServerPolicy.ts`,
checked against the real-world command set in
`packages/domain/src/shieldServerFixtures.ts` on every test run, and the Judge
applies them to every command that starts with `ssh`:

- Only a call that reads as one plain `ssh [options] [user@]host [command]`
  can pass; a command that also runs, redirects, or expands anything locally,
  or runs `ssh` anywhere but first (after a separator, in a substitution),
  goes to the person, since a word check cannot tell which server it
  reaches. The word `ssh` inside a message or a search pattern is not a call.
- An option that names a key file (`-i`, `IdentityFile`) is refused; one that
  can open a tunnel or run a local program (`-L`, `-R`, `-D`, `-A`, `-J`,
  `-F`, `ProxyCommand`, and any `-o` key outside a short list of connection
  timings) goes to the person, as do a login session with no command and a
  user other than the registered one.
- The remote command meets the malicious-call rules except raising privilege
  (`sudo` on the person's own server is what a profile grants), then is split
  into its simple commands, including those inside a substitution, and each is
  placed: a lock-out or destructive part makes the whole command go to the
  person at every profile, then a read of a secret path goes to the person,
  then a tainted thread may only read, then anything no profile names, or
  text the remote shell would expand, glob, or redirect, goes to the model,
  and last the server's profile allows its tiers and sends the rest to the
  person. A program named by a path outside the system's `bin` folders is
  unknown whatever its name; `sed` counts only as an in-place edit (Admin);
  `ip` reads only with `show` or `list`; a package option that sets
  configuration, `pm2 start`, and a `certbot` hook make a command unknown;
  any state change to SSH or network units, a power target, a recursive
  change on a system folder, removing an SSH or boot package, and `kill -1`
  are lock-out actions.
- `scp` and `rsync` read the same way: every `[user@]host:path` operand
  must name a registered server as its user, with options that only tune the
  copy (`-e`, `--rsh`, `--rsync-path`, a daemon or URL operand, scp's `-3`,
  `-A`, `-R`, `-S`, `-J`, `-F`, and non-plain `-o` go to the person; a key
  file is refused). A download is a read; an upload is a configuration change
  (Admin). A deleting sync (`--delete*`, `--remove-source-files`) or an
  upload to a sign-in or boot path is a lock-out action; a secret path on the
  server goes to the person, and a secret file on this computer is refused as
  reading secrets then sending them out, as for any command. Every file on
  this computer must lie inside the Project, else the person decides. An
  rsync option the rules do not name, or a remote path the server's shell
  would expand or run (legacy scp and rsync pass it to that shell), goes to
  the model, and on a tainted thread to the person.

Every `ssh` command an Octant Harness shell runs, at every level, is journaled
under its thread as `shield-remote-commands.ran@1` with the host (left out
when the command names it only at run time, as `ssh "$HOST"`), the
registered server when it is one, the command (credential-shaped text
redacted, cut to 2 KB), and how it ended with its exit code; output is not kept
there. A command whose record cannot be journaled returns no output. Its
output reaches the model as every harness command's does, through the
Watcher. Each harness shell gets the person's SSH agent socket as
`SSH_AUTH_SOCK` when the host process has one that is a live socket, and
nothing that names a key. Work and Code turns on every runtime carry the
thread's servers and their runbooks (the first 8 KB of each, read when the
turn starts) as a notes block that says it grants nothing; a provider
runtime's turn gets the same block a harness turn does.

**Confined commands.** Below Full access, on macOS and Linux, a harness
command that is one plain `ssh`, `scp`, or `rsync` call to registered
servers gets, for that command only, from the host
(`apps/server/src/shield/serverSshAccess.ts`):

- a relay per server it names, which carries bytes to the address the
  person's own `ssh -G <alias>` resolves and nowhere else, so the command
  reaches no other host; a server the person's config reaches through
  `ProxyJump` or `ProxyCommand` gets no relay. On macOS the relay is a
  loopback port, and Seatbelt opens only these ports beside the egress
  proxy. On Linux it is a Unix socket in the host's private folder, which
  the capsule binds read-only, and the capsule's forwarder listens on one
  loopback port inside the capsule per server (from 2201) and carries each
  connection to that server's socket;
- an agent socket the host owns, in a private folder, that passes the
  person's SSH agent only the requests to list keys, sign a login, and bind a
  session to a host key, and answers adding, removing, or locking a key with
  a failure; the command's `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` names it. A server that signs in
  with a key Octant keeps gets, in the same folder, an agent socket of its
  own that lists only that key and hands each sign request for it to the
  credential broker; the server's config names that socket, so its login
  never falls back to the person's agent, and with no key in the broker it
  offers none;
- an SSH config, a known-hosts file, and `ssh`, `scp`, and `rsync` wrappers
  first on `PATH`, written into the command's own script folder, which it
  reads and cannot write. Each server is its alias with the relay's port, the
  registered user, the host keys the person's known-hosts files record for it
  (read by `ssh-keygen -F` on the host), strict host key checking, and
  forwarding, proxy commands, local commands, and connection sharing off;
- on macOS, the user-database lookup `ssh` makes for the person's own
  account (on Linux the capsule already reads `/etc`).

The secret guard's list is untouched: the key files stay unreadable, and the
person's own config and known hosts are read only on the host. A command that
does more than one plain call, or names no registered server, gets none of
this and reaches no server. Rationale: Seatbelt cannot name a remote host, so
per-server loopback relays are the narrowest network grant; the person's own
agent stays the default because it already holds their keys and never hands
them out, and the filter keeps a command from changing what it holds. On Linux the forwarder carries a
server's port straight to its relay rather than through the egress proxy as
a `CONNECT`, as the tool bridge's ports go: the relay already reaches one
address and nothing else, the proxy would refuse that address as private,
and macOS's Seatbelt rule likewise opens the relay beside the proxy, not
through it. A provider runtime's own commands reach a server as below.

**Guarded.** The first connection to each host in a thread asks the person,
naming the host ("First connection to web1 in this thread"), and is never
covered by a remembered approval; once allowed, later commands to that host
follow the level as any command does. The hosts are held in host memory, so a
restart asks again. At Auto, Shield's rules decide first, as above.

**Provider runtimes' own commands.** A runtime's shell commands that reach a
server are recorded as `shield-remote-commands.ran@1` when the runtime names
the command: Codex names every command and reports its exit status, and
Claude Code names a command only when it is a plain `ssh`, `scp`, or `rsync`
call, without an exit status. A Codex command's output from a server passes
the Watcher as `remote-command` outside content. A runtime that names no
command (OpenCode, ACP agents, Pi) keeps Shield's journaled decision as its
record. A failure with no exit status is recorded as `unavailable`, since it
may not have run.

A runtime runs its shell commands itself, so Octant cannot open a path per
command as it does for a harness command. Below Full access, outside Plan
(which runs no shell), each launch of Codex, OpenCode, an ACP agent, Pi, or
Claude Code gets instead, for its life, from the host
(`apps/server/src/shield/runtimeServerAccess.ts`):

- a private folder it reads and cannot write (a read root of its OS
  profile; on Linux bound read-only into its capsule) holding an SSH config,
  a known-hosts file, and `ssh`, `scp`, and `rsync` wrappers first on its
  `PATH`. Each of the Project's registered servers is its alias at the
  address the person's own `ssh -G` resolves, with the registered user, the
  host keys the person's known-hosts files record, strict host key checking,
  and forwarding, proxy commands, local commands, and connection sharing off;
  a server reached through `ProxyJump` or `ProxyCommand` gets no entry;
- an agent socket in that folder, named by its `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, that signs a
  login only on a connection `ssh` first bound, with OpenSSH's
  `session-bind@openssh.com`, to the host key of one of the Project's
  registered servers (the host key's signature over the session id is
  checked), for that session, as that server's registered user, and never
  on a forwarded or second binding. It lists the person's agent's keys and
  passes them only listing and signing; for a server that signs in with a
  key Octant keeps it offers that key and has the credential broker sign,
  and never signs for it with the person's agent. Several registered
  servers on one machine share its host key; the login's user picks among
  them, and so does the key `ssh` offers. It reads the Project's list again
  at each binding, so a server removed meanwhile, or whose alias, user, or
  sign-in changed, signs nothing more in that launch;
- on macOS, the user-database lookup `ssh` makes for the person's own
  account, in the runtime's profile.

A launch receives the folder through the runtime network seam
(`ProviderServerAccessPort` in `apps/server/src/network/providerRuntimeNetwork.ts`),
which the host fills, so no driver reaches the server registry itself.
Claude Code's own process runs outside Octant's profile below Full access,
so a command it runs outside its own sandbox could rewrite the folder; the
agent socket's host-key check, which lives on the host, still decides what
signs. Reaching the address is the runtime's own network: open while Network limits
are off. With limits on, a runtime's own `ssh` reaches no server, since its
OS rules open only its egress proxy, which carries no SSH. A runtime's own
sandbox applies on top: Claude Code's reads only the Project and reaches the
network only through its proxy, and Codex's turns the network off, so `ssh`
works there only for a command the runtime runs outside its sandbox, after
its own approval, as in the provider's own app. Each command still reaches
Shield as the runtime asks about it. _Rationale:_ a launch-wide grant is the
narrowest a runtime allows, so the agent socket, not the network, limits it
to registered servers: a login signs only after the server has proved it
holds a registered host key, so the runtime's `ssh` can sign in nowhere else
whatever address it dials; an `ssh` older than OpenSSH 8.9 sends no binding
and gets no signature. A per-launch relay under Network limits is not part of
this; it would need each runtime's profile to open the relays.

**The credential broker for SSH.** For a server registered to sign in with
a key Octant keeps, the credential broker makes an Ed25519 key the first time
the person asks for it (**Show key** in Settings, `show-server-key` on
`POST /api/shield/servers`, a local window only, for a server whose sign-in
is `octant-key`) and keeps it in a credential namespace of its own (the
`app.octant.ssh-keys.v1` Keychain service, the `octant.ssh-keys.v1` Secret
Service attribute), keyed by the server's id. Its routes (`/v1/ssh-keys/ensure`,
`public`, `sign`, `delete`, in `packages/host-runtime/src/sshKeyBroker.ts`)
give out only the key's public line and a signature, and sign only an SSH
public-key login request (RFC 4252, or OpenSSH's host-bound form) for that
very key; no route returns the private key, so neither the server process nor
a command ever holds it. The person adds the public line to the server's
`authorized_keys` themselves. A server keeps its id when a Project's list is
saved again (by its alias), and a Project's copy of an account server shares
that server's id, so editing a list never orphans an installed key; a key is
deleted once no list names its server with `octant-key`. _Rationale:_ the broker makes the key rather
than importing one, so Octant never reads a key file and a key the person
uses elsewhere never enters Octant; and it signs logins only, so the socket a
command holds cannot sign anything it could use elsewhere.

**Model and privacy.** By default Shield uses the thread's own provider
account with that provider's smallest model, so no new party sees the work.
The person may pick another configured
account and model under Automatic model calls below, a local endpoint
included. Shield
sends no telemetry, and its calls count against the existing spend ceilings.

**Automatic model calls.** The jobs Octant runs on a model without the
person typing, today the Judge and person memory's distilling, share one
Settings surface: Settings › Providers & Models › Automatic model calls. For
each job the person keeps the default (the provider of the thread the work is
about, with that provider's smallest model, unchanged) or picks one configured
account and one of its models, an API-key account included. The Judge's choice
is stored as `CodeSettings.shieldModel` and memory's as
`PersonMemorySettings.distillModel`; the surface is the one place either is
chosen, and both are changed only from a window on this host (a paired device
cannot). The surface says in plain words that what the job reads goes to the
chosen provider: the Judge's input (the person's recent messages, the pending
call and the Project's root, never tool results or outside content) and
memory's (a thread's title and the person's own messages, secrets redacted as
today). Rationale: account selection is fully manual by decision, so there is
no rotation and no failover; if the chosen account is removed, turned off, not
ready or at a reported usage limit, the Judge sends that decision to the person
(`model-account-unavailable`, journaled with the chosen account) and never
allows it itself, and distilling returns the thread to the next pass without
calling another account. A rule that decides without a model (a fast allow, a
hard line) is unaffected. Each call is journaled with its account: the Judge
decision names its model, and the call's `shield-review` or `person-memory`
usage row names the provider account and model, so Usage shows which account
spent it. The surface keeps the two existing stored fields rather than adding a third
setting, so no migration is needed and the default is exactly the old behavior;
"at its limit" means only a limit the provider has reported. The harness's advisor review is a separate, slot-routed job and is
not folded in.

**Journal.** Every Shield decision is journaled with the reviewer, the model,
the rule or reason, and the latency, and shows on the tool row in the
transcript.

**Inheritance.** Subagents inherit the parent's reviewer. A routine may run
at Auto with Shield unattended; anything Shield escalates waits as an
approval for the person.

**Limits.** Shield sees only the calls a runtime asks about. What a runtime
does without asking stays confined by the sandbox, which remains the hard
wall. A model reviewer is not a guarantee.

**Evaluation.** The repository keeps a fixture set of known-safe and
known-unsafe calls, and a release with Shield requires measuring its
false-allow rate on that set. The set lives in
`packages/domain/src/shieldEvaluationFixtures.ts`; every test run checks that
the rule stages answer each fixture as recorded and never allow a
known-unsafe one, and `bun run shield:eval` measures the whole pipeline,
running the model stage only against an endpoint named in its environment.

**As built.** The rule stages, the prompt the model sees, the answer it must
give, and the brakes are pure policy in `packages/domain/src/shieldJudgePolicy.ts`;
the host runs them in `apps/server/src/shield/`. The Judge's input type has no
field for a tool result, a file's contents, or a fetched page, and the
person's messages are read from the thread's own turn prompts, never from what
the agent read, so nothing outside can reach the model. The Project's own
test and build commands are the `test`, `build`, `typecheck`, and `lint`
scripts of its root `package.json` under the package manager its lockfile
names, and the standard commands of a Cargo, Swift, or Go package at the
root; a command passes by rule only with plain arguments after it. Read-only
Git is `status`, `diff`, `log`, `show`, `blame`, and the other subcommands
that only read, with no shell composition and no flag that writes a file.
The model is a tool-less one-shot session started in a scratch folder
outside every Project, on the thread's provider account with the catalogue's
smallest tier by name (a nano, mini, or haiku model, for example), else the
thread's own model; it has 20 seconds. Each model call reserves a small
bound against the thread's and Project's spend ceilings first, so a ceiling
that refuses hands the call to the person, and what the call used is
journaled under the reviewed thread (request shape `shield-review`, on its
own `shield-review-usage` aggregate) before the reservation is released, so
the usage ledger and every ceiling over the thread count it; a call that
reported nothing is recorded as unreported spend. A fast allow reads a
command exactly as written: any quoting, escape, expansion, glob, separator,
redirection, or whitespace other than a space or a tab sends it to the model,
and read-only Git refuses any option, or unambiguous prefix of one, that
writes a file, runs a program, reads outside the repository, or switches
repositories (`--output`, `--ext-diff`, `--textconv`, `--no-index`,
`--exec-path`, `--git-dir`, `--work-tree`, `-O`, and the like). The brakes are kept per thread in
the host process: a restart gives a paused thread back to Shield, which
widens nothing because every counted decision was a refusal. A class the
person already allowed for the session goes through on their word without
asking Shield. On the Octant Harness an allow or deny is journaled as a
settled harness approval carrying the decision, an ask is journaled as the
pending approval with Shield's reason, and the Code transcript shows each
decision as an `approval-reviewed` row beside the tool rows. A Work thread
at Auto is reviewed the same way, judged against its Project folder, with
its own turn prompts as the person's messages and its model calls counted
against its spend ceilings as a Work thread. On the Octant Harness its
decisions are journaled with its harness approvals, and the running turn
shows each as a review row among its tool steps, keyed by the call it was
for. Claude Code, Codex,
OpenCode, ACP agents, and Pi on a Work thread take the path they take on a
Code thread: the approval reaches Shield before it becomes a request, an
allow or deny goes back to the runtime for that one call and nobody is
asked, an ask or a failure becomes the ordinary request for the person, and
the decision shows on the Work turn's transcript as a review row among its
tool steps. Work's Auto reviewer is Settings' choice, since a Work Project
has no override. A subagent asks
under its parent's reviewer, judged against its own worktree, with its own
taint counted beside the parent's. A provider runtime's prompt reaches
Shield with the pending call the runtime described: each driver keeps it
beside the pending request and hands it over through the provider seam's
`approvalCall`, never on the approval event, so nothing journaled, exported,
or shown carries it. Only the fields a reviewer judges cross (the command, its
working directory, the paths and URLs the call names, a sandbox request's
permissions), with credential-shaped text redacted and cut to 8 KB; a write's
contents, a tool's output, and the runtime's own reason stay out. Codex's
request to widen its own sandbox is a privilege change, which Shield hands to
the person. An allow or deny goes straight back to the runtime for that one
call and does not count toward the three refusals that end a turn; an ask is
the ordinary approval. Every automatic answer, and every answer on a child
run's behalf, carries the seam's one-call scope (`ProviderApprovalAnswer.scope:
"once"`): no driver remembers it for the session or the Project or asks the
runtime to, whatever the person's persistence setting, so one allow never
authorizes a later call nobody reviewed. An OpenCode v2 permission's
`resources` are read as the paths, command, or address it targets. Claude Code and Codex keep their own reviewer at Auto
by default; once the person chooses Shield for the account or the Project,
the thread starts without the provider's reviewer, so its prompts reach
Octant and Shield answers them. Mistral Vibe's own auto-approve mode is
built, so Shield is its alternative reviewer; Shield is the only reviewer for
OpenCode, every other ACP agent, and Pi.

The choices are built for Code: Settings › Code › Access has **Auto
reviewer** (Provider's own / Octant Shield, stored as `CodeSettings.autoReviewer`);
the Judge's model is chosen under Automatic model calls (stored as
`CodeSettings.shieldModel`), and a Code Project's overview overrides the
reviewer (`change-code-project-auto-reviewer`, journaled
`project.code-auto-reviewer-changed@1`). The picker offers Auto, marked
Recommended, wherever a reviewer can run: the provider's own, or Shield on a
runtime that routes its approvals through Octant and is enabled; its
description names which reviewer answers. Where none can run (a disabled
provider, a runtime that raises no approvals) Auto is listed unavailable with
the reason and a thread set to it asks first.

**Watcher as built.** The Watcher's detectors are pure policy in
`packages/domain/src/shieldWatcherPolicy.ts`, and it calls no model: a model
reading every result would spend on every call and would itself be what the
injected text targets, while a detector that misses leaves the thread exactly
as guarded as before. Its labels are instructions aimed at the agent
(`agent-instructions`), hidden text (`hidden-text`: tag or bidi-override
characters, a run of zero-width characters, or instructions in an HTML comment
or hidden element), encoded text (`encoded-text`: base64 that decodes to
prose, or an order to decode and run), a request to send secrets out
(`exfiltration-request`), a false claim of authority (`fake-authority`), and a
read of a path the secret guard protects (`secret-path-read`, raised only once
the guard's list is handed to it), and a shell call that printed a
secret-holding environment variable (`secret-env-print`; see
[Secret guard](#secret-guard)). The host runs it over every successful
result of an app-managed tool (the Octant Harness's tools and Octant's own
tools for every runtime) and of a plugin MCP server, before the model reads
it. Each label is journaled as an outside-content ingestion under the source
`shield-watcher-<label>`, so it marks the thread even for a result that would
not mark it otherwise (a file inside the root, a command's output), names the
finding in the person's review of the mark, and is forgotten with the mark
when the person clears it. The result goes on unchanged; a label that cannot
be journaled withholds the result, as a mark that cannot be journaled does.
The Judge's input carries the labels as kinds, never text, and a labelled
thread counts as tainted. A Code tool row whose result was outside content
carries the tag "Outside content", followed by what the Watcher found, in the
warning role; at Full access the tag stays quiet. A Code board card carries a
small mark while the thread is marked, in the warning role when a label was
found. A runtime's own web search or fetch hands its result straight to its model, so
the thread is marked when the call starts and nothing can be withheld. Where the
adapter sees the result text (an ACP agent puts it in the call's content items;
`rawOutput` is never read), it sends an `outside-content-result` event, which
carries the bounded text for the Watcher only: the turn runners run the detectors
over it, journal each label beside the read, and drop the text, so it is never
journaled, shown, or passed on. A label that cannot be journaled stops the turn
as an unmarked read does. Codex's web search item carries `results` (opaque
JSON, codex-cli 0.164.0) when Codex ran a standalone search, and the adapter
hands their string values over on completion; a search the model's provider
runs itself reports `results` as null, so that search is marked but not read.
OpenCode's tool success carries the result as content items (opencode 2.2.0
`Tool.Content`), and the adapter hands over the text items of a call it marked
(`webfetch`, `websearch`, `codesearch`, or a provider-run tool), never a file
item. Both arrive after the model has the page, so the labels inform later
calls rather than this one. The Chat and Work tool rows carry the same "Outside
content" tag as Code's: the turn's tool steps hold the Watcher's labels for a
runtime web tool and for an app-managed tool's result, and a later progress or
result message keeps them. The Judge still never sees the text, only the labels.
The secret guard's list in force is handed to the Watcher and the Judge (see
[Secret guard](#secret-guard)), so `secret-path-read` is raised for every call
of Octant's own tools that names a protected path, and a refused call's row
carries the tag too. A Work tool row's tag is quiet at Full access, as Code's
is. A client built before a tool step carried Shield's decision reads a Work
turn with a review row as an ordinary completed step: clients decode a host's
answer ignoring fields they do not know (`decodeHostAnswer`), and a contract
test decodes such a turn with the older step shape.

**Build order.** (1) Octant Harness; (2) every runtime through the approval
path; (3) the picker and Settings; (4) the Watcher; (5) safe networks; (6)
the server registry and SSH. Work gets SSH under the rule that
[Work and Code are guarded identically](#security-and-authority).

## Package map

| Package                   | Responsibility                                                                                                                                          | Depends on                                                        |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `packages/contracts`      | Effect Schema entities, commands, events, RPC and wire contracts; no runtime logic                                                                      | `effect`                                                          |
| `packages/domain`         | Pure policies and state transitions (modes, tool calls, approvals, remote access, boards, canvas, …)                                                    | contracts, theme                                                  |
| `packages/theme`          | Semantic theme schema, presets, backgrounds, typography, importer, contrast                                                                             | contracts                                                         |
| `packages/provider-sdk`   | `ProviderDriver` interface, normalized runtime events, discovery, conformance harnesses                                                                 | contracts, `effect`                                               |
| `packages/plugin-host`    | Extension manifests, component model, activation ladder, addressing, bundled skills and provider-driver plugins, Agent Plugins loader                   | contracts, `yaml`                                                 |
| `packages/plugin-api`     | Public plugin manifest, component, and contribution schemas for third parties (re-exports contracts/extensions)                                         | contracts                                                         |
| `packages/host-runtime`   | Host paths, owner receipts, service lifecycle, credential broker, host OAuth runners, bridge secret, diagnostics, redaction (shared by desktop and CLI) | —                                                                 |
| `packages/client-runtime` | Authenticated transport, per-feature clients, reconnect, remote pairing, host federation registry and merged reads                                      | contracts, domain                                                 |
| `packages/cli`            | `octant` binary: headless server run, service manager, status, `web` launcher, artifact install                                                         | contracts, host-runtime                                           |
| `apps/server`             | Authoritative control plane: routes, services, journal, projections, providers, tools, extensions, remote gateway                                       | contracts, domain, plugin-host, host-runtime, provider-sdk, theme |
| `apps/desktop`            | Electron shell: windows, menus, native credential-store integration, pickers, signed updates, server process lifecycle, packaging                       | contracts, domain, host-runtime                                   |
| `apps/web`                | React renderer for desktop and paired browsers                                                                                                          | client-runtime, contracts, domain, plugin-host, theme             |
| `apps/mobile`             | Expo iOS/Android remote-control client                                                                                                                  | client-runtime, contracts, domain                                 |

Dependencies point inward: no package imports an app, and `contracts` imports
nothing first-party.

## Current Release Boundary

This section is the one statement of what the first release includes and
defers, and it owns the architectural rules behind it.

**Where the release stands (2026-11-05).** The first release is the Apple
Silicon technical preview with the provider-neutral plugin/skill marketplace.
Builds of `main` are meant to publish daily on the `preview` ring as the second
app Octant Nightly, and on-demand pre-releases of the next stable on the
`candidate` ring as Octant's Preview channel, as GitHub pre-releases named
`v0.1.0-<ring>.<date>.<build>`; each carries a macOS zip and a linux-x64
AppImage. Nightly is a usable client; a scheduled or rollback Nightly run is
built and published only after its secret-free
[usable-client preflight](design/nightly-app.md#the-usable-client-preflight)
passes, and the first scheduled publication still needs a maintainer's
approval. The stable ring (a `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` tag, approved
in the `stable` environment) has not been used, so Octant itself has not
shipped. The first release counts as shipped when a maintainer approves the
first stable version; daily builds stay previews. That first stable release is
the Apple Silicon build, and Linux is not part of it.

The release is signed with a Developer ID, notarized, and updates itself.
Those three are one deliverable: an updater on an unsigned app is an
unauthenticated code-delivery channel, and on macOS Squirrel.Mac refuses a
replacement that does not satisfy the running app's designated requirement. A
ring publishes a signed feed or publishes none. A local package built without
signing credentials a maintainer holds is unsigned.

Cross-platform desktop (macOS, Linux, Windows) remains authorized: the Linux
desktop shell, then the Linux AppImage with its signed feed, then Windows, and
Windows Work and Code only after an explicitly approved Windows confinement
design is documented. Everything on the work board is in scope for the first
proper preview release (maintainer decision, 2026-11-06, which replaces the
2026-10-26 post-preview track): mobile maturity (Android internal builds,
redacted push, capture and voice, public store distribution), a full LSP /
extension host / debugger companion, enterprise directory OAuth and cloud-IAM
provider identity, disposable Linux desktops for headless hosts, third-party
provider-driver plugins, and the EU/GDPR compliance package (legal review is
still required before it ships). There is no separate post-preview track.
Public store distribution, the Windows sequence below, and the full
LSP / extension host / debugger companion are release-scope choices the
maintainers schedule, not safety rules; none of them protects an invariant by
itself.

Also in scope, each design-first (build it only once its owning specification
documents its authority, privacy, and release boundaries):

- Remote SSH development environments (maintainer decision, 2026-10-31,
  replacing the 2026-10-29 out-of-scope rule): a Code or Work Project bound to
  a folder on a registered server is built ([Server Projects](design/server-projects.md)).
  An agent in a local Project reaches another machine with `ssh` through its
  shell with the person's own SSH agent and configuration
  ([Modes](#modes-chat-work-and-code)).
- A hub-and-spoke topology on a person's own devices (maintainer decision,
  2026-10-28): one Octant server (running without the desktop app and serving
  the web app over a private network such as Tailscale) enrolls the person's
  other computers and phones, introduces them, fails over to a standby, and
  runs their wake and push services, including a self-hosted wake service
  ([Hub and spokes](design/hub-and-spokes.md#wake-service)). An
  Octant-operated wake service is not in scope.
- Connectors (MCP servers added by hand, imported from other tools on this Mac,
  signed in to, or chosen from the bundled catalog): user-added packages
  through the published seams and the credential broker, never a hosted
  service ([connector rules](#extensions-and-skills)).
- A Code thread's own Git and pull-request work (push, draft, ready, stacked,
  and force-with-lease on its own branch, a plain force-push the person asks
  for, title, body, labels, drafted replies a person sends, close or reopen
  with approval, and merge, auto-merge, or a stack merge the person allowed), a
  person's merge from any of their windows, phone, or web client, and
  host-local routines (Automation Center, Chat routines included), under the
  rules in [Modes](#modes-chat-work-and-code). Built: a fast-forward push;
  opening a draft, ready, or stacked pull request and editing its title, body,
  or draft state; a person's merge of one pull request from a local window; a
  person's approval or request for changes there; an agent's merge on the
  person's request in the turn, after the person approves that one merge; an
  agent's merge on a Project setting or routine; the Merge when ready and
  Auto-fix switches the person turns on there; and a thread's watch on its own
  pull request, which the person allows. The rest of the allowed actions are
  not built yet.
- Linked external secret stores, built for the 1Password CLI
  ([linked secret stores](#linked-secret-stores)): a pointer in the credential
  broker, the value fetched at use and never kept.
- The [guardrail levels](#security-and-authority) and the
  [key providers' native features](#providers). Built in Code: Ask first,
  Accept edits, Auto (with the key CLI providers' own reviewers), Plan and Full
  access. Built in Work: Auto, Ask first, Accept edits and Full access.
  [Octant Shield](#octant-shield) is in scope; its Judge is built for every
  runtime that routes approvals through Octant, and its Watcher for the
  results Octant hands a model.
- Public Canvas links, under
  [Canvas public links](design/canvas-public-links.md), served by the
  self-hostable reference app at `apps/share` in this repository. Ogard Labs
  operates no share-service instance; each user runs one or points Octant at
  another service they choose.

Out of scope: a merge or force-push an agent starts on its own initiative,
cloud scheduling, an Octant-operated hosted service, Apple physical devices,
and App Store Connect upload, submission and release (maintainer decision,
2026-10-29: Octant drives the iOS Simulator only, and an agent that needs a
device or the store uses its own provider tools).

The authorization covers design and implementation. Creating an account,
spending money, submitting to a store, deploying a hosted service,
or weakening an invariant each still needs a separate explicit action
by a maintainer. Existing scoped exceptions remain documented in this
architecture.

Desktop is one product on macOS, Linux, and Windows; platform differences are
fail-closed posture, never a second app. The desktop process owns its local
server on every OS. server. The sequence is the Linux desktop shell, then the Linux
AppImage with its signed feed, then Windows. Windows packaging, installer,
feed, and packaging CI work may start now (maintainer decision, 2026-11-06,
which lifts the 2026-10-16 ordering gate that held Windows until the macOS
preview had shipped and a Linux self-update from the signed feed had been seen
on a real image). That ordering was a release-scope choice, not a safety
rule. The Linux signed-feed update path is still the shared trust root for
every non-macOS platform, so a Windows feed builds on it and is not trusted
before the path has been exercised on a real image. Windows Work and Code stay
unavailable until an approved Windows confinement design is documented: the confinement port
supports only macOS and Linux and refuses every other platform, so Work and
Code fail closed there. Simulator, the Apple workbench, and vibrancy stay
macOS-only.

**Updates** (`apps/desktop/src/appUpdateService.ts`, `appUpdateFeed.ts`,
`packages/domain` `appUpdatePolicy`):

- Trust comes from the feed signature, never the host. Octant verifies an
  Ed25519 signature over the canonical encoding of the feed's `release`
  object (the wrapper's `schemaVersion` is validated, not signed) against a
  public key compiled into the app, then requires the offered release to be strictly newer and to name
  this app (`product`: `octant` or `octant-nightly`), platform, architecture,
  and the ring the app asked for. A release for the other app is refused as
  `wrong-app` ("This update is for Octant Nightly, not Octant."), on Linux
  too, where nothing after the feed checks which app an image is. Every
  signer emits `product` and every reader requires it; a feed without it is
  malformed. The artifact's
  SHA-256 is inside the signature and the downloaded bytes are hashed before
  anything installs.
- On macOS the platform updater is then handed the verified bytes through a
  loopback feed Octant serves for the install, never the public feed, and
  checks the code signature as an independent second gate. A Linux AppImage
  is not code-signed, so the feed signature and artifact hash are its whole
  trust root: Octant replaces only the image it was launched from (`APPIMAGE`)
  atomically, and refuses a package or archive launch before any request. The
  relaunched image is told which process it replaces
  (`OCTANT_REPLACED_PROCESS_ID`, removed from its environment as it starts) and
  waits, for at most a minute, until that process has exited (on Linux, exited but
  not yet reaped counts) before it asks for
  the single-instance lock, so it never starts a host while the old one is
  still stopping; the old instance keeps its lock until it exits. A platform
  with no signed channel (`supportsSignedDesktopUpdateChannel`:
  macOS and Linux today) refuses with "untrusted-signature".
- Unverifiable is refused, never downgraded: an unparseable feed, unknown key,
  version that is not strictly newer, wrong app, platform or ring, unreachable
  service, or mismatched artifact yields no install, no override, and a
  refusal naming the check. The exact two-field empty document
  (`"status": "empty"`, schema version 1) means no release in this channel,
  not that the build is current.
- Rings are `stable` (tags), `preview` (scheduled `main` builds), and
  `candidate` (on-demand builds of a chosen ref, so a test install exercises
  the real update path) at `<base>/stable/<platform>-<arch>.json`,
  `<base>/candidate/<platform>-<arch>.octant.json` and
  `<base>/preview/<platform>-<arch>.octant-nightly.json`. Settings labels
  the rings Stable, Preview (`candidate`), and Nightly (`preview`); the ids
  stay, since feed paths and version tags that installed builds follow carry
  them. A build's default ring is read from
  its version; the signed ring field is what separates the streams. The base
  is overridable but must be HTTPS. Stable and candidate ship as Octant, one
  binary whose ring is the person's in-app channel choice (Stable or Preview);
  preview ships as a second app, Octant Nightly, with its own bundle id, link
  scheme, command-line name, and icon (maintainer decision, 2026-11-05). Nightly
  shares Octant's data through Octant's running host and never runs a host on
  that folder, so the journal keeps one writer and no nightly migrates data
  Octant must still open. For development and testing it can instead run its
  own host on separate test data. Its command-line tool, `octant-nightly`,
  follows the same rule: it attaches to Octant's host (or, with test data,
  Nightly's test host) and never starts or migrates one
  ([the `octant-nightly` command](design/nightly-app.md#the-octant-nightly-command)). A person's first install is therefore Octant
  ([Octant Nightly](design/nightly-app.md)). The channel split and the
  Nightly-channel install row (packaged macOS Octant, person-started,
  feed signature, artifact hash and a Nightly-specific code requirement) are
  built; a signed install from a published Nightly build has not been
  exercised. Nightly's own host on separate test data (macOS and Linux: its own
  folder, port, logs and Keychain service names or Secret Service `service`
  values, chosen in Settings and decided once at launch) is built; a signed Nightly running it has not been
  exercised. Identity and packaging foundations
  now stamp separate app flavors and restrict each packaged updater to its
  identity's rings. A separate authenticated native window bootstrap can load
  Nightly's own renderer with a short server-enforced lease. It never loads
  the host-owning module, owns a host or migrates shared data; it can ask a
  validated installed Stable to start without a window. Incompatible
  or unsigned builds refuse. Bounded embedded frames and human input use the
  existing native Browser owner; complete Browser parity, other native brokers
  remain unfinished. Current-client retention precedes the existing terminal
  shutdown path; full signed lifecycle acceptance remains separate.
  Packaged macOS Nightly additionally seals its JavaScript entry in ASAR and
  disables alternate Node/loader entry paths. Its existing scoped terminal MCP
  command runs through a fixed bundled role. Stable uses a separately identified
  Node worker for host/tool execution and its fixed physical scoped terminal CLI;
  Code confinement does not acquire GUI-service permissions. This is a prerequisite for peer admission, not
  evidence that a signed Nightly peer or embedded Browser bridge is usable;
  the owning [fixed-entry rules](design/nightly-app.md#fixed-packaged-entry)
  preserve authenticated registration and the functional publication gate.
- Rollback is a roll-forward. The updater accepts only a strictly newer
  version, so a bad Nightly is replaced by dispatching the preview workflow
  from `main` with `rollback_ref`: it rebuilds a published `v*-preview.*` tag
  whose commit is on `main` as Nightly under a new version from the workflow's
  own date and run number. Any other ref is refused before checkout, because
  the build runs the source's own code beside the Apple credentials. The feed
  key lives only in a separate `feed` job that runs the workflow's own commit
  against the uploaded archive. Each published Octant release
  (stable and candidate) also carries `octant-host-features.json`: the native
  client protocol and the brokered features its host offers a Nightly window
  (`NIGHTLY_HOST_FEATURES`), for the Nightly preflight's compatibility check
  ([Octant Nightly](design/nightly-app.md#nightlys-own-updates)). It is
  unsigned and advisory; it must be signed or hash-pinned before it gates a
  release outside CI.
- Release notes for an offered update ride inside the signed release (at
  most 4,096 characters) and fail with it; notes for the running build are a
  bundled file read from disk, so What's New never adds a request.
- The person controls application: an update is staged and applied on a
  relaunch they start, and install waits while agents are active (a thread
  parked on an approval or question is still an active agent) or while the
  desktop cannot confirm what the host is running. A provider that is not
  signed in, not installed, or disabled never holds an install back: quitting
  asks on the same terms, because both read the one `workInFlight` reading of
  the host rather than its `attentionRequired` flag, which also marks the menu
  bar for provider readiness. This conservative reading currently counts open
  provider sessions, including idle sessions kept for another turn, so the quit
  warning describes sessions rather than claiming that each is running work.
  Automatic checks are a setting that defaults to off — a store
  that never recorded the choice decodes to off, and the host starts with
  them off until the persisted choice arrives — then checks daily once the
  person turns the switch on. A check is a
  plain GET carrying only version, platform, and architecture (the ring is in
  the path); it is not a telemetry channel.

An older ban on any updater for an unsigned build
predates the Linux AppImage feed; the rule above, where
the signed feed is the trust root for an image that has no platform signing,
is current.

Artifact replicas, when the person turns sync on, go only to a store that
person owns — a synced folder or an S3-compatible bucket. Octant operates no
storage and no relay for them. The storage provider can read the files. That
does not open a hosted relay or an Octant cloud account.

Public Canvas links are in scope under the rules in
[Canvas public links](design/canvas-public-links.md), served by the reference
share app at `apps/share` in this repository, which each user self-hosts (or
they point Octant at another service they choose; no service address is set by
default). Ogard Labs operates no share-service instance: it is not an Octant
account, a relay, or a sync store, and nothing reaches any service until the
person turns Public links on, sets an address, and approves a publish. Running
the service — its host, DNS, TLS, and operator contact — is the user's own
deployment step, documented in the `apps/share` README.

The connector / OAuth marketplace hold was lifted on 2026-10-20 under the
[Connectors and user-added MCP servers](#extensions-and-skills) rules: a
bundled first-party catalog, sign-in through the MCP authorization flow, and
servers imported from other tools' configuration on this Mac, all as
user-added packages through the published seams and the credential broker.

## Development loop

```sh
bun install --frozen-lockfile
bun run dev        # Vite renderer + Electron with hot reload; server spawned from source
bun run verify     # paths:check, wiring:check, ui:check, style:check, decisions:check, fmt:check, lint, typecheck, test, build
```

- Two stalls are logged once per occurrence so the next one is visible: a
  SQLite statement slower than `OCTANT_SLOW_STATEMENT_MS` (default 20) logs
  its SQL shape and duration, never bound values, and an event-loop lag over
  `OCTANT_EVENT_LOOP_LAG_MS` (default 100) logs the lag. Both log lines are off
  under tests unless the variable is set. The diagnostics export carries
  `hostHealth` counters (a version 2 or 3 packet) since process start: slow statement count and worst
  duration, lag event count and worst lag, in milliseconds, with no SQL text or
  route names.
- `bun run dev` starts Vite for `apps/web` and launches Electron against it.
  Renderer edits hot-reload; server edits apply on the next relaunch. On
  startup the dev script rebuilds `apps/desktop/dist/entry.mjs` whenever
  `apps/desktop/src` is newer, so `apps/desktop/src` edits need only a
  restart of `bun run dev` rather than a manual
  `bun run --cwd apps/desktop build`. It rebuilds the Canvas preview page
  (`apps/web/dist/canvas-preview/`) the same way whenever `apps/web` or the contracts, domain or theme packages
  are newer,
  and hands the host it starts `OCTANT_WEB_DIST_PATH=apps/web/dist`, so an
  agent's Canvas preview returns a picture on a development host; `octant web
--dev` does both as well.
- The server is composed by a root in `apps/server/src/server.ts` that calls
  the per-area wiring modules under `apps/server/src/wiring/` in a fixed
  order, and every module declares the reach it has as a `Pick` of the
  upstream modules' wiring types. The order is the dependency order: a value
  that depends on persistence and options alone is built first
  (`foundations`, `harnessState`, `workRequestState`), an area that holds
  per-window state registers its revocation with the authority, and an area
  that reacts to another's change subscribes to it (GitHub sign-in, pull
  request refreshes, harness questions, a person's harness pause stopping a
  Work goal loop, Chat's attachment purge and tools) instead of holding it.
  A value written at runtime has one owned holder with a read-only accessor:
  the access each running Work turn holds is recorded in `workRequestState`,
  written by the Work turn service and read by the native harness, and the
  Code runtime's running turns are kept in a registry the authority area
  builds and reads a running turn's posture from. The gateway and listener
  the remote area rebuilds at runtime live in that area behind `remoteHost`.
  The Code runtime is built from the Code and device areas, which also need
  it: the Code area hands over a builder for the Code service, which asks the
  runtime for fork points and merge-backs, and the device area hands over a
  binder for its context resolvers and routes, which ask the runtime to check
  a device action's approval. The runtime's area calls both once the runtime
  exists, so every approval and fork answer still comes from the runtime. Canvas is built right after
  the Code area, from the Work artifact projection (a foundation) and the
  image jobs the providers area owns, so Chat, Work, and the Code runtime
  take its agent tool port as a value. Agent runs come before it: Canvas adds
  a managed child's Canvas tools through the agent-run area's tool
  contributions, and the agent-run routes are built where they are
  dispatched, with the Canvas snapshot. Thread hand-off, which writes a
  Canvas from a thread export, is built with thread export in Work. The
  native harness is built right after the providers area and before Code:
  its lead fallback lives in the providers area, beside the driver options it
  builds drivers from and whose lead hook asks it; the harness owns the
  per-turn hooks every mode's turns pass through; it adds a managed child's
  harness tools through the agent-run tool contributions, ahead of Canvas;
  it reads a running Code turn's posture the way the authority does; and the
  Code runtime subscribes to a session leaving recovery. An agent run reads
  its Chat parent through the same persistence-only read `ChatService.read`
  uses.
- No module assigns a value after another has captured it (the composition
  root has no late cells). One forward reference remains, and
  `bun run wiring:check` pins its number so one can be removed but not added:
  dependency getters marked "Wired by wireX; read only after startup", which
  read a value a later module creates per use. Each marks a cycle between
  areas that needs a seam of its own to remove (Chat and the Code runtime
  against Work and Chat's thread-mention and Side Chat reads, and agent runs
  against the provider driver options); lower the ceiling in
  `scripts/check-module-wiring.ts` in the change that removes one.
- A headless Linux station: `octant server run`, then `octant web` (or
  `octant web --dev` for Vite), run as the OS user that started the host so
  it can read the bridge secret and mint the browser's launch link. Linux requires `bubblewrap` and Git 2.36 or
  newer; without `bubblewrap`, Work and Code fail closed. Stored provider
  credentials also need an unlocked freedesktop Secret Service session and
  the `secret-tool` client; without them the host still runs Chat, Work, and
  Code but reports its secret store unavailable. ADE and other boot-managed hosts should run
  `scripts/ade/start-secret-service-session.sh` on each start so the session
  bus and keyring are live (never a snapshotted socket path alone). The start
  script writes `~/.config/octant-host/session.env`; when `start` and
  `server run` are separate processes, source that file in the server-launch
  shell before the host — start-script exports do not cross the subprocess
  boundary. Until a Cloud Agent Saved environment executes the `start` hook,
  run the script manually and source `session.env` the same way. Provider
  CLIs are ordinary host binaries: install one to a user-writable path such
  as `~/.local/bin` and point the provider instance at that absolute path.
- `octant web --dev` changes only the renderer: it starts Vite and attaches it
  to the canonical Machine host. Browser QA and Electron share the same store,
  Projects, threads, and live journal. Destructive tests use an explicit
  `OCTANT_DATA_DIR`; development mode never creates an implicit profile. The
  Vite page is not the host, so the tab remembers the `serverUrl` it was
  launched with (per renderer origin, in tab session storage, judged again like
  a typed address); a reload or in-tab navigation that loses the query keeps
  its Machine instead of reading the Vite origin as one.
- `bun run package:desktop` packages the peer Machine for the build host:
  `out/Octant.app` on Apple Silicon macOS, or an unsigned
  `out/Octant-<version>-linux-x64.AppImage` on x64 Linux (with
  `out/Octant-linux-x64/` kept for inspection). Linux packages skip Darwin
  helpers. The macOS Keychain, Code-file, and device Swift helpers explicitly
  target `arm64-apple-macos14.0`, so a newer compiler host cannot raise their
  deployment target. A dogfood AppImage is not code-signed. Its launcher preserves
  Chromium's sandbox and lets Chromium refuse when the host cannot establish
  it; it never adds `--no-sandbox`. A separate `unshare` executable has a
  different AppArmor identity and is not a prerequisite probe for Octant.
  On restricted Ubuntu hosts, direct packaged acceptance requires an
  administrator-reviewed profile for the installed executable and a real
  sandboxed launch. An existing isolated environment that already supports
  Chromium's sandbox may be used without relaxing host policy; the
  [Linux host guide](https://github.com/Ogard-Labs/octant-site/blob/main/docs/guide/linux-host.md#isolated-desktop-installation)
  records the tested rootless Space installation and its evidence boundary.
  The Linux ADE remains available while desktop prerequisites are unmet.
  An AppImage launch checks
  the signed `<base>/<ring>/linux-x64.json` feed, verifies the signature and
  hash before use, replaces the image atomically (write beside, fsync,
  rename), and relaunches; the new build starts after the old one has stopped.
  A bad signature, a non-writable location, or a
  launch that is not that image fails closed, and the reason is shown in
  Settings. Windows stays out. Override with
  `OCTANT_PACKAGE_TARGET=darwin-arm64|linux-x64` on a matching host only.
- Focused checks: `bun run --filter <package> test|typecheck`; the store can be
  inspected with `bun run --cwd apps/server db:verify`.
- Formatting is `oxfmt`, linting is `oxlint`; Turbo runs the per-package
  scripts. Always run `git diff --check` before opening a PR.
